NOTICE TO CI Taz EDITOR of "The Examiner" invites corre spondence on all subjects of public interest. LSTTERS should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to impart or seek information. not abuse.
Hsu) OyEs.—Several letters, owing to pressure on odr space, are held over till next week.
IRRESPONDENTS. LETTERS must in all cases be accompanied by the
name and address of the writer. _ COMMUNICATIONS received early in the week— except urgent matters—can always be given the best attention.

Simon Peter answered: "Lord, to whom shall we go? Thou hest the words of Eternal Life." Such, too, is the exclamation of the Catholic. s t aProtestants mb eului etovme in a zoivrri,ttatnodtoa tshueby- mean? Do they mean that only the soul of "Christ dieth CChhrriisstt is present? fresreonmt? hodlf y, thewyhderoetashey are dividing no more" (Rom. vi. 9). Is Christ only spiritu- ally present in the Communion, or is He substan- tially present? If only spiritually, then He is really absent, and Communicants derive no benefit through receiving the bread and wine. ' But if substantially present, then we have the Body and Blood of Christ under the appearance of bread and wine. Tte conclusion, therefore, at which we arrive is that in the passage quoted from St. John we have our Lord's words for it that He would give us His Flesh to eat satd His Blood to drink. Christ redeemed His pro- mise when He instituted the Blessed Sacrament, saying, "This is My Body; this is My Blood." He then gave a command, "Do this in remem- brance of Me," leaving power to His Church to celebrate the same mystery for all time, so that "Whosoever eats this bread, or drinks this cup, unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's Body" (Cor. xi. 29). If he is to be punished for not discerning it, it must be there. All these texts are quoted from the Protestant version of the Bible. _

This doctrine of the Real Presence was clearly taught by the Early Church. St. Cyril of Jerusalem (fourth century) writes: "What seems to be bread is not bread, but the Body of Christ; and what seems to be wine is not wine, but the Blood of Christ." If, therefore, Mr. Ogden wishes to continue a criticiser of the Catholic Church and her prac- tices I would advise him not to consult History, or his opinions may change and the light of true faith may shine upon him and number him among the many who are daily seeking the divine guidance of the Catholic Church. After taking all the criticism hurled at me in good spirit, I now find I have a duty to perfprin —to thank the Editor for the valuable space which he allotted to my correspondence, al- though I am still convinced that my correspond- ence miglit have been published more fully and would in no way have been hurtful to anyone, neither would it have sullied the columns of "The Examiner," but, to my mind, would have served the purpose for which "The Examiner" invites correspondence, viz., information. J. D. Warrington, April Ist, 1914.

Sir,—l regret the apparent momentary loss of temper of your correspondent " J.D.," who, if he is not able to reply, should admit his defeat with a good grace. As Mr. Ogden has fully ex- plained how the Lord's Supper was administered among the primitive Christians, it is unneces- sary for me to go over the same ground. But let me point out that there is no suggestion of the Real Presence raised in ecclesiastical his- tory until the eighth century, when the Synod of Constantinople, having argued that there was no image of Christ allowed by Scripture, but the elements in the Eucharist, to which the second Council of Nice, assembled in 787, replied that the sacrament was not the image of Christ's body, but the body itself. According to Car- dinal Bellarmine, the Monk Pascasius Radber- tus in the year 818 was the first defender of, the Real Presence in the Eucharistic elements. The word transubstantiation is not to be found in any book written before the year 1215, when Innocent 111. invented the name and established the doctrine in the 4th Lateran Council. I agree with " j.D." that authority should not be destroyed, but cannot accept his argu- ment that there is not authority in the Protest- ant Polity. We are told to search the Scrip- tures, and that injunction we carry out, but the Roman Church in the Council of Trent decreed that "Inasmuch as it is manifest from experi- ence that if the Holy Bible, translated into the vulgar tongue, be indiscriminately allowed to everyone, the temerity of men will cause more evil than good to arise from it; it is on this point referred to the bishops or inquisitors, who 'may, by the advice of the priest or confessor, permit the reading of the Bible translated into the vulgar tongue by Catholic authors, to those persons whose faith and piety they apprehend will be augmented and not injured by it; and this permission they must have in writing. But if anyone shall have the presumption to read or possess it, without such written permission, he shall not receive absolution until he have first delivered up such Bible to the ordinary. Booksellers who shall sell, or otherwise dispose of Bibles in the vulgar tongue, shall forfeit the value of the books, to be applied by the bishop to some pious use, and shall be subject to such other penalties as the bishop shall judge proper." (Index, Rule 4.) The Council of Trent declared that the ancient and common edition of the Latin Bible should be considered the authentic edition, and that the Bible should be printed as correctly and as expeditiously as possible, principally according to the ancient and vulgate edition. In consequence of this, it was published by Sixtus Quintus in 1590. He himself watched over the work with admirable attention and zeal; he perused every sheet both before it was committed to the press, and after it was printed off. But his edition scarcely appeared before it was discovered to abound with errors. Pope Sixtus published his Bible as infallible head of the Church, commanding 'it to be everywhere received, and cursing all that would charge it beforels93 The e with any errors. But Pope Clement VIII., his es dysier, ebhreoeughhettwoee out n successor, not having the fear of these curses we twoedition Papalin editions is considerabl athnees e; one writer holding there to be 2,000 instances of difference, whilst another states there to be 4,000 pl aces where the Bible of Clement wants correcting. Thus a Bible with four thousand blunders is the best the Council of Trent and the Pope could give to the Church; yet this Bible with so many errors is inerrant! But who shall decide be- tween these two infallible Vicars of Christ? I am pleased to see " J.D." is so proud of St. Augustine, and would recommend to his esteem St. Bernard also, as two Christian characters worthy of imitation. In regard to Kikuyu, I would invite him to wait Patiently, and watch, and take a lesson from the way in ivhich Protes- tants will treat this question. In conclusion, I would further invite him to keep cool and reason matters out for himself.
PHIL SQUOD.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.

of the dumb sing, for in the wilderness shall waters break out," &c. (Isa. xxxv. 6). The numerous joyful prophecies all foretell of the restitution joy that " cometh in the morning." Q.—We read that Christ "gave himself a ran- som for all "; how is it that men are still going into death? (E. R. B.) A.—The explanation is to be found in the latter part of. the passage containing the words quoted—l. Tim. ii. 6—" to be testified in due time."

Clearly this refers to the future, when "at the voice of Jesus, all that are in the graves . shall come forth" (John v. 28). The prophet Hosea likewise speaks of this coming day (chap. xiii. 14) : "I will ransom them from the power of the grave, I will redeem them from death."

At the same time, it might be as well to point out that ever since our Lord's death and resur- rection, all who have believed in the efficacy of his ransom sacrifice have been "justified by faith," and, having taken the further step of " consecration," are reckoned as members of the "body of Christ" (r. Cor. xii. 13). Now, each member goes into death, but it is into HIS DEATH, and thus each "shall be in the likeness of ins resurrection" (Rom. vi. 3-5). "This is the FIRST resurrection," to be followed by what we may term the "general resurrec- tion" of the human race.
" Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection."

div.head: CATHOLIC EVIDENCE.
div.p: CATHOLIC EVIDENCE.

Sir,—Having previously announced my inten- tion of discontinuing the controversy on the lines adopted by "Phil Squod," I find it is necessary once again to unsheath my sword, as it were, and advance to meet the attack of my former opponent, Mr. H. Ogden. His curiosity is aroused concerning my initials. Is it necessary that I should disclose my identity? Perhaps Mr. Ogden would then regard me as undesirable coMpany, if in any way we were brought together. I might say that several of his parishioners are numbered amongst my greatest friends, and I assure you it is not my intention to generate social bitter- ness with their Pastor. But, sir, I cannot get away from the fact that Mr. Ogden's efforts to impart information always take the form of criticisms of the Catholic Church, her practices, and those who wish to defend them. Several passages in Mr. Ogden's letter are very insulting to myself. I would re- mind him that the word ignorant, when used in friendly controversy, is not very complimen- tary, and leads one to believe that his flow of abusive language does not end with this one phrase. Neither is it adopted by individuals professing to be gentlemen. A quotation of mine referring to Mr. Ogden's invitation to attend his church comes in for a great deal of abuse, and, in his estimation, is insulting and no argument. But, sir, is it not true? Where is the professing Catholic who would ever think of attending the Baptist Church to receive Com- munion, when, in his or her opinion, there is no spiritual benefit to be derived therefrom? Mr. Ogden also says that none of the ordained clergy of the Roman Church will gush over their "champion.': But I would remind Mr. Ogden again that I do not profess, neither do I try, to , exalt myself above my co-religionists, by coming I forward as their "champion." But I do think, ' as a layman, I have the right MD, express my humble heliefs and opinion. Surely 'Baptists do not rely entirely upon their pastors to expound their beliefs. If that is so, then we cannot wonder at the falling away in their church attendances.

Mr. Ogden evidently believes in forgiveness of sins, but not through mortal man. Can Mr. Ogden explain away our Divine Lord's commis- sion to mortal man—" Whose sins you shall forgive they are forgiven, and whose sins you shall retain they are retained"? Was this commission to die with the Apostles? If s 0 and Christ founded a visible Church—who is to be the medium for the forgiveness of our sins? The idea of mental confession held by Free Churchmen will not do, and defies the authority and power of Christ (God) as man to give powei to His Apostles to remit or retain sin. No Catholic believes for a moment that priests themselvis forgive the sins. Priests, young or old, are simply the tools of God, made use of to-day and cast away to-morrow. Mr. Ogden tries to defend the actions of cer- tain Church of England ministers who practise the doctrine of confession. Can he fathom the following example of doubt which is prevalent in the Chdrch of England? The Bishop of Liver- pool denies to his ministers the poweto forgive sins. He receives in reply a protest from the Church Union, couched in the following terms: "That the Bishop's statements directly contra- dicts the ipsissma verbs of the formularies of our Church as set forth in the Book of Common Prayer." Mr. Ogden goes on to say: "Better any wide divergence of opinion such as a denial of the Virgin Birth than accept with mental meekness the conclusions that have been settled in clois- tered walls." Does Mr. Ogden believe in the miraculous birth of Christ, or is his belief con- sistent with the majority of Free Churchmen, who deny it? He also says: "In the Early Church and Church practices • there was no altar." History tells us that Augustine came, from Rome in the year 597; also the Venerable Bede, who was a monk, translated the Gospel of St. John into English. With the advent of Augustine and Bede we can truthfully,say- "that altars were at once erected to offer sacrifices." Furthermore, the "conclusions" referred to by Mr. Ogden must have been settled in cloistered walls, Augustine and Bede both being monks, or Monastic dwellers.

We now find ourselves back again to the sub- ject from which emanated the controversy. viz., the Real Presence. In order to understand what Catholics mean by the Real Presence it is necessary first to understand what is meant by Transubstantiation. A simple example will suffice. Now, if a body we are examining be a stone, we can fancy the "substance-" of stone being withdrawn, and the "substance" of wood being put in its place, the "accidents" remain- ing the same. That would be transubstantia- tion. And this is what the Catholic believes makes place at the consecration. The "sub- stance" of -bread and the "substance" of wine are .withdrawn, and their places supplied by " substance" of Christ's glorified and living body, the "accidents" remaining the same as before. Thus we have not wine nor bread, but Christ under the appearances of bread and wine. Christ said: "I am the living bread which i came down from Heaven; if any man eat of this bread he shall live for ever, and the bread that I will give is My Flesh, which I will give for the life of the world." Catholics believe that these words support the Doctrine of Transubstantiation; Mr. Ogden denies this. His Church says that the vrordo of Christ are only to be taken in a fiTarative sense, and not to be taken literally; or, in other words„ Christ did not mean what he said, "This is My Body, this is My Blood." Did the Jews take His words literally? They did, and they began to do what Protestants do—" they strove among themselves," saying, "How can this man give us His Flesh to eat?" Did Christ explain His words away? By no means. He acted as He usually acted, when people understood Him aright, but refused to accept what He said. He insisted, "Amen, Amen. I say unto you, except you eat the Flesh of the Son of Man and drink His Blood, ye shall have no life in y,ou " (St. John vi. 53). And then, as if He wished to close the avenue of escape, He put it in another way: " Whosoever eateth My Flesh and drinketh My Blood bath eternal life," (4;c. "his disciples murmured and said, 'This is a hard saying: who can hear it?' and many left Him" (St. John vi. 66). They understood Him aright, but would not believe, and, turning to His ,twelve Apostle k He said, "Will you also go away?"l

div.head: GOLBORNE-STREET CHURCH.
div.p: GOLBORNE-STREET CHURCH.

Most Successful Special Services. , THE CHOIR'S FINE MUSIC. Large congregations marked each service at thp Golborne-street Baptist Church on Sunday, when the church anniversary services were held. The special preacher was the Rev. L. M. Thomas, of Manchester. In the morning, preaching from the words of tile Prophet Isaiah, the Rev. L. M. Thomas dwelt upon the value of the old Prophet to the Church of the present day. Isaiah lived at a time when people were consumed by their love of pleasure, and the religious effects were spoiled by the indifference of the community. It was in , the midst of all this that the Prophet recalled the nation to their sense of national duty, that the worship of God was the first requirement and necessity of the soul. The members of the Golborne-street Free, Church Lads' Brigade were on parade, under the command of Captain Davies, and the preachei addressed a few words of encouragement to the boys, remikding them that the only true manli- ness was that which was gentle, considerate and kind.

MILES AND SMILES. There was a large congregation at the special afternoon service, when Mr. J. S. Owen occupied the chair, and his subject, "Miles and Smiles," was interesting. Her compared human life to the roads that intersected the land, and which were dotted here and there with the milestones Probably it was easy enough to pass the first, second and third stages, but as the distance tn.- creased, the travellers' strength was reduced, and they became tired. When they were in that state it was almost superhuman to smile, and be optimistic and hopeful about the future, but 1 a living communion with God would give strength and help along the road. Mr. W. H. Sherburn spoke upon the effect of thought upon the body, dealing with the relation between matter and mind. He showed how the mental state placed a permanent impression upon the face, and said that a study of criminology revealed that the face received an indelible impression of the low, crafty and evil thoughts which were constantly surging through the mind. A study of a saint's face showed a look of abstraction and holiness. He advised his hearers, for their own sakes, to allow only exalted thoughts to remain in theft minds, and to remember that constant fellowship and constant living with God would 'not only place its own seal upon their lives, but stamp its impression upon their faces. PAST, PRESENT, FUTURE. Three phases of Christian life—past, present, and future—was Mr. Thomas' subject in the evening. He pointed out that they were prone to look upon the past as either containing the Golden Age, or being responsible for all the present mistakes. There was a class who be- lieved that all the giants were in the past, and that, we should never see their equals again, whilst on the other hand there were those who believed that from their fathers they had re- ceived that legacy which had alienated the masses from the Church, and that the narrow views about God and life, and the glorious things said about heaven to the disparagement of the present life had contributed to lead men away from religion. They should remember that the past suited its day, and that the contributions of yesterday were but a preparation for the :cntributions of to-day. New times demanded new measures, and new men. To-day, as a Church, they must be able to pronounce upon matters which their fathers refused to consider It was sufficient- if they laid the foundation so well for to-day that to-morrow would not mean the destruction of the foundations ere the men of coming days could proceed to build.

div.head: MUSIC.
div.p: THE MUSIC.

The musical items at the afternoon and even- ing services were particularly pleasing. At the former service Miss Jessie Wbodland and Miss Jones were the soloists. "Come unto Him" and "Rock of Ages" were rendered with telling effect by Miss Woodland. Miss Jones taste- fully rendered the song "Babylon," whilst the choir did themselves and choirmaster credit with their anthem. At the evening service the choir gave two anthems, "The Title" and, "Radiant Morn." There was a consensus of opinion amongst the congregation that the choir had never kang better, and visitors, were delighted to have evidence that the choir at Golborne-street is acquiring a name for good Church music.

div.head: PLEA FOR SHOP ASSISTANTS.
div.p: A PLEA FOR SHOP ASSISTANTS.

Sir,—l read the letter of "Early Closer" in " The Examiner." I, too, read' with a certain amount of surprise the article in the "Trades and Labour Gazette," not that I disagree with the principle of trade unionists in boycotting the shops that keep open after 10.30 on Saturday night, because I have been working for this for the last five years against determined opposi- tion. At the •present moment there is before the Town Council a petition from over 80 of the principal drapers, outfitters, clothiers and tailors in the business area of the town for better hours, and all the routine and red tape for getting a compulsory closing order is made necessary on account of half a dozen tradesmen who have the welfare of the public so much at heart that it is impossible to close their place of business before midnight (or after) on Satur- day, and from 8.30 to 9.30 other nights. I say let the public do all in their power to prevent young fellows, most of them under twenty years of age, employed in shops, prowling home in the early hours of Sunday morning, and I am optimistic enough to believe that the tone of our streets at midnight would be raised if we could only close up the few philanthropic shops at a respectable hour. But I note that our trade union friends are, at the expense of advocates of early closing, , pushing forward the claims of shopkeepers, some of whom have persistently opposed early closing for years, and are really responsible for the business places in town as a whole remaining open so long as they unfortunately do. ONE OF THE WORKERS.

ENTERTAINMENTS FOR THE BLIND: HOW COUNTRY RESIDENTS MAY HELP. Sir,—As the result of a recent letter to the Press, I have received a large number of com- munications from people who write to say that they wish to help our campaign for cheapening and amplifying the supply of Braille literature ifor blind readers, but adding that as they live in country districts they are rather at a loss as to the method in which to do so. I have replied to these kindly folk, telling them that a simple way in which to assist in the giving of books to the blind is to get up concerts and other forms of indoor entertain- ment, or, as the summer advances, outdoor entertainments of one kind or another, sending the proceeds to swell our fund. I am glad to say that numbers of people have written expressing their willingness to do this, and I am writing to ask if you will permit me, through your widely circulated journal, to in- vite a similar co-operation from those of your readers who think well of our efforts. Few who have lost the ability to read with their eyes—as I have—can realise what it means to blind people—and particularly to poor blind people—to be without an adequate supply of books and periodicals, which mean so much to them, both from the educative and recreative points of view. Braille books, owing to their great bulk and necessarily costly method of production, are so expensive as to be-out of reach of any but the rich. A copy of "Ivanhoe," for example, which sighted people can buy for sixpence, costs 19s. 6d. to produce in Braille. Our endeavour is so to equip our new pre- mises, which the King and Queen opened on March 19th, with the most ingeniously devised machinery, so that the cost will be somewhat reduced. But it must always remain prohibi- tive, and can only be brought within reasonable limits if people who can see will help to pay for books and periodicals to be read by those who cansiK. ia the Kivg said in his reply to pur Chair- man's address: "There is no sadder affliction than that .which closes to the blind the great channel of common experience and common lintercourse, and cuts off the sufferers from tho 'chief fields of enjoyment and activity We wish you all success in your efforts to bring increased advantages to a yet greater number of our blind subjects. It is commonplace that Imen do not realise the value of that which they have never lost, and I am confident that your appeal for funds to extend and develop your undertaking will stir the imagination of many who unrellectingly enjoy the blessing of sight. I cannot too strongly urge upon all the duty of showing practical sympathy with your devoted efforts to bring down as far as may be the barriers which shut out the blind from a full share of the common interest and pleasures of life. We hope that you will speedily be re- lieved of all anxiety on the score of funds, and we wish God-speed to the work of the National Institute for the Blind." I cannot plead the cause of the blind reader in more eloquent words than these, and I trust that they will touch the hearts of some of your readers, and that we may receive from them heln in some such manner as I have ventured to indicate above.
C. ARTHUR PEARSON. The National Institute for the Blind, 206, Great Portland-street, W.

div.head: CAPTAIN CROSFIELD'S CHALLENGE.
div.p: CAPTAIN CROSFIELD'S CHALLENGE.

Sir,—The correspondence between Mr. 'Barry and myself promises to prove interminable. My contention is that my opponent is grossly exaggerating the opposition in Australia to the principle of compulsory military training, and 'fachet, and suppresses me thatalto- gether nc contrary orY to informa- tion which has an important bearing on the whole question. To most of my points Mr. Barry replies either by ignoring the salient peptraetsesits items or by dragging in irrelevant matter which merely confuses the issue. With the object of testing Mr. Barry's accu- racy on essential points, I will take three of the main questions which have been at issue, and ask Mr. Barry to prove his case on these ques- tions by documentary evidence before a small committee of Warrington citizens. I suggest that the committee should consist of three mem- bers, one to be nominated by Mr. Barry, one by myself, and the chairman to be mutually agreed upon. If Mr. Barry can prove his case to the unanimous satisfaction of this com- mittee, then I will pay .250 to the Warrington Works Bowling Association. The three main issues are as follows:— (1.) The Responsibility of the Labour Party. —With reference to the inception of the Austra- lian Defence Act, Mr. Barry writes: " (a) The Liberal party framed the Bill, based on Lord Kitchener's recommendations." I claim that Lord Kitchener made no official recommenda- tions until after the Liberal Bill of 1909 for National Service had been passed into law. (b) Mr. Barry ignores my statement of fact that in 11907 Mr., W. M. Hughes, Attorney-General in the Labour Ministry, outlined the Labour Party's views in favour of National Service. I challenge Mr. Barry to disprove this fact. (2.) The Verdict of the Last General Elec- tion.—Mr. Barry states that at the last General Election in Australia there were 20 candidates absolutely opposed to compulsory military train- ing. I challenge Mr. Barry to mention the names of these 20 candidates, and to produce copies of the election addresses of at least half of these 20 candidates, showing that they were opposed to compulsory military training. (3.) The Accuracy of Mr. Barry's Figures.— In his letter of March 21st, 1914, Mr. Barry states, as if from an official source : "Number of lads in training, 1,000; prose- cutions to date, 21,300; the prosecutions are 17 per cent. of those training." I challenge him to prove that the figure 122,000 represents the number of all the lads under training in Junior Cadets, Senior Cadets, and Citizen Forces. ,Further, I challenge him to prove that there have been 21,300 different per- sons prosecuted up to date. If he cannot prove that his figures are correct, his percentige of 17 is obviously inaccurate. If Mr. Barry can prove that he is right and I am wrong on any one of the above three issues Lwtiltlhpeany sl the aflolrfeexi tp encate nalt iro. n Be d a rarbyo vt eo . gißvuetuipf going about the country misleading people as to the true facts of the case.
- --- I give Mr. Barry 15 days to accept this offer.
GEORGE CROSPIELD.

We are always on the look-out for opportuni- ties of making our columns attraotive and interesting to all our readers, and have just completed arrangements for a special column entitled:—

EVERYBODY'S BIBLE QUESTION BOX. We realise that there is a growing need for such a column, and are hopeful that it will prove both interesting and instructive to many of our readers, increasing our knowledge of the Bible generally, and shedding fresh light on many of its obscure and difficult features. We all admit that there are many things in the Bible which are perplexing, and questions are continually cropping up which we would like to get a satisfactory explanation of, and also be able to explain to others. This column will not be used to advocate the cause of any one denomination more than an- other; indeed sectarian prejudices will not be considered.

The Bible should be our only standard of appeal, and guide in life„thence the necessity of a clear understanding of its teachings. Our hope is that "Everybody's Bible Ques- tion Box" will be largely taken advantage of, and we invite our readers to show their appre- ciation of this opportunity by sending in their difficult questions. The position we occupy in Publishing "Every- body's Bible Question Box" is 'quite neutral, and so it will be obvious to all that we are not attempting in any way to secure, or to take away, adherents of the Bible, no matter to what denomination they may or may not belong, but simply to assist all to a better appreciation of the Bible, and to a higher and more noble walk in life. Contributors may use a nom-de-plume, and all questions should be accompanied by the sender's name and address, and written on one side of the paper only. . The Editor of this column will esteem all ques- 'tions of equal importance, and answer them in rotation, through this column or by post. • Q.—Please explain I. Cor. xv. 49. Whit is the connection between bearing the image of the earthly and bearing the image of the heavenly? (P.R.8.) A.—The( Apostle is discussing the resurrec- tion of the Church to share in the same nature as her Lord. He is pointing out by contrast the relationship which the members of the Church formerly had with Father Adam, who was a natural human being, and their new relation- ship to the Lord Jesus Christ, the last Adam—a quickening spirit. The first man (Adam) was an earthly being, whereas the last Adam (our Lord) is now a heavenly, spirit being, and the Church is offered a share with Him in that nature, which means a change from corrupti- bility to incorruptibility—from sinortality to immortality; but not a change of identity or individuality (I. Cor. xv. 45-53). This latter re- lationship is obtained by individuals who, exer- cising faith in the Ransom, consecrate them- selves to do the Lord's will, by sacrificing their rights as earthly beings, thereby losing this re- lationship to the earthly Adam, and conse- quently becoming new creatures in Christ Jesus by the begetting of the Holy Spirit to the spiritual nature (see 11. Peter i. 4; I. John iii. 2).

(I.—lf the present unrest, indicating world- wide disturbance, will prove a blessing to man- kind, why did not God send it on us long ago? (N.W.) A.—The Scriptures represent that the Lord , has been holding back this "time of trouble" until its proper time. It will come as the legi- timate outworking of the laws of sin and sel- fishness, as a direct result of the neglect by Christendom of the Sermon on the Mount, Which, to some extent, has been heard and generally neglected. In the symbolic language of Revelation, the Divine power holding back the trouble is represented by four angels who hold the four winds of heaven until the servants of God shall all liv.ve been sealed in their fore- heads—until they are given an intellectual ap- preciation of the Divine purpose regarding them and the rest of mankind. Then the four winds will be let loose and the result will be a whirl- wind of trouble, anxiety, selfishness, strife; "every man's hand against his neighbour"— world-wide anarchy. While sympathising with mankind ,in respect to that awful trouble our hearts are consoled with the remembrance that many of us who have received at the Lord's hands His richest blessings were prepared for these by the laloughshare of trouble. The Lord assures us that the trouble which He will per- I mit to come upon the world will eventuate in such an overturning of human hearts and affec- tions, such a breaking up of the fallow ground, as will make mankind ready, yea, anxious for the blessed message of Divine love, mercy, and hope, which will then be sown broadcast through all the earth, not only for the blessing of those who will be living, but also for the ultimate enrichment of all the families of the earth.

a.—ln what way does the crucifixion of Jesus' Christ affect the human race? (ANXIOUS.) A.—The human race was and is under con, demnation to death on account of Adam's sin. God purposed to release the race by virtue of the substitutionary death of Jesus—a ransom for all. The mere release would be insufficient, however, so He chose a people—the Israelites— who accepted special covenant relationship to Him, in order to train them to be a nation of priests (Exod. xix. 6), who would lift up the fallen race when it should be released from death. Israel, however, broke the Covenant, and brought the penalty of the Law upon them- selves. They were doubly condemned. Jesus was crucified on their behalf (Gal. 'iii. 13), and thus enabled the few faithful Jews to become His followers. The bulk of, the nation rejected Him, but will be regatbered in the resurrection (Horn. xi. 15), and will then "look upon Him whom they pierced," and soon come to acknow- ledge, love and serve Hi. Then they will be used as a "nation of priests" on behalf of the whole human race as they return from the grave.
Q.—What would be the result to the general teaching of the Bible of eliminating or discredit- ing the miracles of the Old Testament? (D.C.L.)

A.—The result would be disastrous and de- stroy faith in the whole of the writings of the Bible as the inspired Word of God, and also its writers should appear as fanatics or dupes. Our Lord and the Apostles would be included amongst these. 'Paul mentions the fiery ser- pents (I. Cor. x• 9), and our Lord mentions the Flood, the destruction of Sodom, the deliver- ance of Lot, Jonah and the whale, &c. (Matt. xii. 39-41; xxiv. 37-39; xii. 40; and Luke xi. 29-32, &c.). The Apostle tells us in Rom. xv. 4 that the things written aforetime were written for our learning, that. we through patience and com- fort of the Scriptures might have hope. Much of our hope, patience and comfort would be gone if the miracles were eliminated. G.—Please explain Psalm xxx. 5: " For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life; weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." (N. 8. A.—Quite a beautiful and simple explanation belongs to this verse. The swiftness of God's condemnation is shown in the first clause when Ile condemned the race in Adam, and "so death (swiftly) passed upon all," yet almost in the same moment came forth the first hint of mercy and hope: "The seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head ";/so His favour was shown as a hope of life. A long night of weeping has Preceded the promised succour and deliverance; but "joy cometh in the morning" (the millen- nial morn), when the Sun of Righteousness shall rise with healing in His beams. "Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue

The Record Achieved by the Wycliffe P.S.A.

div.head: ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: THE ANNUAL MEETING.

The Wycliffe P.S.A. has passed from infancy into manhood, and appears to have a successful future awaiting it. That it is healthy is cer- tain from the reports presented at the annual meeting on Sunday. The Rev. T. T. James, the president, pre- sided over a good attendance. ,Mr. H. Osborne, the treasurer, gave his report, which showed that there was a balance in hand of £lB.

div.head: YEAR'S WORKING.
div.p: THE YEAR'S WORKING.

Mr. B. Farrar, the hon. secretary, in pre- senting his report of • the year's working, said that it was with even greater pleasure than usual that he submitted his report, for they had cause for much joy. In the early autumn they canvassed a wide district round, their church with a,view to increasing their membership,, but though the result was not a great numerical strengthening of the Brotherhood, the 50 new members who joined and the gracious feeling amongst their workers was a hap'py conclusion of the visitations. It could be noticed that when any extra effort was put foah in any good work it always brought its blessings and joy, for they went out sowing and working and. returned re- joicing.

div.head: Sufferings Through Strike..
div.p: Sufferings Through Strike..

_ The suffering of the women and children in Dublin consequent upon the great strike ap- pealed to them, and they had sent on two occa- sions a donation of a guinea to the relief funds. As a Brotherhood they took no sides with the contending parties, but with suffering humanity wherever it was found they were bound to open their hearts. and offer the hand of friendship. Subscriptions had also been sent to Dr. Bar- Inardo's Home and. Dr. Stephenson's Home. They had recently celebrated their 21st anni- versary. They looked back upon the early days ' when they spent a large amount of time and !money and were thankful, for the results were gratifying, as. they reached a membership of 1,200. Their membership began to, dwindle be- cause of outside efforts—the meetings for •men all around them, which had been inaugurated since their own was sufficient to fill them with joy and thankfulness, because Wycliffe's activi- ties from 1890 to 1896 were preparing the ground for the other men's meetings. The interest of many of their workers decreased with their membership, and the steering of the Brother- hood was left in the hands of a faithful few, the majority of whom were still identified with the P.S.A. They thought well of those who helped them at the commencement, but they thought !better of those who had• continued to work.

Seeking Betterment. They still sought the betterment of men, their desires were still to make homes happier and brighter, and to make the hearts of wives and mothers easy and cheerful, and to cause sons and daughters to look up to their parents with respect and hold them in great honour. The object of their desires were to influence the town for righteousness, and to fix their faces against all evil, so that evil-doers would know which side the Wycliffe P.S.A. was fighting for. They desired that the weak would find in them a source of strength and the troubled ones a plentiful supply of sympathy. They thanked their President (Rev. T. T. James) for his con- stant and earnest work on their behalf and his regular attendance at their meetings. They had always had the sympathy and help of the various Mayors of the town, whilst alder- men and councillors had also helped them. Indeed, their Brotherhood had become part of the work of the town, a part in conjunctions with all the churches and chapels •in setting forth the Christian ideals.

The prize books obtained by the members for the year ending August laid numbered 328, mak- ing the total number since the formation of 14,851 books. Their weekly collections had en- abled them to appear with a credit balance of over £2O, against a debt previously of £lB or £l9.

_ He entreated them to go forward as indi- viduals and collectively; they had had 'glorious times and results in the past, and these should only be a stimulus for greater things in the future. Mr. J. Himsworth gave the absentee report, .Mr. Archer the sick club report, and Mr. A. Littlewood the savings bank report. The officers for the past year were thanked for their ser- vices.

DECREPIT HORSE TRADE. The following resolution was unanimously carried, and a copy was directed to be sent to Mr. H. Smith, M.P.:— " That this general meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Brotherhood (which consists of 300 mem- bers) deeply deplore the existing state of the decrepit horse traffic, whereby horses in a worn- out condition, suffering from decrepitude and disease, and physically unfit to undertake any journey, are shipped abroad and subjected to untold suffering, and hope that you will strain every effort to support the Bill of Colonel Hall Walker, at present before Parliament, and, if necessary, support amendments in Committee to render the Bill more stringent, and so assist to abolish what is now termed `England's shame.' "

div.head: LATE MR. H. GIBSON.
div.p: THE LATE MR. H. GIBSON.
AN IMPRESSIVE FUNERAL.

The funeral of the late Mr. Hhrry Gibson, whose sudden death was recorded in last week's " Examiner," took place on Sunday afternoon amid many marks of sympathy and respect. The service was conducted by the Rector, the Rev. Canon Willis. The coffin, which was of massive oak, was carried by six of, his fellow workmen at Messrs. Rylands Bros.', and a number of other employes of the firm were present as ti deputation. The mourners who 'attended were:—

Mr. Alfred Gibson (father), Mr. JoSeph Gib- son and Mr. Ernest Gibson (brothers), Miss Lily Gibson (niece), Mr. Samuel Pimblett, of Eccles (uncle); Messrs. James A. Gibson, James Gibson, Joseph Garner and 'Robert Turner (cousins), Messrs. Jonathan, W. Jeffery, William Box, Jack Ashley, Harry Newton, J. Webb, Tom You'd (Frodsham), George Mason, and William Mounfield. Floral tributes were received from:—

" Those at home," "Joe and Polly," Miss S. Sparks, Mr. and Mrs. S. Pimblett (Eccles), Mr. and Mrs. R. Turner, Mr. and Mrs. H. Newton, the late Mr. and Mrs. George Allen's family, Mr. and Mrs. Box and family, Mr. and Mrs. Garton Stone, Mr.W.Mounfield and Miss M.Fair- hurst, Miss Wickstead, Mr. and Mrs. Stretton, "Annie and Alice" (Farndon), Miss S. White (Rugby), Mr. and Mrs. F. Hayes, Mrs. Greaves, and Mrs. Tipping, Mr. and Mrs. Jack Booth, Councillor and Mrs. J. T. Locker, Bailey Parker and Newton, Mr. and Mrs. Whittaker, Mr. and Mrs. W. S. Barker and family, Mr. and Mrs. George Mason, Mr. and Mrs. Bramhall, Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Jeffery, Mr. and Mrs. 'll P. Thros- sell, Mr. and Mrs. James Gibson (3, Mill-street). Mr. J. A. Gibson and Cousins, Netting Depart- ment of Messrs. Rylands Bros.', Engineering Department of Messrs. Rylands Bros.', Inde- pendent Order of Rechabites (Warrington Dis- trict), Mr. and Mrs. J. Garner, Mi. and Mrs. Fletcher (Burnley), Mr. and Mrs. T. Yould, Mr. and Mrs. J. Webb. Messrs. J. Mounfield and Sons carried out the funeral arrangements.

div.head: UTILITY POULTRY CLUB.
div.p: THE UTILITY POULTRY CLUB.

The report of the twelve months' laying com- petition at Sedlescombe for the period of four weeks ending January 29th, has been issued from the publishing offices of the club, 68a, Lin- coln's Inn Field, W.C. Mr. J. N. Leigh points out that, in spite of severe frost, accompanied by very cold east winds, the egg yield continues to increase, the month's total being 3,660 eggs as against 3,423 in the previous period of, four weeks. The increase of 237 eggs is almost en- tirely in the semi-intensive section, but. the birds in this section are still producing less than their sisters in the small pen section, i.e., 1,795 eggs against 1,865 eggs. It is a satisfactory feature that the proportion of the first grade eggs (20z. and over) is steadily increasing. The report contains tables showing the results to date of the pens in both sections, and in com- paring these tables it is of interest to remember that each competitor has a pen under the same number in each section, and to notice the different results their birds are giving under the different conditions in the two sections.

Among the pens which are giving the most even results in both sections are pens 15 (white Wyandottes) and 11 (white Leghorns). The former are third in the semi-intensive section (eggs 239, value 1,1 13s. 91d.), and fifth in small house section (eggs 234, value £1 175.), and the latter are fifth in the semi-intensive section (eggs 203, value £1 18s. 51d.), and sixth in the small house section (eggs 234, value £1 14s. 51). The leading pen in the small house section is a pen of white Leghorns, with a score of 267 eggs (value £2 Os. 61d.). Their sisters in the semi-intensive section are eighth, with a score of 169 eggs (value £1 6s. sid.). In the semi-intensive section the first pen is one of white Wyandottes, with a score of 270 eggs (value .Rl. 18s. 61d.), while their sisters in the small house section are ninth, Nyith a score of 222 eggs (value £1 10s. Hid.).

div.head: ST. lIELENS PIT SHAFT TRAGEDY.
div.p: ST. lIELENS PIT SHAFT TRAGEDY.

Sequel to a Remarkable Accident. Coroner Brighouse, at St. Helens on Saturday, held an inquest on Edward Owen (24), of 138, Berry's-lane, Parr, who died at St. Helens Hos- pital two hours after falling down a shaft at Collins Green Colliery, where lie was employed as a haulage hand. lie was married. Evidence was given, that the deceased had to work near the top of the Staple Pit, where he had to manipulate the brake of the mach- inery by which boxes were lowered down the pit. On Thursday morning he went down the main shaft at 5.35 and set out to walk to his post at the Staple Pit, down which he fell, either froM slipping under the fence at the top of the shaft of by walking too far and going over.

Elijah Derbyshire, of Brick-street, Earles- town, said he followed deceased towards the top of the Staple Pit on Thursday morning, when deceased and his light suddenly disappeared. He heard voices from down the shaft, which showed that people were attending to someone who was hurt. The top of the shaft was pro- tected by fences, and when he arrived at the place the fence near the iron landing-plate was down in its proper position. The Staple Pit was 37 yards deep. There was a shelf on the fel side of the place where the men put their food as soon as they arrived at the place. Deceased had not done this, so he concluded that he had fallen down right. away. Ife might have slipped on the landing-plate, or he might have slipped in reaching over to put his can on the shelf.

James Lowe, fireman, of 49, Pairclo—ugl;.:s-tieet, ; Earlestown, said he heard something fall down the shaft. Tie jumped aside, and when a heavy body fell on the ground he found deceased with One arm torn off and the other fractured. Tic was delirious and unable to say anything. That shaft had been going over twelve years, and the present fences were the same as had been always used. They were bars of wood that worked on hinges, and were lifted up and down. By Mr. Tinker (miners' agent) : A man fell down this shaft two years ago, but he was car- ried off his feet by some full boxes running down on him from behind. The fence was two feet from the floor. The Coroner: If a man slipped on the iron plate and fell on his back, he could easily slip down the shaft under the bar. The Coroner asked Mr. Murray, the Govern- , ment inspector, if he could help to explain the matter. Mr. Murray said lie did not know that he could. • The Coroner: Did. the fencing comply with the rules and regulations? Mr. Murray said he thought so. Now that a man had gone through the fences the manage- ment would do something to make the fence more efficient. Tie had gone down the shaft, and it never struck him that the fences well) not adequate, but there was a space of nearly two feet open which ought probably to have been fenced. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and recommended that the fencing be completed so as not to leave an opening at the corners.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914. FIRM AND GARDEN.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914. FIRM AND GARDEN.

SWINE FEVER AND PIG FAMINE. 'Mr. Charles Bathurst, M.P., said at Glouces- ter on Saturday that it would be more useful to allow swine fever to take its course, with such advantages as might be derived from serum treatment, than to continue the wholesale slaughter under the present regulations. The steady increase of swine fever threatened a pig famine, a serious matter for working class con- sumers of the country. In other countries there were no substantial restrictions of movement or isolation, and the pig population was steadily increasing. Until scientists could say what was the period of infectivity, there was no logical justification for any of the restrictions of the Board of Agriculture.

div.head: STORE CATTLE PROBLEM.
div.p: THE STORE CATTLE PROBLEM.

The outlook for graziers has undergone no material change, says "The Times." Their anxiety is not concerned with the pastures but with the problem of procuring animals to stock them. The prospects as regards grass are un- usually encouraging, there being already a thick carpet of herbage where the aspect is favourable and the soil of a kindly nature, but store cattle are difficult to buy now, and will reach prohibi- tive prices as soon as the demand attains normal activity. Specialisation in farming has its ad- vantages, but in certain eventualities it has also serious drawbacks. Our dependence upon Ireland for a large proportion of our lean stock to eat the grass in summer and the roots in winter is the result of concentration upon cer- tain pursuits to the exclusion of others. Although the dairy farmer is held to be chiefly responsible for the deficiency by sacrificing the bulk of the calves born in his herd, the grazier himself is not free from blame since he shows no concern about the provision of lean stock until he needs them in spring or autumn. Ho cannot in fairness reproach the owner of a dairy herd for adopting a principle of restriction in scope and foresight similar to his own. There is little probability of store cattle from Ireland being available for another Month or six weeks at the earliest, and in view of the seriousness of the situation it may be interesting to reflect that we have in this country ready to hand the means for producing the full complement of requirements of store animals—that, indeed, calves are born in sufficient numbers and that the scarcity arises from failure to rear them for the store market.

div.head: MORE "VETS." WANTED.
div.p: MORE "VETS." WANTED.

Mr. Runciman, President of the Board of Agriculture, speaking at Cambridge on Satur- day, said one of the real troubles they were suffering from in England was a deficiency of veterinary surgeon recruits. This was due to the belief among existing "vets." that motoring had killed the profession. The Board proposed to combat this with the help of the Develop- ment Commissioners by remunerating more fully the clever young men entering the veterin- ary profession.

County Council and the Live Stock Scheme. It was reported that the executive committee bad protested against " the injustice to the farmers f Lancashire caused by the delay in putting into operation the improvement of live stock scheme."

Sir Sydney Oliver had written explaining that the delay was due to the fact that the Lanca- shire County Council had not arranged to co- operate with the Cheshire County Council in the formation of an advisory council for advis- ing the Board of Agriculture on matters per- taining to agricultural education and the im- provement of the live stock industry. Mr. Runciman regretted that he could not meet the wishes of the association for a temporary scheme in Lancashire similar to that arranged in Che- shire until their elected representatives i.e., the County Council, co-operate with the Board. This letter was referred to the executive com- mittee.

div.head: VALUE OF HEDGEROWS.
div.p: THE VALUE OF HEDGEROWS.

In a letter to the " Times," Sir Herewald • Wake; of Courteenhall, Northampton, contro- verts some statements of that journal, that "the new ideal of the English cultivator is the Cana- dian prairie "—and also " that it is not easy to say .anything very convincing in defence of the English hedge." From the severely practical point of view Sir Herewald writes: " I venture to point out that, were our hedgerows done away with, the farmer would not get rid of either sparrows or rats. That the rats make use of the hedges and ditches as a summer., resort is only because the hedges are there to make use of. The sparrows never breed in the hedges, and were there no hedges at all, unless properly: waged war against and kept down in numbers, those numbers would never decrease. Wild creatures of all varieties can, and do, adapt ! themselves to circumstances. Were wire-fenc- ing substituted for our hedgerows where live stock is kept, such contagious ,or infectious diseases as ,anthrax or foot-and-mouth disease would be passed all over England in as many days as it now takes months for them to spread. Isolation would become impossible. Valuable live stock of all kinds would constantly be get- ting injured. I had a valuable Shire horse colt myself, which got seriously injured and its life' shortened owing to a gap having been stopped by a piece of barbed wire, and a neighbour hav- ing turned some mares out in the next field. Were all our hedgerow timber to disappear, with the hedges, we should have far more severe droughts ewry summer than we have now. div.head: SOME GOOD BORDER PLANTS.
div.p: SOME GOOD BORDER PLANTS.

Plants bearing beautiful flowers, suitable for the herbaceous border, are very numerous, but for the ordinary garden the following small col- lection will do for the beginner. They should all b 6 got in their flowering quarters at the earliest opportunity. The Phloxes are general favourites, being especially attractive and showy during the months of July, August and September. The soil should be deeply dug, and during dry short manure. of seasons they are greatly benefited by a mulch

Peonies are very showy in June; Achillea PtarMiCa The Pearl has conspicuous heads of white flowers; the Geums are good border plants, while Artetuisia lactiflora is stately, producing tall spikes of creamy white flowers late iu the summer.

The Larkspurs, or Delphinums, are most effective planted in bold groups. Tdere are now a variety of pleasing colours, ranging from creamy white to deep purple. Japanese Anemones, both white and Pink Varieties, make a nice autumn display. Gaillardias, in various shades of colour, from yellow to rich brown, are admirable border plants, and particularly useful for cutting. Lychnis chalcedonica, the flowers of which are bright red, planted in bold groups, are desir- able. The Oriental Poppies make a gorgeous show, and frequently bloom twice each year. The Campanulas are a splendid race of plants, and amongst the most showy of summer-flower- ing perennials. There are numerous varieties, of varying heights. The Ox-eye Daisies are indispensable for cut- ting, as also are Pyrethrums. The Dropmore variety of Anchusa italica is considered the best blue-flowered perennial. It flowers for a long time, and the individual blooms are produced freely. in full bloom the Plant is a dense mass of rich blue.

div.head: "ST. HELENS WESLEYAN CENTENARY.
div.p: "ST. HELENS WESLEYAN CENTENARY.

The centenary of the St. Helens Wesleyan Sunday School was this week celebrated by a series of meetings and services. Locally the Wesleyan Methodists have held services in the town since before 1782, for during that year John Wesley visited St. Helens and preached in the house of a local Wesleyan. In 1810 efforts were made to form Sunday schools in the town, the population then being 4,294, against 100,000 at the present time. The first Wesleyan meeting-house was in Market- street, and in 1814 the foundation-stone of a good-sized chapel was laid in Tontine-street, and washeld since that time the activities of the association have spread throughout the district. : teaOciiiieSrast nightuat;iddayhe nd a s re-union ohf old scholars, the Wesley Church after tea in the schoolroom. Mr. WB. Houghton presided. Addresses were delivered by several old scholars—namely, the Rev. F. 1). perki„s, Mr. Joseph Smith, Councillor W. A. Brooke, the Rev. Thomas May (Luton), and Mr. J. IL Houghton. On Sunday the Rev. Moffat Gautrey preached special sermons in the chapel.

A MOTOR IN THE ANDES. The motor car which a few years ago was known only in the streets of cities and the country roads of the most important countries of the West and America, is gradually finding its way to the remote parts of the globe. On several Antarctic expeditions _the motor sledge has formed part of the equipment,. and in Asia Minor, Central Africa, and other regions too numerous to mention, the car is no longer re- garded by the respective inhabitants as a strange curiosity. A remarkable mountain climbing feat is recorded from South America, where the great Continent has just been crossed by motor car for the first time. The route was from Buenos Ayres to Valparaiso, via San Luis, Mendo.sa, and Santiago, following the line of the Trans-Continental Railway. The whole journey is approximately nine hundred miles, which were negotiated after 28 days' hard work. For a great part of the distance the only road is the railway track, and the country is practi- cally uninhabited except by natives. The crossing of the Andes range took the travellers to an altitude of 13,000 feet, more than three times that of Ben Nevi.

div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
A AVarning to Prospeethe lio3crs of Bicycles.
CHEAP AND EXPENSIVE MACHMES.

I am often asked what is the exact difference between the lowest-priced machine in certain catalogues and the corresponding models de luxe? The answer to such a question is rather difficult, but the superiority of the expensive ! bicycle can really be summed up in the phrase "do luxe." Apart from a few unscrupulous individuals who make bicycles at an absurdly low figure for customers as doubtful as them- selves, manufacturers have adopted a certain standard of materials and workmanship which is observed in every bicycle without exception. Such items and processes as quality of tubing and brazing will probably be the same in alt machines; where the high-grade machine has the pull being in the excellence of plating, enamelling, &c., which certainly prolong the life of a bicycle. First grade tyres accompany a first grade price, and the same may be said of saddles, brakes, pedals, lamps, &c. The novice has no need to doubt the reliability of the cheap machine from the works of an established maker, but he must not expect the service guaranteed for the more expensive patterns. ; A Timely Warning._

• _ Just at present, when many of our readers are purchasing bicycles for the coming season, per- haps a word of warning may not be inoppor- tune. There seems to be no limit to the pitfalls in the way of the hnsuspecting novice. First, there is the alluring advertisement of the gentleman about to go abroad, and consequently desirous of selling his 15-guinea cycle, hardly over ridden, Sze., &e., or the countryman lately moved to London, who finds the traffic of the Metropolis too much for him. We do not mean to insinuate that all such advertisements are bogus, but a thorough examination of the machine offered for sale by an expert' cycling friend will sometimes prevent the beginner from throwing his money away. Then we come across advertisements offering brand new machines at an absurdly low figure. Here, again, beware! Such machines are turned out in their thous- ands at an absurdly low figure and sold to retailers at' about £3, or even less. Very often, too, the decoy machine, which should certainly carry a heavy insurance to its unfortunate buyer, is fitted with one or more standard accessories as a further inducement.

Lady Drivers. Notwithstanding various assertions to the con- trary the number of lady drivers is only increas- ing very slowly. True, the lady taxi driver has arrived at last, but I hardly think there is much possibility of the lineal descendant of the original Jelm being ousted from his occupation. tp to the present. ladies have not shown much desire to probe into the vitals of such a compli- cated mechanical contrivance as the petrol engine, but the greater reliability of the motor car of to-day, with its comparative immunity from breakdowns, must beget confidence, and we shall doubtless see far more lady drivers in the near future. There is not the slightest reason why a woman should not drive as well as a man, once the old-fashioned prejudice of such things not being " ladylike" is got rid of. Why, it only seems a little time ago since Mrs. Grundy protested against the woman cyclist. Her strident remonstrances were treated with the contempt which they deserved, and so it will be of the lady motorist.

div.head: Short Measure.
div.p: Short Measure.

Motorists, like most other members of the community, are liable to be defrauded, but with petrol at its present outrageous price, short measure in petrol tins is far too serious to be overlooked. Sometimes as much as a quart has been known to be missing, and even though 0;4 average deficiency is much less than this, the matter is sufficiently important to demand: attention. The weights and measures authority unfortunately has no jurisdiction over the filling of the cans, being only concerned with their actual capacity, so motorists must just tackle the problem themselves. Probably several causes are at the bottom of the shortage leakage from the can itself—evaporation, careless filling, and, last of all, deliberate fraud. But whatever the reason the result is the same. Everything except fraud can easily be guarded against. div.head: CYCLISTS' NOTE BOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLISTS' NOTE BOOK.
Spring Again Appears With its Hopes for Riders, Young and Old.
BY SILVER-STREET.

Now that the Grand National is over, and the main roads of Warrington are once more safe for the oldest and still the most harmless race of cyclists, our machines may come out again and receive the usual spring clean, the new coat of enamel and the elbow grease neces- sary for the handle bars. Those of us who have been riding all the winter have the cycles in such good order that only the mudguards want cleaning out, and a couple of pairs of new brake blocks, to make all ready for the spring and summer seasons, and repair the damage that five months of sloppy riding have done. Although the last thing I said in October was "Don't put your cycles away for the winter," almost every other person I speak to has to say, " No, my machine is all in pieces yet; I'm going to put it together next Thursday afternoon, when I've a bit of time. And this winter has been an unusually mild one—a winter when cycles need not have been out of use a day. Not once has the snow stopped us cycling to work and back, and whilst we have read of snow all over the country, Warrington in its low valley has enjoyed, as it generally does, more than its share of mild temperature. WOOD PAVING.

-- - _ However, regrets as to past omissions are of little use, and the only way is to do better this year, for no matter bow young you are, you won't be on the right side of 30 long. And now I must have another growl. It is more than 12 months since I spoke of the fearful state of all the wood pavements in Warrington except the one along Sankey-street and Church-street,' which is not yet two years old. Not a single road has been relaid. Wherever a church or school or vicarage abuts on the main road, there we must plunge and rear and rock on the vile wooden setts outside. In front of the Infirmary the same pot-holes! The cyclist or motorist who uses the Causeway suddenly dashes on to a piece of surface in front of St. James' Church and Vicarage that makes his teeth chatter, that is enough to loosen every spring and shatter every lug on the machine. It is the same in front of St. Mary's, Latchford; on the Liver-

I shall return to the question of roads next week.

CYCLE CLUBS. I should very much like to ask any of the members of the Warrington Teachers' Cycling Club what has become of it. Is it still in tho land of the runners, or is it drown-dead, as Mr. Peggotty used to say?

The Warrington Wesleyan Cycle Club is lively enough, after its winter's sleep. Three runs have been takeq already to Swinyard and Arley for the afternoon only, and last Saturday to Rostherne for the evening also. Nineteen riders for a March run is not bad. Two photos were ! secured by the secretary, one at Massey Bridge ! and the other at Rostherne Church door. Booth Bank was reached at 4 o'clock, so after ordering tea to be ready at 4.45, the remaining mile and a half were soon covered to Rostherne Church. There the party explored the churchyard for new and quaint epitaphs, the stone coffin was again admired, and the splendid view over the lake evoked the usual adjectives. After tea the return, via Bucklow Hill, was enjoyment indeed, for the S.E. wind had strengthened and blew us over the High Legh road in fine style. - AN EASTER HOLIDAY.

Before another column of these notes appears Easter will be on us. Do any of my readers want a charming spot for their holidays? Well, you know the old saw about "gorse being in bloom"? Now the Lleyn Penipsula is the land of the gorse, and it is just now in perfection. How do you get there? Well, cycle through Chester to Wrexham, Llangollen and Corwen, to Bettws-y-Coed, 70 miles. Turn up the Lledr Valley to Pont-y-pant, Dolwyddelan, and over the hill to Ffestiniog and Maentwrog. Through Portmadoc to Criccieth. Four miles further take off your cap, for you are at Llanystumdwy, the home of David Lloyd George, where he was a boy, and where he has now built a beautiful house on the hillside. Cross now to Morfa Nevin, where lodgings can be found cheap and good. The furthest town on the peninsula is A berdaron. which should on no account be missed. The road back is over the Rhiw Moun- tain, and if ever you see in England or Wales a sight like the view of St. Tudwars Bay from the top, just let me know—l'll be off to see it. The gorse follows you everywhere, for the Peninsula is otherwise rather barren, except for trees and rock scenery on the coast. • Lamp time to-night 7.45; next Saturday 8.10.

div.head: AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHY.
div.p: AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHY.
Topical Notes of Local and General
Interest.
BY "SILVER-STREET."
In this column we shall present our readers with a weekly review of interesting matters affecting the amateur photographer.
The notes will be written by our well-known contributor, "Silver-street," a guarantee that they will be thoroughly well done and highly entertaining.

div.head: "AR" EMPIRE NUMBER.
div.p: THE "AR" EMPIRE NUMBER.

I expect this splendid publication is by now out of print, although only published on March 16th. Still every photographer should see it, even if he has to go and specially ask for it at the Free Library. The speaking likeness of Captain Scott, the two sea pieces by F. J. Mortimer, and the page of Colonial snap-shots are studies worthy of anyone who wants to make a success of this ever-growing art. This number of the premier photographic journal of Britain is especially noteworthy, because every illustra- tion but three is from the Colonies, thus making it worthy of the title "Empire Number." A page is devoted to the recital of our photo- graphic terms in French, German and Italian. When one finds that the Germans call a dark- room lamp, an ordinary one, not one that the " nuts " buy for two guineas, that will do everything for you except swear, that they call it a "dunkel kammerlampe"; or that the French ask for a packet of "papier au gelatino-bromure" when they really want bromide paper; or that the Italians make a still bigger mouthful, " carta al bromure d'argento," one gets resigned to the trials of being an unassuming English camerist and pities the ignorance of these " f urriners."

THE PLATE AND NOXIOUS EMANATIONS. Several times recently we have noticed various writers advocating the use of dead black varn- ishes mixed with turpentine, apparently in ignorance of the fact that turpentine is now well known to have radio-active properties detri- mental to dry-plates. It is very necessary to use media that are inert this respect, and while alcohol, amylacetate, and acetone appear to be quite innocent of any fogging propen- sities we cannot be so sure in regard to other materials. Solutions of shellac in alcohol, or of celluloid in amylacetate or acetone, are quite effective as the vehicle for the black pigment, and have no disadvantages compared with tur- pentine, the lower cost of which is more than balanced by the waste of plates which will occur if the apparatus is used too soon, and by the waste of time if the apparatus is put on one side to "air" for A time sufficient to make it safe. Another mateiial that should be avoided where ' near contact with sensitive plates is probable is the type of patent adhesive sold under various names, but apparently consisting in the main of fish glue prepared with aniseed. A number of very useful adhesives of this class exist and they are most valuable for many purposes, but when a dry plate is allowed to become too intimately acquainted with their emanations it sometimes shows insensitire markings. When repairing dark-slides or plate-holders it is, therefore, better to use ordinary glue, reserving such things as seccotine, mendine, &c., only for places well away from the plate.—" British Journal of Photography."

div.head: WARRINGTON PHOTOGRAPHIC SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON PHOTOGRAPHIC SOCIETY.

I was asked to give one of my lectures to the Photographic Society of a county borough not a hundred miles from Warrington the other week. When I started I had an audience of ten and two more subsequently dropped in, making with myself the unlucky number. A club that can only secure such an audience from a town twice the size of Warrington is a contemptible one, and not worthy of the name of a society. A ve y different state of things prevails in our own often-maligned town. With a membership of 80 for the present year, no stranger has had to speak to less than 30, and often 40 members have been present during the session that has just drawn to a close, or will do on April 24th, with the annual general meeting. Week by week, in the columns of this journal, the doings of this society have been chronicled, and the most tasty bits from the lectures given. On April 7th the meeting will be held, at which the summer rambles will be arranged. Beginners especially are welcomed, and only need the introduction of a friend who is already a member to be invited to spend many days and half-days during the summer in company with friends of the magic shutter. The society's year begins on May Ist. I will _
- - willingly send a syllabus and be sponsor to any- one who writes to the Editor of " The Warring- ton Examiner," giving name and address.

div.head: PRINTS AND LANTERN SLIDES.
div.p: PRINTS AND LANTERN SLIDES.

At the Secretaries' and Lecturers' meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Photographic Union it was decided to give another month for the sending in of the prints and slides compet- ing for place in the portfolio and the slide box of the L. and C.P.U. So that the last day for this competition is April 30th.
