div.head: TOWN HOUSING.
div.p: TOWN HOUSING.
FIRST ARTICLE.
BY B. SEEBOHM ROWNTREE,

A Member of the Land Inquiry Committee. The first part of the Land Inquiry Commit- tee's Urban Report is devoted to the subject of Housing, which is reviewed in all its aspects. We are reminded that four-fifths of the popula- tion already dwell in towns, and the proportion is constantly increasing. The question, there- fore, is of the utmost importanee, especially as from the health standpoint an unsatistactery house in the town, in a congested area, is ,worse than an unsatisfactory house in the country Furrounded by open sv toes. Urban housing cot' litime have improved of late years, especially silace the passimg a the Housing, Town Planning, &c., Act. 1409, Liit in spite of this, the standard of housing to-day falls far short -of the minimum widen prudent and judicially-minded housing reformers consider it not only desirable, but practicable to attain. Probably the number of slum dwellers must be counted in millions. Over three million people, according to the 1911 census, are living under over-crowded conditions, while the great majority of the working classes ibvell in long and featureless streets, with no gardens or adequate playgrounds for the children. But though their houses leave much to be desired, working people are obliged to pay a large proportion—probably upon an average ' from one-sixth to one-fifth of their whole in. come—for the privilege of occupying them. Another grave fact confronts us in that the supply of houses in about half of the towns of ! England and Wales falls short of the demand, land this shortage leads not only to overcrowding, but to the occupation of dwellings which are really not fit to be occupied. These facts alone, supported as they are in the report by abundant evidence, constitute an , overwhelming argument for a great forward movement in housing reform, both ameliorative and constructive.

div.head: PROPOSED REFORMS.
div.p: THE PROPOSED REFORMS.

. _ What are the reforms which the committee recommend? They offer no single panacea with a promise that it will cure all housing evils; and on this account the recommendations, though the result of exhaustive inquiry, may fail to strike the imagination. That fact, how- ever, possibly commends them all the more to the practical person who has learned to distrust Panaceas. The committee's first recommendation is that it shall be a statutory duty resting upon all local authorities to see that acrequate and sani- tary housing accommodation is provided for the whole of the working-class population employed, or reasonably likely to be permanently resident, within their area. This recommendation, al- though at first sight it may seem very sweeping, only involves a slight addition to the duties which already rest upon local authorities, al- though at present they are seldom enforced by the Central Authority. If it be accepted and acted upon, the existing shortage and its attend- ant'tvils will disappear. The second recommendation deals with the planning of new building areas. The com- mittee propose that the adoption of a prelim- inary town planning scheme shall be made com- pulsory. This does not mean that every town shall prepare such a detailed town plan as can only be drawn up after the most exhaustive ' local investigation and complicated arrange- ments with innumerable owners. What is pro- posed is a general scheme, providing, among other things, for the width and direction of the principal roads, and a restriction upon the number of houses to be built per acre.

If, during the next few years, such prelim- inary schemes were adopted for every town, the worst evils of uncontrolled town development would cease to exist. A restriction upon the number of houses per acre would prevent the erection of row after row of mean streets with- out open spaces and without gardens—mere deserts of brick and slate. It would give the working man a little breathing space round his house, and a chance to cultivate a few flowers• and vegetables.

div.head: PRICE OF LAND.
div.p: THE PRICE OF LAND.

Of course, if working-class houses are to have more land attached to them, it must be avail- able at a reasonable price. The proposed restric- tion upon the number of houses would in itself prevent that forcing up of land values which is possible when 40 or 50 houses may be built to the acre. But the price of building land can also be reduced by increasing its available area. To this end the committee suggest several means. One is that transit facilities should be provided to render available for building cheap land which at present is too far distant from the centres of industry. A difficult and complex question arises as to the best methods of pro- viding and financing these transit facilities, and the committee recommend that an official in- quiry should be made into this subject. Among other means of increasing the supply of cheap building land, alterations in the rating system, and improved facilities for compulsory acquisition of land by local authorities are re- commended. These subjects, to which consid- erable space is devoted in subsequent parts of the report, will be dealt with in other articles of this series. BAD HOUSING AND POVERTY.

Space does not permit me here to dwell on all the committee's recommendations; but there are one or two more which should be mentioned. One is concerned with the intimate relationship between bad housing and poverty. At present many thousands of families are living in insani- tary dwellings simply because they cannot afford sanitary ones. If they are to live under healthy conditions, either their incomes must be suffi- ciently increased to enable them to pay more rent, or they must be housed by the community at a loss. _ . _

_ The committee point out that in the case of the rural worker the same difficulty presented itself, and the Government decided to meet it by insisting upon the payment to agricultural labourers of a wage which would not only cover the necessaries of physical efficiency, but an economic rent for a sanitary dwelling. There is no logical reason why this policy should not be extended to the town, and rapidly expanded. If this were done, and if at the same time steps were taken to, lessen the amount of casual labour, one of the chief obstacles to the solution of the housing problem would be re- moved.

div.head: SURVEY OF CONDITIONS.
div.p: A SURVEY OF CONDITIONS.

- - - Another important recommendation of the committee is that a survey should immediately be made in every town of the actual conditions under. which the workers are dwelling, that the results of this survey should be published, and that subsequently every local authority should he obliged to prepare a scheme for remedying the defects which it had revealed. CONDITIONAL GRANTS IN AID.

--..—... --•-- - - - The Gtwernment has already promised to make a substantial grant in aid of local rates, from the Central Exchequer. The committee recommend that this grant should be made con- ditional upon the satisfactory performance of the statutory duties imposed upon loco) author- ities, including those which refer to the housing of the workers. If this policy were adopted, it would pay a local authority better to do its duty than to neglect it, and consequently lose the grant. Thus backward authorities would receive a stimulus, while those who would gladly carry out all their duties but for the fear of imposing ! too heavy a burden upon the rates, would have the help they needed. Many other recommendations are contained in the committee's report, including among others one for the re-planning of congested town areas; but space precludes their enumeration ' here. They are based on a great volume of evi- (knee, and have been carefully drawn up after consultation with men of practical experience and authoritative knowledge. If adopted, they would not only remedy the worse defects of existing housing, but prevent the serious mis- takes of the past from being repeated in the future:

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.
TYE WAKES WEEK PROPOSAL.
The Scheme First Outlined in "The Examiner" Practically Adopted.

div.head: MATTER ADJOURNED FOR DETAILS.
div.p: MATTER ADJOURNED FOR DETAILS.

There seems every likelihood that Warring- ton will have a Wakes Week. In fact, the pro- gress towards such an end was very rapid, for on Tuesday afternoon a large and representative gathering of the parties concerned assembled in the Town Hall at the invitation of the Mayor and approved of the principle of such a scheme, which, as announced exclusively in "The Examiner,", originated at a recent meet- ing of the Trades and Labour Council. The date fixed was from the Thursday before Walking Day (July 3) until the following Mon- day week.

• DIVIbED EMPLOYERS. The MAYOR, who presided, said the Trades and Labour Council thought it was desirable, in the interests of the employes, as well as in the interests of tradespeople, that there should be one holiday week instead of so many broken holidays.. It was stated that some of the firms stopped work for stock-taking purposes at the Walking Day period, others in August, and others at different times, and that in conse- quence everybody suffered to a certain extent. The firms in Warrington had been communi- cated with, and out of 28 there were only ten or eleven who were definitely in favour of a week's holiday.

Some said Walking Day week—Alliance Box Works, Monks, Hall, Richmond's—:and whilst the letter from Messrs. Pearson and Knowles was somewhat indefinite, they had a letter from the secretary of the Iron and Steel Workers' !Union stating that Monks, Hall and Pearson and ! Knowles agreed to close the week after Walking Day. Ile, the speaker, could not understand Pearson and Knowles' letter, in face of the one from the secretary mentioned.. So practically eleven firms agreed on a Wakes Week holiday. The others were either against it or were willing to fall in with the general wishes of the town. They said they could not close down if others did not do so, but they were anxious to see the result of a representative meeting of traders;

• MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S VIEW. Mr. LAYTON (Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd.) said his firm were quite agreed that it was not agreeable to be shutting down on numerous occasions. -Whitsuntide week or the first week in August would suit them—prefer- ably the latter. The MAYOR: It WOU1(1, perhaps, be as well if Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' representattve gave us information. Mr. MURRAY (Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Ltd.): What is the date of Walking Day? The MAYOR: Friday, July 3rd. Mr. MURRAY: The schools are in at that time. The MAYOR: If the firms agree upon the holi- day the school holidays will be altered. That is one of the -grievances which has brought about this request. Some firms close Walking Day . week and the children cannot go with the par- ents, and when the children are out in August the parents cannot go with them. Mr. MURRAY: Will Walking Day or the school holiday be altered? • The MAYOR: I don't think Walking Day would, but the holidays would if the firms , agreed on that week.

A VERY SOUND PRINCIPLE. Alderman BENNETT : Find out if the meeting is in favour of the general principle, which seems to me to be a very sound one. It gives the working men in the town an opportunity of having a week's holiday like anyone else. A Member said that those people who had a fixed Wakes Week had to take their holidays that week, no matter what was the state of the 'weather, and sometimes their holiday was spoiled. Mr. FELIX 111nonm said the same might apply to any part of the year. Holidays were not fixed in a moment, but were fixed for some time before. (Hear, hear.) Whatever arrangement was made it should not interfere with Walking Day. (Hear, hear.) He was prepared to fall in with the general feeling. His own view on the matter was that it was greatly to be desired that a fixed holiday should be instituted for Warrington, instead of the short and irregularly arranged holidays spread all over the year. Walking Day gener- ally occurred at the end of the half-year, and he thought that would be a most desirable time to have the holiday, the following week, (Hear, hear.) It would only mean extending the holi- day of the local school festival. He preferred one fixed holiday. People were now asking for leave of absence all through July, August and September, and during those three months one could never get one's place to work at full pres- sure: From the financial standpoint he had a strong preference for one week and "have done with it." (Hear, hear.)

WHAT ABOUT THE SHOPKEEPERS? Lieut.-Colonel B. EURCLOUGLI, speaking on be- half of the Territorial Battalion and the Army Service Coy men had gone to camp at the beginning of Ps, said that for many years past the August for 14 days, and lie hoped the meeting, in coming to a decision in reference to the holi- days, would bear that fact in mind. There Were 1,100 Warrington men who would be more or less affected by tilt proposed change. . Alderman BENNETT : The first course is to de- cide about the principle, and I propose we agree to the principle of a Wakes Week. Mr. J. ELWELL: I second. Mr. J. JARMAN (Co-operative Society): Does this refer to tradespeople or the works? The 111Avoa: I think it is the works. Thii others will follow.
Mr. C. DUKES (Trades and Labour Council) asked what was the basis of representation. The MAYOR: All the firms have been asked, the Trades and Labour Council, and the minis- ters, ac.
Mr. DUREN : And the tradespeople? The DEPUTY Tovni CLERK replied that the tradespeople had not been asked to attend the meeting.

Mr. Duties: They are the people who are affected. We shall have a greater difficulty with them than with any other section. Mr. J. JARMAN said the position would be that the shopkeepers would have a matter for them- selves. The works might close down withotit Warrington being empty. The people who re- mained would require food. Walking Day week would be the most suitable, time for the holiday. Their own experience was that they were short- handed from the beginning of April -Until the end of September or October. If by any pos- sible means there could be a concentration into one week SO that they knew trade would be slack they could dispense with half their shops. The small shopkeepers might do as they did in Bol- ton—close for half the week.

CENTRED IN ONE WEEK. 3/c. Dram said, it might be news to those pres- ent that the Trades and -Labour Councils in other towns were actively interested in the matter. Be had no hope for a reasonable, holi- day except Walking Day week, but they (lid not think it ought to be chopped into two weeks. He did not see why. Walking Day could not be on the Monday. If the holiday extended from the Thursday it meant two broken weeks., He thought they ought to have a Wakes Week, if it did not interfere with the statutory holidays. Mr. C. BUNCH (Messrs. Pearson and Knowles) said they had a rather difficult matter with which to contend in regard to Wakes Week, because of taking their tilinual stock. It would suit them if they could have the holiday this year from the Monday, June 29th, to July 4th, inclusive, to suit stocktaking, when. the men had an enforced holiday. If that could not be arranged it looked as if the men would have to take a fortnight's holiday, and it would be dis- astrous to the men and the company to stop for a fortnight. EMPLOYERS' REPRESENTATIVES DIFFER.
The MAxoa .Are you in favour of a Wakes Week? Mr. BUNCH : I cannot say we are in favour of a Wakes Week. If it could only be made con- venieut for -thy men to take" the holiday when

the stocktaking was on we should be pleased to do that. Mr. LESLIE (Messrs. Rylands Bros.) said be could not agree with Mr. Bunch. They had to decide about the Wakes Week permanently. ,So tar as Rylands Bros.' were concerned, ever since Walking Day was established—he was told 50 years ago—they bad closed the works on the Thursday before Walking Day, and they had no wish to alter that. In fact, they would take a firm stand in regard to the matter, and ad- here to their practice. Mr. MURRAY Under these conditions how would the school children be affected? The MAYOR: If all the works close a certain week the schools would close at the same time.

NO DIFFICULTY WITH THE SCHOOLS. Councillor Itonsirrs said he did not think the question of the schools Would be a difficult one. The matter could. he arranged. While most of those present Were in favour of a Wakes Week, they were not agree when it should be. The broken week involved by Walking Day was a difficulty they wanted to overcome if they cpuld. Walking Day had been established to his know- ledge for nearly 60 years. They were, as he had said, prepared to support a Wakes Week, but as a matter of convenience they were entitled to suggest that it would be better to have it either in the Whitsuntide week (following Manches- ter) or the Bank -Holiday week in August. If it were fixed for Walking Day week they had the difficulty with Whit week and other broken wee, and it seemed to him that unless they could -concentrate on a week that would save some time and have the advantage of a long holiday, they had better remain as they were. Colonel FAincLovon asked if Walking Day could be altered? It seemed to him that the majority of those present were in favour of a Wakes Week, which was a greater question than Walking Day, and be would like to know if they could move Walking Day to coincide With the greater question.

div.head: FROM A BUSINESS STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM A BUSINESS STANDPOINT.

Mr. DUNES said there was a difficulty as to Wheth eylrifrom tofuilnt. oill(iralaea;as euaoughtcsnei(siiiseiesttvsyoe.srtcyaOhnTfidsiriipmdeoyei rnmtv,,teo.lrelreer epgr(joitUrniieinlSagktriiioitli.lgyolstrictl. about find difficulties. Chorley, Oldham, and the other towns had met the difficulties, and they should get some opinion which would work in with the majority of the people, rather than with purely business enterprise. A holiday was a holiday, and if it were going to be a matter of purely business convenience there was never going to be any solution of the problem. A matter of a holiday went further than mere business necessity. Mr. MAGINN: In regard to the holiday, the children should not be overlooked. I put in my plea for maintaining Walking Day. On a vote being taken, 12 voted for the prin- ciple of a Wakes Week and seven against. Several gentlemen did not vote.

VOTED CONDITIONALLY. Councillor llonEßTs : We are voting condition- ally. We are all in favour of a general holiday. (Hear: hear.) The principle, which is spreading and will spread, is that men should have an annual holiday. The humanitarian side of the question was a big one. Thh only difficulty, I think, is to get over the strong local prejudice in favour of Walking Day as it stands.

div.head: DATE OF PROPOSED HOLIDAY:
div.p: DATE OF PROPOSED HOLIDAY:

. Mr. Ltsm moved: "That the holiday be from tile Thursday (July 2nd) until the following Monday week." F. W. MONKS seconded, and said the ques- tion of a week's holiday was coming, whether they 'liked it or not Councillor ROBERTS: Subject to the Board of Education allowing us to alter the holidays, I don't think there will be any difficulty. Mr. MONKS said the time was a most suitable one, because they got long days and nice weather. Their people had agreed to work Easter Monday and Whit Monday, in order to get a real week. Mr. BUNCH: If the resolution is carried it will be a ten dayS, holiday. Mr. JARMAN : If the Walking Day is in the middle of Wakes Week it will spoil the holiday absolutely. The ten (lays does not amount to anything, as the works close for Walking Day now. (Hear, hear.) Mr. MURRAY: In Glasgow the works close down from the Friday until the Monday week, and if Scotsmen can do it surely Lancashire men can. (Laughter.)
MINISTERS' VIEWS,

The Rev. Father WILSON said that if the parents of the children were away in consider- able numbers it would interfere with Walking Day, and it would be almost impossible to hold that festival. It would be better to hold it on the Friday as now. The Rev. 11. OGDEN said the matter of firms working Easter Monday might be considered. In another Lancashire town that attitude was adopted, and perhaps they went to the extreme in working Good Friday---(laughter)—in order to have the Wakes Week. The ten days, with Walking Day on the Friday, was not an exces- sive demand, granting that the other holidays were supplanted and included in the ten days.

div.head: TERRITORIAL OBJECTION.
div.p: TERRITORIAL OBJECTION.

Colonel PAIRCLOUGH moved an amendment that the August Bank Holiday Week be selected tot the Wakes Week, and he did so to show how sincere he was in regard to the work of the Territorials. He could not allow that meeting to conclude without bringing forward the claims of the local Territorial battalion and the Army Service Corps, (Hear, hear.) The Rev. W. BRACECAMP (chaplain to the bat- talion) seconded, and said that, in his opinion, it would be a very serious thing indeed if they could not get the men to go to camp. Mr. JARMAN : Is it not a fact that not one of the holidays interferes with the Territorials? What difference can it make? If it is a question of going to camp, I don't know that the Empire would be hurt whether the Territorials went in June or August. They would .he ready for the invasion and be earlier in June. Colonel l'Anici.ounn: It is not a question as to whether We Wish or Ilit; we have to go to camp. . Mr. JAlimAx : In that particular period? Colonel VAIRCLOUGH : lii that particular period. Mr. JARMAN : The holidays don't fit in with you now. Councillor ROBERTS: I don't think Mr. Jarman realises that .this week in camp exists as a fact. We are asking for another week in addition to that, and it would be a serious matter for some firms—who are quite willing under present con- ditions to allow their men to go to camp—if in addition to that week they had to provide foi still another week. (Hear, hear.) . Mr. JARMAN : Some Territorials go to camp in Easter and others at Whitsuntide. It is a matter of arrangement with the War Office to have the date altered. Mr. MoNxs: If• the firms refused to let them go down the War office would have to alter it. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: GOOD-RYE TO LOCAL BATTALION.
div.p: GOOD-RYE TO LOCAL BATTALION.

Colonel FAIRC—LOU77H.-SaTiilliat the Warrington Battalion went with other battalions at the same time, and if the Wakes Week were held afk suggested by the resolution it would jiractically mean giving up the local battalion. If the Wakes Week were going to be held at any time other than August Bank Holiday Week it would he "good-bye" to the local battalion. I am, added the Cillonel, absolutely convinced that business men and heads of firms and companies will not allow their men another week's holiday, or possibly a fortnight's holiday, in addition to the Wakes Week. Therefore, from purely patriotic motives, I ask you to support the amendment I have just now submitted. Mr. Dosss : If you are going to bring the camp week in the Wakes Week it means the men will not get a holiday. Councillor ROBERTS : It is not our suggestion. . _ _
Mr. DUKES: You suggest Wakes Week for the tamp, uud I say the men who go to camp would

div.head: not get any other holiday. You are working them. They would not get any other holiday. The MAYOR: They don't now.
div.p: not get any other holiday. You are working them. They would not get any other holiday. The MAYOR: They don't now.
A LIVELY EPISODE.

Mr. DuKea: We are now trying to get these men a Wakes Week holiday. A man who goes away to do duty as a soldier is working, and he should be paid for it.. We should not attempt to squeeze it out of him. That is not patriotism— it is sweating,

-Councillor-ROBERTS (heatedly): I object to that. The gentleman who has just spoken does not understand camp life. If he did he would know that the great hulk of the men who go to camp are only too pleased to do so. They spend their time in camp and derive an immense advantage, physical and otherwise, from doing so. It is, therefore, not fair to introduce ele- ments of the kind which have been introduced.

div.head: WHICH_ PREFERENCE?
div.p: WHICH_ PREFERENCE?

. _ Mr. DUKES : Would Councillor Roberts prefei going to camp or Bettws-y-Coed? Councillor ROBERTS: The men would prefer it,. They would prefer to go tp camp, because it is generally pitched in a delightful centre. More- over, the labour in camp is not of an arduous nature, and it is a complete change for men, who thus live under ;mist healthy conditions, I claim to know as much about the local Terri- torial Battalion as Mr. Dukes, and a great deal more. I have been associated personally with men and officers connected with the battalion for nearly the whole of my life, and I know that the men are quite prepared----and all credit to them for it—to make sacrifices. Great sacri- fices have been made in order that the battalion might keep up its reputation. (Hear, hear.) A large number of the men who form the batta- lion are quite prepared to take their holidays in camp. The only holidays they have are spent in serving their country. I ,am proud of them foi , it. (Hear, hear.) Mr. ELWELL : We have to consider the women and children. If we are going to make the holi- day just to suit the men we are failing in the object. (Hear, hear.)

AN / EMPLOYER'S IDEA. Mr. MAGINN : I think it is a slight on the Patriotism of the employer. I.am not in a large way, but I am prepared to let the Territorials in our employ go away Wakes Week and a week when' training. I think everyone here will be prepared to let their men go at the beginning of August whether the holiday is in July or not, Colonel. FAIRCLOUGH: I thank you for those sentiments.

The Rev. H. Oansx : What do other towns do? Does their holiday harmonise with the training? If it does not, surely it is not insurmountable here. If other towns met the difficulty, Surely Warrington could. (Hear, hear.) Colonel PAIRCLOIiCaI : I meant when I asked for this, if it were possible to get the Wakes Week to fit in so that the men could go to camp fol August without asking the employers for an- other week. •

SUNDAY SCHOOLS' POSITION. Mr. F. W. MONKS : Have you approached the Sunday School Authorities and ascertained if they will fall into line? \ The MAYOR : They have been invited to attend the meeting. Mr. Moiars : The objection to August is that it is a crowded month. They want to get away from the tyranny which obtains during that, month. Four members voted for the amendment and 15 against it, so that the date was fixed foi Walking Day Week, as originally suggested. Alderman BENNETT said the meeting had agreed to the general principle that a Wakes Week should be held, but there was a difference of opinion as to details. Therefore, he thought it would be advisable to adjourn the meeting tc. enable the various authorities of the town to be consulted, and more mature information about the subject obtained. (Hear, hear.) Ample time would be afforded for a fuller con- sideration of the subject than had been given to .it by the meeting that afternoon. tHear, hear.)

EMPLOYES TO CONSIDER. Councillor RomaTs suggested that the em- ployes of the different firms should consider the question for themselves. After further discussion the suggestion was approved, and the adjourned meeting was fixed for April 21st (Tuesday) at 4 p.m., and in the meantime the shopkeepers, Chamber of Com- merce, Trades und Labour Council, Sunday School Authorities and others interested in the question will be consulted as to the final decision in regard to the date.

div.head: ST. HELENS PUBLICAN'S DEATH.
div.p: ST. HELENS PUBLICAN'S DEATH.

An inquest was held at St. Helens on Robert Burrows, aged 42, licensee of the Princess Royal Hotel, Park-road. The deceased had fallen and hurt his head, but Dr. Unsworth, who made the post-mortem, said that death was due to natural causes. There were no signs of injury, but deceased was not a healthy man, and 'death was caused by apoplexy. A verdict in accord- ance with this evidence was returned.

On Saturday Mr. Walter Nuttall, bandmaster of the famous Irwell Springs Band, received a letter from Lord Derby in which he expresses his thanks to the band for the enjoyment their playing gave to the Royal party at Knowsley.

At a Rochdale inquest on Saturday on Arthur Howard (56), grocer's assistant, of Moston, who committed suicide while of unsound mind, it was stated that when his body was found in the canal the pockets of his clothing were filled with large stones.

div.head: WOULD NOT HEAR HIM.
div.p: WOULD NOT HEAR HIM.
The Education Committee Refused to Listen to Councillor Pemberton.

div.head: CONCENTRATED "SCENE."
div.p: A CONCENTRATED "SCENE."

A brief scene ensued at the meeting of the War- rington Education Committee on Monday evening, but it was extinguished by the prompt action of the Chairman, with almost the unanimous support of the members. Councillor Pemberton refused to withdraw the remark which led to the abrupt termination of the meeting a fortnight previous, and the Chairman (Councillor Roberts) promptly told him the meeting would not hear him. Councillor Pemberton sought to parley with the Chairman, but the meeting declined to listen, and with the exception of Councillor Pemberton unanimously adopted an amend- ment to remove his name from the deputation to be sent to London. Councillor Roberts, on the motion of the Mayor, seconded by Canon Morley Stevenson, was thanked for his services as chairman of the Committee. The only voice to interject a " No" to the unanimous " Ayes" was that of Councillor Pemberton.

The first meeting was a continuation of that which was interrupted and adjourned by the scene of a fortnight before. It will be recalled that during a discussion with regard to the ap- pointment of a deputation to the Board of Edit. cation the nomination of Councillor Pemberton was opposed. Mr. Pemberton declared that all he had done was to prevent unfair treatment of outsiders, and exclaimed that things were done' in that committee that would not be tolerated in a third-class gambling hell. AN AMENDMENT WITHDRAWN. •
As soon as Councillor Roberts- 1;i-d- taken the chair, he said; • _ -

We resume our business to-night at resolution E 1,126 on page 13 of the agenda. (This was the resolution about the deputation which led to the former scene)" I do not know whether Council- lor Wilkinson has anything further to say in regard to his amendment. (This amendment proposed to consult the Town Clerk as to the legality of sending a deputation of three mem- bers and the Director of Education to London.) Councillor WILKINSON: I only say I wish to withdraw the amendment I moved at the last meeting, and I think the protest I made has served my purpose. The matter no doubt will come before the Council. I move that the amendment be withdrawn.
Councillor JENK. INS : I second. (Cries of "Agreed.").
TO DELETE NAME.
Mr. jARMAN : Have Nve no further suggestion to make or do we hold with this recommenda- tion?

The CHAIRMAN : If there are no further re- marks I shall put the minutes. Mr. JARMAN: I move that the name of Coun- cillor John Pemberton be deleted from this deputation, leaving it in the hands of the sub- committee concerned to appoint someone else in his place. • _
The CHAIRMAN: Does anyone second the amend- ment?
Mr. PLINSTON I'll formally second it, sir. ..A SHORT, SHARP SCENE.
Councillor PEMBERTON : But, Mr. Chairman, this amendment is not in order.

The CHAIRMAN (sharply): Are you going to withdraw the expression you made use of at the last meeting? COUlleillOr PEMBERTON : NO, I'm not. The CHAIRMAN: Then I decline to hear you! Councillor PEMBERTON : You cannot stop me from taking part in these proceedings. On the contrary, I am probably representing the rate- payers here, and I'm not going to be put down. ("Chair.") THE PROPOSAL CARRIED.

The CHAIRMAN : Has any other member any- thing to say in favour of the amendment? Councillor PEiusEuToN: I have to say The rest was drowned in cries of "No" from the members in answer to the Chairman's ques- tion.
The CHAIRMAN : Then I Put it—all in fat-our say " Aye:" _
o0111“i1i0E PEMBERTON : This can't be forced in this--
"Aye, aye," called the members. The Cumangy: I declare the amendment to be carried.
Councillor PEMBERTON : I say it is not carried. The CHAIRMAN: I put it as a substantive motion. Those in favour—(" Aye, aye.") It is carried.
Councillor PEMBERTON : It isn't. I shall claim every time to be heard here. The meeting proceeded to the next business. A SOLITARY "NO."

The MAYOR pr-0-110-S4B-;"ote of t-banks to Coun- cillor Roberts, the retiring chairman. We know, he said, the difficult position you have to fill and the way you fill it. I can feel very much for you, because I have had trouble in the chair —(laughter)—though not so bad as you have had. (Laughter and applause.) Canon MORLEY STEVENSON, in seconding, re- ferred to the skill Councillor Roberts brought to bear on educational matters. He has, added the Canon, presided over our deliberations with courtesy, fairness and tact. (Applause.) Those are three points, and members of my craft are generally allowed three points, and if We take a fourth you grumble, so I shall say no more. (Laughter.) The MAYOR All in favour say "Aye." "Aye !" came a nearly united cry. Councillor PEMBERTON No! The resolution was thus carried with one dis- senting voice.

COUNCILLOR ROBERTS REPLY. . Councillor ROBERTS, who feelingly replied, said : I thank you, Mr. Mayor, and all the com- mittee very sincerely indeed for this expression of your appreciation of my conduct in the very honourable and responsible position as chair- man.

• - I value very highly indeed this expression of opinion, and it is no exaggeration to say, as I have said on a previous occasion, that any pub- lic work I have been engaged upon has given me satisfaction and pleasure, and more so has the work I have been privileged to do in con- nection with this Education Authority been a special gratification to me. Mr. Mayor, as pro- poser of this resolution I can assure you I appre- ciate it. (Loud applause.) On the motion of Mr. PLINSTON, seconded by Mr. A. J. JoLLEY, Councillor Roberts was re- elected chairman. In replying, Councillor Roams said he would not allow any incident to interfere with the pleasant relations he had with the members, and he trusted the committee's business would he conducted on model lines.

div.head: lIOW LABOUR WAS CONSULTED.
div.p: lIOW LABOUR WAS CONSULTED.
Deputation's Speeches and' Pre-con- ceived Ideas Prevented Progress.

To the Editor of "The Examiner." briefly refer this week to the subject of can onlyofthe second Warrington deputation to Ireland and their report. You will probably remember that only on reading your issue on March 14th, and when they had commenced their journey, was I made acquainted with Mr. Bellian's desire to be supplied with the name and address of my Belfast correspondent, al- though he had probably been some days, if not weeks, arranging the tour. However, Mr. D. R. Campbell placed himself in communication with him, and an interview was arranged for followingthe les' ridayevening (I think) at the Hotel,Prince Belfast, at 6.30. Mr. accompanied by his friends, Mr. e o f Wales' 'and Mr. Mitchell, arrived punctually, JohnstonCaipbe Campbell, but although Mr. Campbell told Mr. Bellian he had an important engagement at 8 p.m., he was kept hanging about until 7.30, when he was ushered into a room where a number of gentle- men were smoking, and subjected to some questioning. As he had to leave so soon, he left his friends behind him to continue the conver- sation, but offered his services from two o'clock next day until midnight to act as their guide, to show them things, ,and otherwise substantiate the statements made in your columns. Need- less to say, this offer was not accepted. Mr. Johnston and Mr. Mitchell • stayed with the deputation until 9 o'clock, Mr. Johnston telling them tlitt the fact of the deputation coming at the eleventh hour to gather information on the subject, and, after a few hours' sojourn in Belfast, to assume to be authorities on the question, "was really the whole case for Home Rule." These gentlemen have come to the con- clusion that the deputation spent too much time in making speeches themselves and airing their preconceived opinions, and their visit was not dictated so much by desiring to acquire know- :ledge as it was to endeavour to refute criticism of the previous visitors, and report in a manner palatable to the taste of the organisers of the expedition, and this view will, I believe, be zealously promulgated amongst labour circles in Belfast. May I add how grateful I am to the deputa- tion, and Mr. Bellian particularly, for referring to the incident of the tarring of the memorial to the men of Cork, who gave their lives on behalf of the Empire in South Africa? The act, whilst disgustingly silly and vicious, may have been the result Of vandalism, hooliganism, or "Sheridanism" (curious how it occurred contemporary with the visit of the deputation). But, of course, it appealed to the visitors as possessing grave political significance and against Nationalism. Did it dawn upon the patriotic intelligence of the deputation that the memorial was dedicated to the sons of the South of Ireland, who gave their lives for the Empire in the hour of her need? That it stands in the midst of their parents, their brothers, relatives and friends, many of whom, living in the im- mediate vicinity, served with them? Had not their lives and their death no political signifi- cance for the deputation? No; they can wax eloquent over the mischievous smearing by tar, but they have only a gibe and a sneer for the "hated- and despised" South, West and East, who gave their lives with the "Dublins," "Monsters," "Leinsters," " Connaughts," and "Royal Irish," who did not confine themselves to "lip loyalty," but fought and died whilst others talked and sang about the glory of the Empire. With all clue respect to Mr. Bellian, my criti- cism of that telegram has not yet been refuted. PATRICK O'BRIEN. 125, Wilderspool-causeway.

div.head: THE
div.p: THE
Ah ULSTER VIEW.
How the " Liberals " Studied the Liberal Case in Belfast.
"QUICK CHANGE ARTISTS."

The "Ulster Guardian" of last Saturday, dealing with the visit of the second Warrington deputation to Ireland, who are described as " quick-change artists," says : This also claimed to be composed of Liberals, and we assume cbUsequently that they were all men who voted for Home Rule in 1910, and who up till a fortnight ago were in favour of the , Home Rule Bill. We are, of course, open to correction on this point. As soon as news ar- rived in Belfast of its approach both the Ulster , Liberal Association and the Belfast Trades Council put themselves into touch with those in charge and arranged for an interview with the deputation when it arrived here on its way back from the South of Ireland. In accordance With instructions, four Ulster Liberals (all Protestants) waited on the deputation at the hour appointed. They were to be given half an hour, after which they were to make way for the representatives of the Trades Council, who, presumably, were to be given the same time to set forth their views. The 'time-table was not strictly adhered to, the Ulster Liberals being accorded three-quarters of an hour. Assuming that the Trades Council secured the same exten- sion of time, we find that an hour and a half out of two days were thus spent by the deputa- tion in learning the views of Liberalism and Labour in Belfast. If the same proportion was given by the Tapiff Reform deputations in Ger- many to discovering the opinions of Free Trade Germans, we can understand why so many con- versions to Protection were to be found amongst their members.

div.head: Breach of Faith.
div.p: A Breach of Faith.

When the Ulster Liberals entered the room where the conference was to take place, they found present a Unionist reporter. As they had not been informed that a report was to be taken of the proceedings, and consequently had come unprovided with a reporter, they natur- ally objected to this arrangement. The depu- tation by a vote decided quite fairly that the Unionist reporter should withdraw on condition that the "Ulster Guardian" should publish no report of the proceedings, an undertaking being given that the Unionist Press in Belfast should do likewise. It is worthy of note that all the Belfast Unionist papers next day contained a summary of the arguments laid before the depu- tation both by the Liberal and Labour repre- sentatives, and also of the views held by the deputation in regard to these arguments. While we have every right to regard this as a breach of faith, we shall still observe our part of the contract.

div.head: Not Much Loss.
div.p: Not Much Loss.

The members of the deputation have signed a report stating at length their reasons for changing their views upon Home Rule. We have no intention of combating those reasons in detail. They are the old stock arguments against Home Rule, and a man need never have tett Warrington to find in them ample justifica- tion to his intellect for becoming a Unionist. Dublin slums, Nationalist disloyalty, boycot- ting, these things form the stock-in-trade of the Unionist Press agency in Great Britain. Are there no slums in English cities? Was not South Africa as well as Canada disloyal before it got self-government? Is boycotting in agrarian disputes in Ireland any worse than the treatment a blackleg gets in an industrial dis- pute in England? The Home Ruler who be- comes a Unionist because he finds that Irish Home Rulers are not perfect angels, but human beings, who act just as people in other coun- tries act under similar circumstances, is not much Of a loss to us or a gain to the other side.

div.head: Unionist Habit.
div.p: The Unionist Habit.

There are many signs in the report which indicate the spirit of partiality towards Home Rule in Which the deputation is presumed to have set out, did not long survive the channel crossing. Thus the " squalor" in Dublin is ascribed to Nationalist incompetence, but the country districts where land purchase prevails were "never in a better condition." But the majority of the farmers are Nationalists. Why are they, too, not incompetent? The explana- tion of these inconsistencies, of course, is that in the one case the desire is to deal a blow at Home Rule by demonstrating the incapacity of Nationalists. In the other the desire is to deal another blow by showing that the country is so prosperous that Home Rule is unnecessary. It did not take the deputation long to acquire the Unionist habit of argument.

An " Opportune " Outrage. There is only one more point in the report with which we mean to deal. It states that: The day we avere in Cork we had a practical instance of the feeling which prevails among the Irish Nationalists. The instance was the tarring of a memorial cross erected to Cork soldiers who fell in South , Africa. The deputation accuse the Irish Nationalists of Perpetrating this outrage. What proof have they got? Not the slightest. As well might we retort that it was done by some Unionist aware of the coming visit of the depu- tation for the purpose of discrediting the local Nationalists, more especially as the Unionist Press reporting the incident gloated over how " opportunely " it had odcurred. On the very lowest grounds, would an Irish Nationalist, how- ever disloyal in his heart, select such a time to vent his spleen, the only effect of which would be to alienate the sympathy of English Home Rulers? But on higher grounds, the memorial was to Catholic and Nationalist soldiers and was erected by all creeds and classes in County Colt. What earthly motive would Nationalists have in committing such a dastardly action? The truth of the matter is that men who could thus, on no evidence whatever, lay at the door of Irish Nationalists the guilt of an action which was plainly the work of some irresponsible mis- creant, must have been prejudiced at the outset against the cause of Irish Home Rule.

div.head: Heaven Save Warrington.
div.p: Heaven Save Warrington.

_ Could not the deputation have spared a little time from raking in the muck-heap to raise their eyes and see if there was at least one small atom of good in an Irish Nationalist? While down South they passed through a country where nine Catholic lifeboat men gave their lives the other day in an effort to save the Protestant crew of a Norwegian vessel—a glar- ing instance, surely, of Nationalist depravity! They were in Limerick. Did they meet the Bel- fast Protestant who three weeks ago was elected County Surveyor in preference to Catholic ap- plicants by a Nationalist County Council?--, another proof of " Catholic intolerance"! Did they ask for the views of Mr. Holiday, a Protes- tant member of the Limerick Harbour Board, who stated the other day in reference to these charges against Roman Catholics: "Whether Home Rule came or did not come, there would be no change in their relations. He did not fear persecution from them, and this charge of intolerance was a falsehood and a lie. All those stories that had been circulated through the country for political objects, by political trick- sters, were false and untrue."

_ No, they heard nothing, or, if they heard, like Festus, they cared for none of these things. Dublin slums, tarred monuments, Nationalist incompetence and intolerance—that is the per- spective through which they view three-fourths of Ireland. Heaven save England in general and Warrington in particular from visitors who go over to ferret out all the bad spots and shut their eyes to the good.
Small Blame to Them.

But we must refuse to be tempted into lay- ing the blame upon the deputation. After all, it takes a strong man to fight successfully against his environment, and when one has been feasted by Unionist hosts and fed with Unionist Continued in next column
IR, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.

div.head: POLITICS IN THE ARMY.
div.p: POLITICS IN THE ARMY.
Mr. Asquith Becomes War Minister and Confounds
the Opposition.
LITTLE DEMAND FOR ELECTION NOW.

Far and away the niost interesting event of the week is Mr. Asquith's decision to take over the War office himself. This—though Mr. Glad- stone in a similar case accepted the view of his Law Officers, against the judgment of his Lord Chancellor, that the assumption of a second office without salary did not vacate a Minister's seat —makes it desirable, if not imperative, that the Prime Minister should offer himself to the suffrages of his constituentsior re-election. Lord Curzon, discarding the methods of Mr. Bonar Law, declared in the House of Lords that Mr. Asquith's decision did him nothing but honour, and was a public-spirited act on his part. The War Office, it is hardly necessary to explain, was left without a head owing to Colonel Seel) 's resignation, offered and refused last week, but eventually persisted in for sufficient and highly honourable reasons. Sir John French, Chief of General Staff, and Sir J. S. Ewer+, Adjutant- General, have also resigned their appointments, not with any desire o embarrass the Govern- ment, to whom they have given loyal service, but ' t through a punctilio of honour. Lord Morley on Tuesday explained how it was that he did not follow Colonel Seely into retirement. Even bitter political onponents could not but feel satisfaction that Lord Morley is still able to represent the Governtnett in the House of which he is a most distinguished ornament.

takes a supererogatory General Election on the Irish question and wins, the Opposition will not overtly support Ulster resistance. They -do not pledge themselves to refrain from a more or less discreetly veiled campaign to seduce the Army from its duty to enforce the decision of a majority of British electors and of the Imperial Parliament.
AN ELEVENTH HOUR APPEAL FOR A SETTLEMENT.

On Tuesday the motion for the Second Reading of the Home Rule Bill a-as the Order of the Day in the House of Commons. Its rejection was moved by Mr. Walter Long. Sir Edward Grey replied with a speech which, by its gravity, sincerity, and calm strength, profoundly im- pressed the House. Sir Edward Grey made an earnest appeal for an eleventh hour endeavour to arrive at an amicable solution. But it is necessary, if any progress is to be made, that the Government proposals, even when unacceptable, should be recognised as made in good faith, not denounced as a hypocritical sham. The Gov- ernment proposals would ensure that a General Election would ensue before the Irish Parlia- ment was established, and another General Election before the six years of exclusion for the counties which demanded it would have elapsed. Sir Edward Grey suggested that, if the Opposition desired peace, negotiations should be re-opened to devise a Federal solution before the end of the period of exclusion was reached.

div.head: DEFINITE CHARGE AGAINST THE OPPOSITION.
div.p: A DEFINITE CHARGE AGAINST THE OPPOSITION.

He supported the charge with a mass of relevant and convincing quotations.

div.head: MR. BOMAR LAW "QUALIFIES."
div.p: MR. BOMAR LAW "QUALIFIES."

Mr. Boner Law's principal contribution to Monday's debate was a recantation, or " impor- tant qualification," of what he had said in the discussion of the Government's proposed con- cessions to Ulster a few weeks ago. Mr. Bonar Law had said that, if a General Election on the Home Rule issue gave a majority to the Govern- ment, they would ho justified in coercing Ulster. Mr. Bonar Law now " qualifies" that admission. Of course, such an admission carried with it the implication that, if it is "unthinkable" that the Army could be used to coerce Ulster before another General Election has been held, the Army is'to be the arbiter when and on what issues a General Election is to take place. To- day Mr. Bonar Law says that if the Government
A VERY PARTIAL SENSE OF DUTY

The Gessau.: "I don't mind operating against this Home Rule chap, if it's necessary, but I don't admit that it's any part of my duty to interfere with the Ulsterman." JOHN Bra (sternly) : "Your duty, General, is to obey your orders and to stand between the two and prevent either one or the other from breaking the law or disturbing the peace."
AN ULSTER VIEW—continued.

stories for a week, small blame if one is con- verted and declines to be re-converted by an hour and a half's hurried talk with Home Rulers at the close of the tour with an Ulster Unionist present at the beginning of the con- versation and another present at the close. A courtship in Spain under the eagle eye of a duenna is a light task compared with getting any member of these deputations out of reaCh for a little of the crook of some of their Union- ist shepherds. In conclusion, we would say that even if the whole of Warrington or the whole of England were brought over to Ireland and subjected to the same lightning conversion, the Irish pro- blem remains. And remain it will till Home Rule be granted. The Warrington deputation may have become impressed by the determina- tion of Ulster Unionists to resist Home Rule, as if threats of violence should carry weight with any honest democrat. They heard no threats of violence from Ulster Home Rulers, for the simple reason that the latter still place their trust in constitutional methods of agita- tion. But if the present Bill is defeated by these threats of resistance, we would advice them to come across again and they will see that determination is not confined to the other side.

div.head: SOLEMN WARNING.
div.p: A SOLEMN WARNING.

As for the temporary Army "crisis," Sir Edward Grey expressed the hope that the new Army Order and the Prime Minister's assump- tion of the responsibilities of the War Office would close the affair for ever. But, he added, in solemn warning, if ever it should really be the case that the Army, or any large section of the Army, took active sides between the poli- tical parties, the country would be face to face with a question more serious and grave than it had known for three centuries. And Sir Edward Grey declared that if it ever tame to be a ques- tion whether Parliament alone was to govern and decide policy or whether it was to be inter- fered with, he took his stand as strongly as any one with what was said last week, even from the Labour benches—a significant allusion to Mr. John Ward's now historic pronouncement
'WILL COMMON-SENSE PREVAIL?
Bill Must Be Pressed Forward if Unionists Remain Obdurate.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."
Sir,—Mr. Bonar Law, March 26th, said :

"The right hon. gentleman [Mr. Lloyd George] has not realised that there is some work that gentlemen, whatever their rank in life, will not do. . . . He has come up against the Army and finds that no inducement of self-interest will make them do the political work of the Govern- ment when they think that is dishonourable." " The soldier has got to decide whether he will obey the constituted authority, or do something that is against his conscience."
" The Government . . . without the consent of the country are trying to do something which the Army will not be their tool in doing." March 23rd:—

"The House knows that we on this side have from the very first held the view that to coerce Ulster is an operation which no Government under existing conditions has a right to ask the Army to undertake, and, in our view, of course, it is not necessary to say that any officer who refuses is only fulfilling his duty." We have here a doctrine taught directly and by inference by a Unionist leader, which strikes at the roots of orderly government. It puts the officer above the Executive, his inclination takes the place of his oath, and, aCcording to Mr. Bonar Law, in refusing to obey orders, if against Ulster, he "is only fulfilling his duty." His conscience, not his duty to the King, is to decide his action. Conscience is an elastic element; it can be stretched to any length and in any direction. At its bidding certain women are burning houses, and defacing the nation's treasures; the private soldier could plead a conscience as a reason why he should not take part in quelling a civil riot if the rioters be- longed to his class.

div.head: CONCILIATION IN THE aAIR.
div.p: CONCILIATION IN THE aAIR.

The peaceful mood continues in the House of Commons, wrote the Parliamentary correspon- dent of the "Daily Chronicle" on Wednesday night. Mr. Dillon, who is in the apostolical succession of the Irish Nationalist movement, opened the debate to-day in a speech of fine spirit and pacific temper. Later in the afternoon a more militant note was struck by Mr. Harry Lawson, who did much less than justice to Mr. Dillon's zeal for a peaceful solution. Subse- quently the peace spirit again asserted itself in two striking utterances from men who are as far as the poles asunder in political and religious opinion, namely, Sir Mark Sykes, a Tory and a Catholic, and Mr. Silvester Horne, a Noncon- formist Liberal. Sir Mark made a most elo- quent appeal to the leaders of his own party to promote a settlement, and Mr. Silvester Horne pleaded with the Protestants of Ulster to show faith in the Protestant principle of liberty. Both hold that an honourable solution can be reached along the federal road. The feeling in the House now is that a settle- ment by consent is within sight and reach In‘that event a General Election will not take place until next year. Sir Edward Carson is expected to deal with the federal suggestion on Monday, when the second reading division will be taken.

div.head: (Reproduced by kind permission of the "Westminster Gazette.")
div.p: (Reproduced by kind permission of the "Westminster Gazette.")
MARKING TIME.

Thursday in the House of Commons we have been marking time, writes the Parliamentary correspondent of the "Daily Chronicle." The Conservatives, who are now concentrating all their energies on the demand for a General Election before the passage of the Home Rule Bill, are incensed because Sir Mark Sykes last night gave their case away by showing that an election would settle nothing. Hence for the time being the voices for peace on the Tory Benches are silenced. So far as the Opposition are concerned, the movement towards a settle- ment by consent is therefore arrested, though a group of Conservative federalists continue to meet for the exchange of ideas. Mr. Balfour did not help the peace-makers by , his speech this afternoon. On the Irish question he is unteachable. He had not one word of helpful advice to give; it was all pure negation. He has no sympathy whatever with the Federal idea, and would only tolerate it as avoiding the calamity of civil war. He pressed upon the Government to submit the Home Rule Bill to a Referendum.
On the question of the Army, Mr. Balfour laid down the doctrine of optional obedience.

with his oath, is to me incomprehensible. I do not think this would ever have occurred but for the suggestions of Unionist politicians, and their responsibility and blame is great. It is well for the country that this matter has been brought to an issue by recent events, even if accompanied by serious muddling at the War Office.

Unionists' False Position. The proposals of the Government ought to have received definite consideration by the Unionist party and the people of Ulster. They have put themselves in the wrong by scornfully and precipitately rejecting them. These went a long way to meet the objections of the Irish minority. I have more than once publicly ex- pressed the opinion that it was a mistake not to have left an open option at the end of six years. To hang this matter up, and to bring the two, or four, counties, as the case may be, into the Union against their will did not, and does not, seem to me to go td the making of a united Ire- land. But what is the use of anyone pressing his views on his party, when the Unionists treat the great advance made in the spirit manifested? There are indications in the Unionist \parti of a more reasonable attitude. Mr. F. E. Smith's words at the end of his speech on Monday holds out some hope, but the responsibility is at pre- sent with his party. If 'they will not even dis- cuss the Government proposition it is useless to

div.head: Muddled Sequence.
div.p: A Muddled Sequence.

Mr. Law affirms that these cavalry officers `f have a great contempt for politicians of all kinds," and yet in the same speech he tells us that the Army men will not obey orders because they think the Government has not the approval of the country. What a muddled sequence of thought is here revealed! First the Army has a contempt for politics and politicians, and then it is a matter of conscience with them, and they should not obey if, in: their opinion, the Government has not received the country's approval for a pro- posed law. Surely soldiers, whether they hold politics in contempt or not, should not set thew- selves up as both judge and jury of a political question. But it is difficult to resist the tempta- tion when it comes as a suggestion from the leaders of a great political party. Allow, for argument's sake, that the question is open to doubt as to whether the country has been suffi- ciently consulted, such a question is wholly political. It is not one in which the soldier has any right to intrude; his responsibility is to the Executive for the time being of which the King is the head, and to this only. We have heard a good deal of loose talk about the Army shooting down their fellow-country- men in Ulster. It is clear there can be no shoot- ing until the Ulster Unionists begin it. I have never been able to understand who it is the Ulster party mean to shoot. Is it the Home Rule Protestants? Is it the Catholic National- ists? Is it the Irish Constabulary? Is it the Army sent to defend life and property should the civil authority be in danger of being over- powered? I have asked many Unionists, both here and in Ulster, but have never got a satis- factory answer. They acknowledge they do not know. Circumstances being as they are, there I can be no shooting in Ulster unless and until the Ulster revolutionists begin. As soon as force is employed and shooting begins, you have a state of civil riot, which the constabulary must put down with the exercise of whatever force is required, and the Army must be at hand to assist in the defence of life and well-being, and resolutely quell civil commotion. That any soldier should hesitate under such contin- gencies, and in anticipation should commandeer his conscience and refuse to act in accordance

div.head: ZAM-BUI
div.p: ZAM-BUI
Torture.

AN outbreak of itchy pimples on Mrs. A. L. Savage's face started a long and severe attack of eczema. Writing from GO, Chestnut Street, Leicester, Mrs. Savage says : "My skin got inflamed and dry, and the burning, smarting sores practically covered my face. I daren't go near the fire nor face the least wind. The doctor's treatment failed. Common ointments, creams, etc., were no better either.
" After nine years of indescribable misery and disfigurement, I felt I should never be cured.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914. R. W. WOODS, I COMMON-SENSE IN POLITICS. SOUTHPORT & WARRINGTON. OPEN Exceptional Value in STORE. Easter Wedding Presents. 5, MARKET PLACE (Next Door to Post Office). WALK ROUND AND INSPECT OUR GOODS.

A little over a week ago the Unionists, under the impression that they had made peaceable government impos- sible, were openly gloating over the result of their reckless manceuvring. But they counted without their ASQUITH and they forget the solid foundations upon which modern democracy is building its superstructure. Both Leader and army are determined that whatever happens the country shall not be robbed of the fruits for which they have waged a long and sometimes weary battle. It is a question whether. the weakness of the case for the Opposi- tion or the strength of the case for the Government had most to do with bringing about the dramatic change, but the fact remains that so altered are the condi- tions that the demand for an election has not been so pronounced, and the resignation of the Government, which was confidently foretold, has been adjourned indefinitely. It is certain that the Opposition digged a pit for others, and with great speed slipped into it themselve. Meddling with the Army for political ends is a dangerous pastime in these days, as they soon dis- covered. But we must take some credit, as a party, for the discomfiture of the enemy. The party instinctively recog- nising the seriousness of the position, closed up their ranks, and before the Opposition had time to realise what had happened, their Leader had himself undertaken the pot of danger at the head of the War Office, and submitted himself to the judgment of his consti- tuents. Well may ALDERMAN TINNION say that if ever the Liberal party had reason to be proud of its Leader they have reason to be proud of Mr. ASQUITH. It may be saying too much to claim that Mr. ASQUITH is the strongest man that ever held the reins of government in his hands, but when the history of our time comes to be written and historians are able to say that it was Mr;ASQUITH'S exhibition of undaunted courage that was the deciding point in the fortunes of the Irish cause, ALDERMAN TINNION'S superlatives may stand justified. Cer- tainly we have nothing but admira- tion for the man who, in the midst of. oceans of calumny, remained calm and serene and finally triumphed over every difficulty by sheer strength of

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.
BIRTHS. MARRIAGES. D

character, aided, of course, by an unassailable cause. We record the fact that Mr. HAROLD SMITH has paid the town another visit during the week and that he still stands where he did. He seems to find greatest comfort in the reflection that he fore- told "awful " results in Ulster to follow any attempt to, drive Ulster from the protection of the flag. It is the old re- actionary story over again. We have in his speech a return to the old ques- tions now dead as the Dodo. Home Rule or no Home Rule is a settled issue. Whether the Orangemen—whom Mr. SMITH persists in calling Ulster, although half of Ulster is in favour of Home Rule—are bluffing or not does not matter now. All that does matter is that the Irish question has got to be settled one way or the other, and that soon. Sir MARK SYKES, the Conserva- tive Member for Central Hull, sees this as other Conservative Members see it, but he has had the good sense to say In the House of Commons, on Wednes- day night, he said In politics they had drifted on passion; they had divided class from class, creed from creed; the Throne even had been involved in their politics. He felt that there was a terrible future before the country unless the Irish ques- tion could be settled now. If that could not be done he feared that nothing could save the country from disintegration. If the Liberal party won at the next election they would have a mandate to coerce -Ulster; if the Unionists won they wo'uld have a mandate to thwart the hopes of 30 years now just on the verge of fruition. Therefore, whichever way the election went, he saw no prospect but that of bloodshed in Ireland sooner or later. The Army would be compro- mised in politics, and then it would never be the same again, whether democratised or not, and the Navy would follow. Once blood had been shed faction would grow more violent.

In view of the very serious outlook, the HON. MEMBER appealed for a settle- ment by consent. There is no theatrical "We will .not have Home Rule" about this gentleman; no streets flowing with ,blood unless he can have his own way. He accepts existing facts, and wishes to grapple with a known situation. The sooner it is recognised that the demand of the majority in Ireland has to be met and a solution found, the better it will be for all parties—and not least, we are certain, for the Unionist party.

div.head: ANOTHER TRIUMPH FOR FREE
div.p: ANOTHER TRIUMPH FOR FREE
TRADE FINANCE.

On Tuesday the financial year closed. Once more a Free Trade Budget, framed on the lines of the historic Budget of 1909-10, on which the Lords gaily challenged the verdict of the country, "damning the consequences," in LORD I\ llLNER..epigrammatic phrase, has vindicated its , resources and elasticity. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE budgeted for a revenue of £194,825,000. He was denounced for recklessness and "incurable optimism." by the Opposi- tion Press. He has obtained al revenue of £198,242,897. There has been an increase in every item except under the two headings of Stamps and Telegraph Service. The national revenue has increased by nearly 9i millions, and an increase of nearly 3i millions over the amount budgeted for. Owing to Supplementary Estimates, due to ex- ceptional circumstances, the total esti- mates`of the year's expenditure would have exceeded the realised amount of the revenue. Certain savings have been effected, and the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER has a surplus of £749,928. Once more the Cassandras, who raved about the bankruptcy of Free Trade finance and the shock to national credit and prosperity from the present Gov- ernment's " predatory " methods, have been made to look very foolish.

div.head: PASSIM WEEK.
div.p: PASSIM WEEK.
PARR HALL ORGAN IN SIGHT.

Satisfactory progress is being made with the, effort to raise sufficient money to provide Parrl Hall with an organ that will not be a reproach to the place and the town. At a public meeting held early in the week it was decided to pro- ceed with the project, and' the committee then appointed got to work yesterday upon a scheme by which it is hoped the necessary money will be got together. The original idea was to build an instrument to cost £1,600, but it is generally felt that the building is worthy of something on a more expensive scale. As £6OO has already been promised, the committee may be placed in possession of sufficient funds to proceed upon more generous lines than those proposed when precautions had to be taken to make the least possible demands upon the rates. This is rather reversing the ordinary procedure, which is held to fairour a more lavish hand when public money is involved. However, an excellent start has been made, and those who have the honour of appearing upon the first list of subscriptions are :—Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfleld, Mrs. Charles E. Parker, Mr. J. C. Parr, Miss M. G. Bylands, .ClOO each; Mr. J. J. Crosfleld, Capt. George Crosfleld, .R5O each; le Mayor, Dr. Joseph, Councillor H. Roberts and the Misses White, £25 each.

div.head: POLITICAL SITUATION.
div.p: THE POLITICAL SITUATION.

Locally, as well as nationally, the events of the past fortnight have put added strength into the Progressive forces, and much enthusiasm prevails. The Opposition having failed to suc- ceed by a flank movement, and having already, failed in the frontal attack, there seems to be little left for them but to acknowledge the logic of facts, and agree to the reasonable terms that the Government are willing to offer. There is, , we are glad to note, a spirit of conciliation in the air, with which we should not dare to inter- fere, but we should like to see our opponents make a good start for peace by forgetting their habits of bluff which only irritate. The sugges- tion that Mr. Asquith will only be opposed in Fife if he makes a too militant speech is particu- larly ridiculous. They know, or ought to know, ' by this time that Mr. Asquith will both do and say what appears to him to be necessary, and they can oppose or not oppose as they please. His majority, if there be a contest, will give them an idea of what the country thinks about Ireland and their tactics. We will, in the inter- ests of peace, leave the matter there.

We have dealt in our leader with Mr. Harold Smith's idea of the position reached in the con- troversy, and, still in the interests of a peace- able settlement, forbear to say more. On the ridiculous deputation, however, which does not count one way or the other, we may call our readers' attention to the manner in which, on page 5 of the present issue, our correspondents in Ireland show how worthless is their report. We see that Mr. Smith believes that the deputa- tions have proved something—presumably in favour of the lost cause they were sent to bol- ster up. All we can say is that as Liberals we hope more deputations of the same kind will be sent. But the parties concerned must hurry up, for Home Rule will soon be law, and their occupation will then be gone.

div.head: TOWN HOUSING.
div.p: TOWN HOUSING.

The report of the Land Inquiry Committee, on its town aspect, has been published this week, and to-day we publish the first of a series of articles by experts on the subject. It deals with urban housing and is written by Mr. B. Seebohm Rowntree, a member of the com- mittee. Next week the subject will be "Acquisi- tion of Land," by the head organiser of the inquiry, and subsequent articles, will be, on Tenure, Rating, and the Report as a whole, by gentlemen who have served in various capaci- ties on the committee. It is a valuable series upon a subject that will be in the very fore- front of politics when Home Rule has been granted and Ireland is at peace.

A BOWLERS' SCHEME. The new system adopted by the Warrington and District Bowling Association at their annual meeting on Thursday that teams consist of seven a side will be welcomed by a number of clubs, and particularly those who have not been able to enter this Association owing to not hav- ing a sufficient number of players to constitute a team of twelve.

SICK CORPORATION EMPLOYES. The Warrington Corporation are about to fall into line with the custom prevailing amongst other public bodies in regard to the payment of full wages to their employes dur- ing sickness. They intend, however, to deduct the money allowed under the Insurance Act, which means that the workers when sick will be paid the same wages as if they were well and at work.

EXTENSION OF LOANS. Councillor Pemberton is to ask the Council on Tuesday to approve of a resolution in which he proposes that the loans to Corporations for private street works should be extended for re- payment from seven to 20 years. thinks this would induce private enterprise to erect suitable dwellings for the working class and re- lieve the present scarcitjr of houses. If the Council approve of the resolution, Councillor Pemberton suggests that a copy should be sent to the Prime Minister, the President of the Local Government Board, the local Member, and to all urban authorities.

div.head: FRIENDS OF DEMOCRACY AND PROGRE! MUST EVER STAND ON GUARD.
div.p: FRIENDS OF DEMOCRACY AND PROGRE! MUST EVER STAND ON GUARD.
BY ARTHUR H. CROSFIELD.

Before I come to define and consider the two centres of re-action referred to at the head of this article, I think it will be useful to take a preliminary survey, beginning with the year 1899, and the negotiations that took place in the summer of that year, prior to the South African War, in the course of which negotiations the Boers conceded, as Mr. Chamberlain admitted and avowed, nine-tenths of our demands. Some of the coolest heads on the spot in South Africa, and some of the ablest judges of the situation were satisfied that long before generation had passed away the Union of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State with the rest of South Africa would inevitably take place; and yet, not con- tent with such concessions and such a situation, the man Niielding the highest authority in South Africa did not scruple to telegraph home, inviting the Government to proceed to extreme measures—as disastrous a message as had been sent in modern times. The high authority I refer to as responsible for that message was Lord Milner. The Tory Government listen6d to him; the goers were goaded into war, and in the course of that prolonged struggle there eame another extreme message to England when Lord Milner, as if not satisfied with the havoc and disaster for which he himself had already so large a shire of responsibility, actually re- quested the Government to suspend the Consti- tution in Cape Colony. This was more than even Mr. Chamberlain, the then Colonial Secretary, would face, and the request was refused; but let us take note of the fact that it was Made, and who made it.

In 1902 Mr. Chamberlain paid a memorable visit to South Africa, which he found desolated by the prolonged war and all its appalling con- sequences—desolated like a stricken field of battle. Shocked by these results, and, as it were, to cover up the wreckage, he resolved on his return to make a new departure. It is not only Liberals' who have made the assertion; I have heard Tories in high places—some of whom bitterly rue the consequences of it—say, roundly, that but for the South African War there would never have been any attempt to re-introduce Protection into the United Kingdom. But the attempt was made—an attempt to launch a policy so crude, so ill-thought out, so contradic- tory, and so reckless that it drove the most responsible, experienced, reputable and capable Conservative leaders, one after another, out of the Conservative Ministry. Mr. Balfour, indeed, remained as a brilliant exception, but as time wee' on it became tolerably evident that he t-Lily hated the whole proceeding. It was the wilder spirits, the more thoughtless and reek- • .;ss on the one hand, the more cynical and selfish on the other, in the Tory party who put the drive and force into the movement known as the "Raging, Tearing Propaganda"—to quote the description of it which Mr. Arthur Chamberlain prophetically and accurately gave. Again let us take' note of the fact that it was with these extremists of the Tory party Lord Milner, on his return from South Africa, was found in close alliance, and Lord Roberts with him.

1906 came, and the Day of Reckoning with it, and these reckless men of the Tory party re- ceived their crashing and unexampled defeat. Beaten in the constituencies they sought refuge in the House of Lords, and measures of the highest importance, passed by the largest majorities recorded in our Parliamentary his- tory, and, be it added, by Members of Parlia- ment who had freshly drawn their authority from their constituencies, were thrown out by the Lords with their customary contemptuous arrogance. The memorable Budget of 1909 fol- lowed, a Budget which has already proved itself of infinite value, and, indeed, indispensable to the whole nation, providing as it does on the one hand for the dreadful and deplorable, but, for the time being, inevitable increase in our expenditure on the defensive forces of the Empire; and on the other for all that far-reach- ing social reform which we have taken in hand of late years and which every man who looks one inch below the surface of things, whatever party he belongs to, must surely recognise as a crying and vital necessity for our people. But that Budget touched the pockets of plutocrats and aristocrats, and offended deeply against the spirit of selfish re-action. And so, the wilder
