div.head: MEMBER'S VISIT.
div.p: THE MEMBER'S VISIT.
Mr. Smith Addresses a Meeting in
St. Austin's Ward.
IRELAND AND THE DEPUTATIONS

The little schoolroom of St. Luke's, Liverpool- road, was only partially filled on Thursday even- ing, when Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., gave an address on the Home Rule question. Councillor Broadhurst presided. _

_ Mr. SMITH said the resignation of the Army officers had staggered not only the British Isles, but the Empire. It was their duty to inquire why that catne about. Why, if they had committed a wrong, were they put back in their commands, and if they had done no wrong, why did they resign? General Paget either repeated the orders he received from the War Office when he got back to Ireland, or he did not. If he did, then the Government ought not to stop in office another hour, and if he did not then the officer ought not to have been in office another hour.

The Government dare not for one moment con- sider dismissing the officers, because they knew the officers were in the right, and that the blunder they made was the blunder of the Gov- ernment. (" No ! No !") It was a criminal and ghastly blunder. In order to save their own skins the Government threw over the War Secre- tary and two distinguished soldiers like sheep to the wolves, in order to retain the position they had held for so long, contrary to the wishes of the British public.

div.head: ARMY v. PEOPLE.
div.p: ARMY v. PEOPLE.

But during the crisis the Government were saved. They found a new cry in the middle of the trouble. When the Government were anti- cipating going to the country one or two Labour members made speeches in which they raised so wicked, almost criminal, and certainly untruth- ful, cry, " The Army against the people." He was not going_to point out the awful conse- quences of such a cry as that, if it were ever adopted by the English people. It was purely an electioneering cry, a natural successor to "The people against the peers," by the revolu- tionary party. That was the cry the Govern- ment were going to make had an election taken place.

div.head: "COERCION" OF ULSTER.
div.p: "COERCION" OF ULSTER.

What really emerged from all the trouble was that coercion for the Loyalists of Ulster with- out an appeal to the British electorate was im- possible. "Perhaps," added Mr. Smith, "I ought to qualify that and say it is impossible so long as Ulster maintains her resolute and determined position, and remains aloof from all ordinary party politics, and so long as she remains prepared, and so long as we who sup- port her are prepared and determined, then my firm and considered opinion is that we are able to say that coercion of Ulster is an impos- sible thing. Much as there is to be regretted in the grave crisis through which we have passed, we can congratulate ourselves that Ulster's tri- umph is almost complete, and that Ulster can

div.head: Excellent Water.
div.p: Excellent Water.
Reporting upon analyses of Warrington water, Dr. Thresh, of London, says it is "excellent and pure for public supply."

Knocked Down By Motor. Lucy Taylor (seven), 21, Glazebrook-street, was knocked down by a motor in Manchester- road on Saturday and sustained a fractured leg. She is, making a good recovery at the Infirmary

Warrington P.S.A. Open Meeting.
Dr. Stanley Mellor will be the speaker at an open meeting on Sunday. Mr. W. H. Sherburn will preside.
Scarlet Fever Cases.
Sixteen cases of scarlet fever were reported during the week ending March 28th, and there are 60 patients in hospital suffering from this disease.

div.head: Latchford Without Burial Ground.
div.p: Latchford Without Burial Ground.

.... At the Latchford Without Parish Meeting the only question raised was the provision of a burial ground. Messrs. Fairclough, Pilling and Roberts were appointed a committee to consider the matter and to report to a later meeting.

Pupils' Success. The following pupils of Miss JeFsio Farrar, A.T.C.L., have been successful in passing the recent examinations held in connection with the Trinity College of Music, London: Miss Mary E. Archer, junior grade, and Miss Bessie Rushton, elementary grade.

Book for Good Friday. "The Seven Cries from the Cross," a book that contains a true spiritual message from the pen of the Rev. E. Morgan, Padgate, is perhaps the most appropriate book for reading amidst the religious peace of Good Friday. It is cheap at one shilling.

New Chief Fire nuttier. The Fire Brigade Committee recommend to the Council that Mr. Frank IT. Turner be ap- pointed Superintendent of the Fire Brigade. He is the son of Mr. Turner, who recently resigned the position, is a born fire fighter, and has been associated with the Warrington Brigade for 31 years. Life and Death. During the week ending March 28th 40 chil- dren were born in Warrington (15 males and 25 females), whilst the total number of deaths was 28 (16 males and 12, females). The increase in births over the corresponding period last yea' was two, and there was one more death. The death-rate is equal to 19.4, and the birth-rate 27.7.

St. Ann's Sale of Work. During Easter Week an important sale of work in aid of the Curate and Lay Readers' Fund will be held. On the Wed- nesday the sale will be opened by Mrs. Rylands, and on the Thursday by Mrs. Melville, Appleton. The stalls will be supplied with all kinds of suitable and pleasing Foods, marked at reason- able prices. There will be musical entertain, meats both in the afternoon and evening, under the charge of Mr. W. H. Rigby. As last year, the refreshment room will be entirely separate and will be well provided.

div.head: Warrington Market Prices.
div.p: Warrington Market Prices.

_ The prices at die Market on Wednesday were: Wheat firm at late prices, with not many offers. Oats a little easier, prices 2s. 6d. to 2s. 84d. per 451 b. Markets very slow with hay and straw; local demand quiet, very little business done; good prime clover hay .1:3 ss. per ton, meadow hay ..t2 10s. per ton, wheat straw 255. per ton, oat straw 255. to 265. per ton. XX flour, 235. per 401 b.; offals a little easier; bran Is. 2d. per 201 b.

Warrington Junior Liberals. A successful whist drive was held on Tuesday evening, about 60 persons being present. Dur- ing an interval refreshments were partaken of, the catering being in the hands of a Ladies' Committee, under the supervision of Miss T. Booth. Mrs. Lloyd Jones presented the prizes to the following: Ladies-1, Mrs. Raiford; 2, Miss Gordon; 3, Mrs. Brown; gentlemen-1, Mr. D. Ward; 2, Mr. J. Dickenson, jun.; 3, Mr. J. L. Jones. - -

div.head: Notable Successes:
div.p: Notable Successes:

_ We are pleased to note that Mr. Alfred Taker, a student of Wood's College, has been successful in securing an appointment as shorthand typist (in open competition) with a large engineering firm. Mr. Taker, after only some eleven months' training in shorthand, has attained the high Speed of 120 words per minute. It is interest- ing to note also that no less than ten students of Wood's College have been placed in remun- erative appointments during the last eight weeks.

Out-relief in Warrington. In the House of Commons on Wednesday Mr. Lees Smith asked the President of the Local Government Board whether hci would give the number of households and of persons, distin- guishing adults from children and males from females, in receipt of outdoor relief in Septen her, 1913, in the Borough of Warrington.—Mr. Herbert Samuel: The number of persons was 658, of whom 63 were men, 216 were women, and 379 children. The 658 persons represent 239 case's of relief, i.e., families received or persons relieved singly.

Ebenezer Church Band of Hope. The Band of Hope at Ebenezer Church was brought to a close for the session on Monday evening. A tea party and entertainment was held. The tea was well attended by members and friends. At the entertainment the chaii was occui.ied by Mr. A. E. Reece, in the absence of Mr. H. Thornton. A recitation, "If I were a man," was given by Daisy Boughey, and "Arthur's victory" was recited by Miss Lily Hibbert. Solos were rendeied by Miss Birchall and Miss Lily Hibbert. A song, "Poor Thomas Brown," was well sung by members of the Band of Hope. An action song, "The hoop song," was well presented, and a dialogue, "The ten virgins," was also given. All the items were well appreciated.

Ragged School Mission. The Ragged School Mission, which has been greatly improved in the hands of the decorators, was re-opened on Sunday. The Mayor presided in the afternoon and an excellent address was given to the children by Mrs. Dodds. The Mayor said that any work Mrs. Dodds was interested in was good work, and it gave him great pleasure in joining in it. • Those responsible for the : conduct of the school were not wealthy, and there was an uphill battle all the time. During the 27 years Many cases of distress had been assisted. He was very thankful to find that there was an institution in Warrington which cared for those who were somewhat neglected by other denominations. , In that institution they were taught the simplest truths and it would be well to encourage the children to keep in touch with the institution when they were grown up.

Mr. Elliott Married. Mr. A. S. Elliott, our highly esteemed Assistant Director of Education, was married on Thursday at Rumford Congregational Church, the happiest of happy brides being Miss Ethel Gertrude Muskett, LL.A., fourth daughter of the late Mr. William Muskett, of Romford. The Rev. F. Simmonds, minister of the church, officiated. The bride was attired in a dress of cream mousline de soie, with lace and pearl trimmings, while the dress of her brides- maid, Miss Elsie Muriel Beatrice Muskett (sister), was of flowered crepoline. Mr. T. H. Elliott (brother) was the best man, and among others present were Mr. and Mrs. R. B. Roberts (now of Woking) and friends from Bradford, Southend and London. A reception was held at the Carlisle Institute, and the newly-married pair left, in brilliant Spring weather, to spend' the honeymoon in Tbrquay. Before leaving they received, as their friends will be prepared to learn, a small sheaf of congratulatory telegrams.

div.head: PARR HALL ORGAN.
div.p: PARR HALL ORGAN.
A Committee Appointed to Raise the Necessary Funds.
A SUM OF £6OO PROMISED.

There seems no reason to doubt that a new organ for the Pair Hall will be forthcoming. At a town's meeting on Tuesday night at the Town Hall, at which the Mayor presided, a committee was formed to raise funds for the pur- pose. It was announced by the Mayor that .X 550 had been offered. The MAYOR said he had received from Mrs. Parker and Miss M. G. Rylands offers of £lOO each, and Mr. Reynolds had received a like offer from Mr. J. Charlton Parr. A letter had been received promising a joint subscription of £lOO from Mr. and Mrs. A. H..Crosfield, and Coon- . cillor Roberts offered £25 for his non-attendance at that meeting. (Applause.)

LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD DISAPPOINTS. Mr. REYNOLDS said it was disappointing, after h Y the Deputy-Mayor and cer- tain effmembers of the Council, and especially after a favourable tender had been received, that the Local Government Board refused to allow the Council to borrow the necessary money. However, they had to accept facts, and these were that the matter was absolutely dead so far as the Council was concerned, so that it now came down to a question of raising the money by public subscription and private gener- osity. In 1834 there were three musical societies in sections, ve ther e choral the town, which, through the energies of the R amalgamated the li and weovrke . a i - mon ic. That was really the beginning of the clifoinra two Powys,Musical Society, which was with them at pres- ent. The first organ was obtained about that time, and he understood that parts of that in- strument were to be found in the present organ. Coming down to the 'sixties and 'seventies, they found a great advance had been made, and other societies came into existence. A series of high-class concerts were given, and the Musical Society formed an orchestra and started ele- mentary classes. Ii 1877 the Warrington Orchestral Society was formed, and in 1883 the late Mr. T. J. Down started his band, which was now conducted by Mr. Arthur Down. They had also the Male Voice Choir, Messrs. Cros- field's Band, and numerous other bands and societies in the town. Warrington was a far better place than it could possibly have been, as a result of the great number of hours devoted to musical culture. Nothing short of true Christianity had a greater power than music foi raising the moral and intellectual tone of the people, and on the strength of that he urged that they should have an organ in the Parr Hall, for without a really good organ they were not able to reap the full benefit of the hall. Mr. Payton and Mr. Pearson had been ap- proached by various people to officiate at func- tions in the hall, and also with a view to recitals being given, but they had to report that there was no organ available. The Musical Society was at present debarred from presenting certain musical works which would be acceptable to its members and to the public, through the lack of a good organ. He moved a resolution stating that there was a real necessity for an organ, and that steps be taken at once; the money to be raised by private subscriptions and private generosity. This was seconded by Mr. J. JARMAN. FREE WINTER CONCERTS.

Mr. W. H. PAYTON supported, saying that the Corporation engaged bands for the summer months, but nothing was done municipally to cater for musical enjoyment during the winter. Mr. JARMAN asked if it was the intention, if the scheme was carried through, to provide con- certs and recitals during the winter months, to which a large proportion of free or cheap seats would be allotted to the general public. If that could be guaranteed he thought there was no doubt that the committee of the Co-operative Society would ask the members to help the effort. The DEPUTY-MAYOR said that although there was no resolution to that effect, it was generally understood by the Council that one of the main objects of the scheme was to arrange free or cheap recitals.

ALDERMAN BENNETT DISGUSTED. Alderman BENNETT said he was disgusted with the position. He was not at all anxious to rcwhen wh ii t c h came w were to e the re not simple to h e throw cold water on the scheme, but he could not help commenting upon the idiotic absurdity of the position with reference to the Local Gov- we ernment Board. They had a town of over 70,000 inhabitants and assessed at about a mil- lion and a half, a town supposed to be capable of importance, d o i mn gvarioustan e, things yet matterallowed ot fo borrow t b g an ol organon emoney. they . There is a great .deal of talk about Home Rule, declared Alderman Bennett, but, upon themy word, aotife thneigsattniloomf Home Rule, tulee; it e seems t consider- able m. It is a de- liberate insult to a municipality like Warring- ton to have to be dictated to as to the precise manner in which they should pay for a simple luxury of this kind. He was also indignant with the Town Council, who, finding they were not able to borrow the money, did not rise to the occasion and consent to the money being taken from the rates. He objected to shelving their responsibility upon other people—generous people. It made him ~think that the town was full of shirkers. It , made him right down angry—(laughter)--but he hoped there would be no difficulty in raising ' the money by public subscription. The proposition was carried.

div.head: Frodsham Pleasure Grounds.
div.p: Frodsham Pleasure Grounds.
Overton Hill Pleasure Grounds, Frodsham, will be open on Good Friday and Easter Mon- day. Crosfield's Band will be amongst the many attractions.

div.head: Cinemas on Good Friday.
div.p: Cinemas on Good Friday.
The Watch Committee have granted permis- sion to the picture palace proprietors to open on Good Friday from 6 to 10 p.m., provided the Pictures shown are suitable to the day.

div.head: Tram Employes' Wages.
div.p: Tram Employes' Wages.
In consequence of the loss in Wages to the tramway drivers and guards through the altera- tion in the Sunday services, their wages are to be increased id. per hour.

div.head: Bank Quay Working Men's Mission.
div.p: Bank Quay Working Men's Mission.

The Sunday school anniversary will be held to-morrow in Parr Hall,. services at 2.30 and 6.30. Mrs. J. Crosfield will preside at the afternoon service, and in the evening the Rev. J. W. Lowe, Sheffield, will preach. Special music will be provided by the children and choir.

Memorial to Late Mr. Frederick Monks. A tablet to the memory of the late Mr. Frederick Monks, which has been provided by the employes of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.; will be unveiled in the Nurses' Home, Arpley- street, at 12.15 to-day. Mr. F. W. Monks will perform the unveiling ceremony.

div.head: Dr. Hutt's Book on Health.
div.p: Dr. Hutt's Book on Health.

Her Majesty Queen Alexandra, whose great sympathy with all charitable objects is well known, has been graciously pleased to accept a COPY of Dr. C. W. Hutt's work, "Hygiene for Health Visitors, School Nurses, and Social Workers," recently published by Messrs. P. S. King and Son.

div.head: RaihA aymen's Concert.
div.p: RaihA aymen's Concert.

- The event on Good Friday in Warrington will be the tea and concert in aid of the Railway- men's Widows' and Orphans' Fund. This will take place in Cairo-street Schools, tea at 4.30 and concert at 7 p.m. This is a most deserving cause and ought to be well patronised. The fund does a noble work, and in Warrington alone £4O was, paid out of the fund towards the upkeep of the orphans of local railwaymen. An excel- lent musical programme has been arranged and the artistes will be: Miss H. Howell (soprano), Miss C. Rigby (contralto), Miss A. White, Mr. W. H. Rigby (baritone), Mr. Rutter (cornet soloist), and St. Ann's Juvenile Choir.

div.head: Splendid Holiday Guide.
div.p: A Splendid Holiday Guide.

Easter holiday-makers and those who are thinking of spending an early vacation should secure a copy of "Holiday Haunts" for 1914. This popular official handbook is now ready for distribution, and it would be difficult to imagine a more comprehensive and practical guide book for travellers over the Great Western Railway system. Profusely illustrated and interestingly written, the 1914 "Holiday Haunts" is a vade- mecum of useful travel, information, designed not only to furnish particulars for travelling facilities, but to make holiday of vital interest and peculiar pleasure. The book is obtainable at all G.W.R. stations and offices, price 3d., or from the Superintendent of the Line, Padding- ton Station, W., 6d. post free.

div.head: Bishop Welldon in Warrington.
div.p: Bishop Welldon in Warrington.

The Warrington Church Society Lectures were continued yesterday in the Parish Church. Addressing a large congregation of women in the afternoon, the Ven. Archdeacon Spooner took for his subject "Home Life." In the even- ing Bishop Welldon gave an inspiring address to a large number of men, taking for his subject "Behold the Man." At the outset he said they were on the verge of that week which commem- orated the most solemn and awful events in the history of mankind. It was a strange fortune that that Holy Week should be marked, at the present time, by all the emotion and agony of an election. They hoped that election would be uncontested in one way, if only to save the harrowing of men's minds during Holy Week.

div.head: Coming Trades' Exhibition.
div.p: Coming Trades' Exhibition.

There is always something intensely interest- ing about a Trades' Exhibition, but that which is to open in the Parr Hall on Tuesday will be particularly attractive. Not only will the lead- ing features in different trades be illustrated by the best exhibits it is possible to gather under one roof, but there will be many other attrac- tions. Working exhibitsi will prove interesting, as well as educational; then there are the Potter's Wheel, Hall of Mirth, electrical exhi- bits, and each evening the programme will be completed with the fairy fountain display. , With the exception of Good Friday the exhibi- tion will be open daily from Tuesday until the 17th of April. It will be well worth a visit.

div.head: Trips for Eastertide.
div.p: Trips for Eastertide.

Easter is fast approaching and many of oui readers will probably be undergoing the annual Perplexity of where they are to spend the holi- days. Whether they are desirous of spending a week on pleasure bent, or the humble week-end, they will find all their desires catered for by the London and North-Western Railway Co., who, as usual, are running cheap excursions to all parts. Specially cheap rates will be charged the visitors who intend to travel to the Metro- polis and the South of England pleasure resorts, and also to the West of England, the Lake District, and Wales' beauty spots. Those wish- ing to travel further afield will find conveni- ences to fulfil their desires, for the bookings to the centres of attraction in "Bonnie Scotland" and in "Erin's Isle" can be had at exceptionally cheap rates. The London and North-Western \and Great Western Joint Railways are arranging a number of day excursions on both Good Friday and Easter Monday to Frodsham, Halton, Helsby, and Chester. For further particulars see the companies announcements. •

div.head: Gymnastic Display.
div.p: Gymnastic Display.

The annual musical drill and gymnastic dis- play were given in the Gymnasium on Thursday night, when the Mayor (Councillor P. Peacock) presided. The programme commenced with a dumbbell exhibition by the small boys and girls, and was followed by a tug-of-war between elder boys and girls, in which the former avenged the defeat of last year. The spring board jumping was keenly contested, J. 'larding winning with a jump of 4ft. llin. The Champion Eight gave an exhibition on the rings, and Mr.' T. Jennings an exhibition of weight-lifting. The smaller boys and girls' tug-of-war resulted in favour of the girls. An exhibition in the noble art of self-defence was given by Messrs. L. Nlarnon and J. Farrell, and proved most inter- esting, as did the club solo by Miss W. Jones. The bar-bell exercises by the ladies' class was particularly smartly performed, 24 ladies taking I part. The Mayoress presented the prizes to the winners as follows :—Champion eight—W Haigh (champion), S. 'Linde, J. Sanders, S Daniels, L. Lawton, W. Sisson, Thomas W. Ward and D. 11. Ward; boys' class—l A.Board- man, 2 W. Gartland, 3 S. Jones; girls' class— ]. K. Bollingworth, 2 M. Bennett, 3 M. Souther- den, 4 11. Sergeant. The display reflected credit on the instructor, Mr. A. Mottram. Miss A. Clayton was the pianist.
Liberals Make a Great Demonstration Everywhere Between London and Edinburgh.
THE DAYS OF GLADSTONE RECALLED.

div.head: PREMIZR AND SE CRETARY FOR WAR.
div.p: PREMIZR AND SE CRETARY FOR WAR.

• -Not since the days of Gladstone has such a great ovation been extended to a British Prime Minister like that accorded to Mr. Asquith on his journey North to East Fife yesterday. At every stopping place along the 400 miles of rail- way track between London and Edinburgh the Premier received the greatest of enthusiastic greetings. His journey was one long triumph, and it is doubtful if even Gladstone received such a testimony of public opinion, although his journeys were marked by great enthusiasm. At King's Cross Station, London. thousands gathered, and so dense was the throng, eager to wish God-speed" to him in his by-election in Fifeshire, that it was with difficulty a large staff of police cleared a way. Many of the Prime Minister's admirers who were near enough slapped him on the back or shook hands with him. Those surrounding him sang For he's a jolly good fellow," and the singing was taken up by the spectators lining Euston-road. The train departed'amidst an extraordinary demon- stration of enthusiasm.

you back to us with redoubled authority to maintain the traditions of the Army, the author- ity of the Crown, and the power of the people." Mr. Asquith was deeply touched and briefly ex- pressed his thanks.

Grantham.—Address assuring Premier of un- swerving Liberal loyalty presented. In course of reply Mr. Asquith said: "We are prepared to persevere to the end in the great struggle we have undertaken." Scenes of enthusiasm. York.—Presentation of illuminated address. Premier expressed his thanks. Train departed amidst vociferous cheering. Newcastle.—Address presented by Sir Walter Runciman to Premier for his " untiring vindi- cation of democratic principles." Mr. Asquith replied. Suffragette attempted to board train as it moved out. Pulled away by a constable and injured. Edinburgh.—Welcomed by deputation of Scot- tish Liberal Association and large and enthusi- astic crowd, which recalled the crowds who used to welcome Mr. Gladstone.
The Prime Minister arrived at Cupar, Fife. shire, last evening, and was equally as enthu- siastically received. He is the guest of Sir James Lowe, at Kilmaron Castle.

div.head: JOURNEY IN BRIEF.
div.p: THE JOURNEY IN BRIEF.
London.—Presentation of address expressing the wish: "May the electors of East Fife send

Mayor was elected chairman, with Mr. liey- nolds as secretary, and Mr. Fairhurst treasurer. A number of ladies were co-opted members, and a scheme was adopted for collecting funds. It was stated that 4;600 had been promised.

div.head: To the Editor of "The Examiner."
div.p: To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—Having followed this scheme up very closely since the commencement, I feel it my duty to write publicly to thank the Mayor (Councillor peacock) and the ex-Mayor (Dr. Joseph) for the efforts and energy they have put, and are still putting, into the matter. One cannot help, on looking down the list of subscribers, but remark, Where are the Musical Society amongst the donors? Have they offered any guarantee, or are they going to give a con- cert in aid of this fund? As they will reap the benefit and pleasure of the instrument in the future, I think they ought to do their share. With reference to the committee appointed at the meeting on Tuesday last, I think a better committee could not be appointed, as it in, eludes all denominations as well as councillors.

I think, in the interest of the ratepayers and subscribers, that all previous tenders for the instrument and specifications of the organ ought to be cancelled and fr6sh contracts sub- mitted and placed before the committee to be discussed and voted for at some future meeting. Might I ask what is to be done with the old "Box of Whistles"? It should be arranged with the contractors of the new instrument to buy it, but I have no doubt the committee will see to this. Hoping to see a new instrument erected 07 the next concert season. INTERESTED ORGANIST.
TALENTFD YOUNG MUSICIAN.

div.head: MISS MARIE HAWLEY.
div.p: MISS MARIE HAWLEY.

Miss kla;:ii;-Hawley, daughter o-f- Mr. Felix Hawley, of Knutsford-road, Warrington, has just added to her already long list of musical successes. She has passed with high honours the Senior examination in pianoforte playing of Trinity College of Music, obtaining 98 marks out of a possible 100. Miss Hawley is only 14 years of age, and this result must be very grati- fying to her and to her teacher, Mr. William Cooke, the organist of Lyn= Parish Church.

Rebuked. Miss Phmbe was; going out of town for the week-end and had barely time to pack her suit case and catch the train. "I'll make that train or die for it," she said to Rose, the chambermaid, who was assisting her. - _
"Don' say dat, Miss Pbcebe; don' say dat," remonstrated Rose. "Et yo' was to miss dot train yo' could take anoder, but ef yo' was to die yo' might have to go befo' de Lo'd unpre- pared."

div.head: ASQUITH THE STRONG MAN Alderman Tinnion's Tribute at the Liberal Club. THE BILLIARDS HANDICAP.
div.p: ASQUITH THE STRONG MAN Alderman Tinnion's Tribute at the Liberal Club. THE BILLIARDS HANDICAP.

Alderman Tinnion presided over a meeting held in the Billiards Room at the Liberal Club on Monday night, and presented the prizes that were won in the Christmas handicap. Among those present were Councillor Wilkinson, Coun- cillor Firth Lindley, Mr. Critchley, and Mr. Herbert Johnson (honorary secretary).

The prize-winners were: W. Woods, T. Newns, J. Durkin, F. Jordan, H. Hayes, H. Greenhalgh, P. Johnson, F. Walker, J. Davies, H. Gilbert, W. Patrick, A. Crowe, I. A. Simpson, F. Stilling- fleet, and S. Gough.

A TREMENDOUSLY HIGH STAKE. Alderman TINTUON, who was received with cheers, said it was with pleasure that he com- plied with the request that he should present the prizes, as be knew the club was one of the greatest auxiliaries they had to help forward the Progressive work in town, which he had so much at heart.

"I think," said Alderman Tinnion, in a short sentence that was followed by ringing cheers, "that if we as Liberals were ever proud of a man as leader of our party we are proud to-day to march forward towards progress under the able and splendid leadership of Mr. Asquith." These few days would be very eventful ones, not only in the history of the party, but of the country. Our liberties were at stake. What- ever advantages were gained, whatever progress was made, whatever guarantees of liberty were procured by the passing of the Parliament Act, all were in jeopardy, unless they a..iberals were prepared to support Mr. Asquith fn saying once and for all that the aristocracy, neither in the House of Lords nor the Army, should be allowed to take away the liberties of the demo- cracy. Applause.) He could not for the life of him understand the suicidal policy of the Conservatives—who had always pretended to be the party of law and order, the party of land- owners and owners of property, who had most to lose—why they should gamble with the stake they played for so tremendously high. The democracy, however, had a greater stake at issue—the rights we now enjoyed—than any- thing the privileged classes could possibly have. That being so, he was very pleased to note the hearty manner in which they had received the name of one who was the strongest man who had ever been responsible for the government of any country. (Cheers.) Mr. W. PATRICK agreed with all Alderman Tinnion had said, and referred to the pensions 1 that were now available for old folk at the end of an arduous life. He thought members of the club ought to take even a more active interest in politics and do their utmost to see that the !people should prevail. (Applause.) Councillor GOUGH, having replied to some good-natured "chaff" on the part of Alderman Tinnion, saying that in all he did in the Coun- cil he tried to serve the interests of the rate- payers, Councillor WILKINSON proposed. a vote of thanks to Alderman Tinnion, aading with respect to his apt remarks regarding Mr. Asquith, " Them's my sentiments." (Laughter and applause.)

div.head: NO LONGER TO BE WRONGLY REPRESENTED.
div.p: NO LONGER TO BE WRONGLY REPRE- SENTED.

The vote having been heartily carried, Alderman TINNION said he was pleased to find the club in such a healthy state, and proud that so many young men were taking an interest in Liberalism. The health of the club reflected the health of the party.

"We would rather welcome a contest in the immediate future," concluded Alderman Tinnion, amid a further outburst of cheering, " because I have every confidence that when the fight does come we shall be quite ready and Warrington will no longer be wrongly repre- sented by a Conservative member."

div.head: BOUNDARY BATTLE.
div.p: BOUNDARY BATTLE.
Lancashire and Cheshire County
Councils' Great Fight.
LAND AROUND WARRINGTON.

The great fight, ill which Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils are chiefly concerned, over the question of the boundary between the counties near Warrington, opened in the Man- chester Town Hall on Wednesday, and is likely to last some time.

Major C. E. Norton conducted the inquiry on behalf of the Local Government Board. The principal authorities affected were legally repre- sented as follows: Lancashire County Council, Mr. Harcourt E. Clare (clerk to the Council); Cheshire County Council, Mr. George Rhodes, K.C., and Mr. Har- old Rhodes; Irlam District Council, Mr. Vesey Knox, 8.C.; Partington Steel and Iron Works, Mr. Forbes Lankester, K.C., and Mr. Harold Smith, M.P.; Bucklow Union and others, Mr. A. Macmorran, K.C., and Mr. F. B. Merri- man; Runcorn Union and Rural District Coun- cil of Runcorn, Mr. A. T. Miller; Grappenhall parish and Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. A. Lister-Kaye; Lord Barrymore (property owner in Grappen- hall), Mr. Walter C. Richmond; Barton Rural District Council, Mr. J. W. Whitworth; Ship Canal Company, Mr. Frank Kershaw; Man- chester Corporation, Mr. P. M. Heath (deputy town clerk); Barton and Warrington Guardians, Mr. T. G. Russell; Thelwall Parish Council, Mr. Herbert Hatton; Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company, Mr. H. Greenall ; Altrincham Justices, Mr. H. Leonard Harris; and the War- rington Rural District Council, Mr. Sutton.

A THREE HOURS' SPEECH. Mr. Clare, who outlined the Lancashire County Council case, spoke for three hours. The Ship Canal, he said, was the suggested new boundary. The effect of the proposal would be to transfer from Cheshire to Lancashire £9,628 of assessable value and 918 acres of area, and to transfer from Lancashire to Cheshire only £B2O of rateable value and 217, acres of area. Hence the net loss to Cheshire, taken as a. whole, would be £B,BOB of rateable value and 700 acres of area. Mr. Clare examined the application in detail, urging that in the matters of govern- ment, particularly as regards police work, the, grant of the order asked for would add to the general efficiency of local administration. He disclaimed any idea that the application was prompted by a desire to acquire further terri- tory or rateable value.
The Lancashire Chief Constable, Mr. Lane, and Dr. Sergeant, medical officer, gave evidence.

THURSDAY'S EVIDENCE. On Thursday brief evidence was given in sup- port of the inclusion of certain parts of the Grappenhall and Thelwall districts in Lanca- shire, one reason advanced being that the War- rington Rural District Council were more likely to attend to the sanitary work than the present authority. Most of the day was devoted to the case for the inclusion of that part of Partington which is on the north side of the Ship Canal in Irlam. Mr. Vesey Knox, K.C., said the population of the district was increasing rapidly. It was expected that the Partington Steel and Iron Works would ultimately employ 1,500 men, and these, together with the employes at new caustic soda works for a company which was to bring soda from British East Africa, would accentuate the housing difficulty which had caused the Irlam Urban District Council to submit a scheme for the approval of the Local Govern- ment Board.

CHESHIRE FIGHTS FOR ITS RIGHTS. Yesterday Cheshire began its light for what one witness called its sole rights and liberties. For Cheshire, Mr. G. Hhodes, K.C., said they felt strongly that the alteration of the boundary between two counties--especially .two counties as Lancashire and Cheshire, which had always worked together—ought not to be made except by agreement, unless very grave reasons were given, or it was shown that the district was not administered in a proper manner by the county council from whom it was proposed to take it away. The .Manchester Ship Canal for _thirty out of its forty miles of, length ran through Che- shire, but the benefit of the canal was mainly for Manchester or the Ma.ncliester end of the waterway, and it was there that the great im- provement in the value of property had taken place. But as far as Cheshire was concerned, it got very little immediate benefit. They in Cheshire had felt all along that if any alteration should be made in the boundary with regard to the Ship Canal, in justice to Cheshire—seeing that the canal could not have existed but for Cheshire—the northern bank of the canal should be fixed as the boundary in- stead of the centre of the canal. Dr. Hodgson, of Crewe, vice-chairman of the Cheshire County Council, and chairman of the County Education Committee, said he thought Lancashire's application was ill-advised. The hearing was adjourned.

div.head: LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
Latchford Ward Wotkers Make Merry.

I One of the most successful functions ever held in connection with the Latchford Ward Liberal I Association was held on Tuesday evening at the Winamarleigh Cafe, Sankey-street. Under the new organisation, both the ladies, led by the I captain, Mrs. T. Locker, and the gentlemen, led by Mr. John Dodds, chairman; Mr. E. W. James, deputy-chairman; and the energetic secretaries, Messrs. J. Mather, G. Toulmin, E. H. Jones and W. Merrill, joined forces to make the arrangements complete, the 'result being that over 100 workers sat down to an excellent I dinner, which was thoroughly enjoyed. After dinner a whist drive and concert occu- pied the rest of the evening. There was de- lightful singing by Mrs. Sanders, beautiful violin solos from Miss May Mather, and capital and mirth-provoking humorous songs from Mr. J Nurse, whilst Mr. George Tendlebury and Mr. C. Baxter were accompanists of special merit. Those who could not play whist occupied their time by draughts and dominoes and listening to the musical items. Mrs. T. Locker presented prizes to the successful card players as follows: —Ladies: Mrs. A. Shakeshaft, silver sugar bowl (kindly given by Mrs. James Walker), whilst the following received books: Mrs. Percival, Mrs. J. Mather, Mrs. A. Critcbley, Mrs. Newell, Mrs. Ryder, Miss Merrill, and Miss E. Short; conso- lation, Mrs. Powell. Gentlemen: Mr. W. Hughes, tin of tobacco (kindly given by Mrs. Sanders), and the following also received books: Mr. A. Critchley, Mr. Hulse, Mr. E. Walker, Mr. A. Denny, Mr. Fairhurst, Mr. Patterson; consolation, Mr. W. Merrill. The consolation prizes, which caused endless amusdinent, were kindly given by Mrs. Osborne, who, at the close, addressed the meeting.

TO KNOW EACH OTHER. Mrs. OSBORNE, amid applause, said she was pleased to see so many Latchford friends. That was the first ward social which had been organ- ised for the workers, and her only regret was that the idea had not been thought of long ago. They wanted to know the workers, and the workers to know one another, and with that end in view it was intended to have a social for every ward. She thought their workers had been neglected in the past, but the new organisa- tion had altered all that. They could not help in their enjoyment but think of the Leaders of the Government who were engaged against the vile attack of the Opposition. (Cheers.) She thought the time was due when they ought to ask themselves if they were ready for the fight when it began? They should ask them- selves if there was nothing they could do to strengthen their forces in Latchford. Person- ally she would like to see the number of workers doubled before the election came round. (Ap- plause.) They could not all do the same work. but there was a place for everybody, and she trusted that the Latchford Ward would do its best to return Mr. Crosfield as Warrington's member once again. (Applause.)

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
TUESDAY.

Before Councillor Roberts (in the chair), Alderman James Evans, Mr. T. Locker, and Mr. C. Jackson, Holmes. Left His Wife.—William Timms, late of Man- chester, was charged with running away from Newton-in-Makerfield and leaving his wife and two children chargeable to the Union.—Mr. Shearer gave details of the case, and Mr. Auk- land, relieving officer, said the man had given his wife little money, and he (the officer) had relieved the family to the extent of 225. 9d.. outdoor rgief.—The case was adjourned for four. weeks. A Sad Cate.—John Bennett, Enfield-street, was , charged 'with neglecting his four children.— Mr. A. Btowne, for the N.S.P.C.C., said Mr. Wainwright had exercised a great amount of patience in the case. He had warned the prisoner, who was a labourer at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works. The man did not turn up his money and the family went short of food. Mr. Wainwright had relieved the family severall times. On Saturday night the Inspector found the woman and the children in the street.— Inspector Wainwright told a sad story of neglect. On Saturday the man was drunk and the wife and children were perished with cold.— The case was adjourned for a week, and would be adjourned afterwards from week to week, when Inspector Wainwright would report. To Avoid a Summons.—George Ogden, 8, School-brow, was charged on remand with at- tempting to commit suicide by drinking lini- ment.—On the husband promising to sign the pledge the case was adjourned for four weeks.

div.head: JUVENILE COURT.
div.p: JUVENILE COURT.
WEDNESDAY.

Before Messrs. S. Wright (in the chair), J. Upson, T. Pemberton, and A. J. Jolley. Daring Young Thief.—A twelve-year-old boy answered two charges of stealing money from children, and also one of attempting to steal.' —Superintendent Williamson said the boy had stopped a policeman's little daughter, who was sent to buy something, and took a paper out of her hand containing 2s. sd. He said there was a man further down the street who was taking money from little girls. He put the fivepence back in the paper and kept the 2s. He had stolen 2s. from a lad in a similar manner, and had attempted to snatch a bag from a little girl after saying he would give her twopence to show him where the Maypole was. The lad admitted several offences and had given his mother.erums varying from fivepence to eightpence, saying he had earned it.by carrying parcels at Bank Quay Station.—Mr. J. Moore Murray said the boy was a truant and quite indifferent to school.—The lad was committed to the Macclesfield Industrial School until he was 16 years of age.

div.head: FRIDAY.
div.p: FRIDAY.
Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bol- ton, Burton and James Evans, and Messrs. S.

Wright, A. J. Jolley and W. Furness. A Licence Question.—Mr. Longton applied for the confirmation of the removal of the licence belonging to Matthew Cunningham from 29, Froghall-lane, to the brewery premises in Owen- street. He said that at the adjourned Licens- ing Sessions the removal was granted subject to an undertaking being given by Mr. Cunning- ham. This had been given.—The Chief Con- stable: It must, of course, be thoroughly under- stood that only the beer licence and not the wine and spirit licence would be removed, as the Owen-street brewery would have to be on the same lines as other breweries.—Mr. Long- ton said that he was under the impression that the beer and wine and spirit licences were or- dered to be removed, but he. did not press the matter of the wine and spirits.—The Bench de- cided that only the beer licence should be re- moved.

div.head: DEALER AND INVESTOR.
div.p: DEALER AND INVESTOR.
A Curious Case in Warrington County Court.
VERDICT FOR PLAINTIFF.

An unusual case was heard at the Warring- ton County Court on Thursday, when, before his Honour Judge Stanger, James Illingworth, formerly of Rotherham, but now a photogiaphl enlargement dealer, Knutsford-road, Warring- ton, claimed ..tl2 from Daniel Webster, cycle mechanic, 8, Church-street, and residing at 5, Lord Nelson-street. Mr. Sidney Wallhead appeared for the plain- tiff, and Mr. A. Browne for the defendant. Mr. Wallhead said the defendant advertised in a newspaper that he wanted someone to in- vest £5O or £lOO in a business. Plaintiff an- swered the advertisement, and came from York- shire to see defendant. He came over another time to make further inquiries, but never agreed to go into the business. Shortly afterwards de- fendant wrote to plaintiff and asked for £2 as a deposit, which plaintiff sent, saying he would come over and make further arrangements. He came to Warrington a few days later and let the defendant have £lO on some terms.

div.head: "WANTED TO INVEST."
div.p: "WANTED TO INVEST."

James Illingworth said he replied to the ad- vertisement, "Wanted, a man to invest from ..4;50 to .2100 in a business," but denied that the advertisement (produced), "Good opening; handy man with £5O or £lOO in business; wages and profit sharing," was the one he answered. Mr. Browne: That advertisement has been running all the time. Plaintiff corroborated what Mr. Wellhead had said, and further stated that he thought defend- ant wanted him to "dodge" about his shop at 30s. per week. He paid the deposit, but did not decide to go into the business. He wanted time to think the matter over. Defendant said he wanted the .flO to buy frames in Liverpool, and he (plaintiff) lent him the money and got a receipt for it. He had now removed from Rotherham and gone in another business. De- fendant wanted him to sign the agreement.

"WOULD HAVE NO 'TRUCK.'" Mr. Wallhead: whp. -did you not sign the agreement? Plaintiff: Because I was not satisfied about the security. After I had taken up Hi& other business I told defendant I would have no 'truck" with him, and he promised to pay the £l2 by instalments if I promised to take the matter out of the solicitors' hands. If I did not, he said I should not get anything. Mr. Browne: Did he tell you it was to put a patent reflector on the market? Plaintiff: He said he had a patent reflector. Mr. Browne: Did he ask you to travel for the reflectors?
Plaintiff : He wanted me to go running "bikes' about and selling them. _ _

Mr. Browne: Did he say he would provide you with a motor car to go and get orders. Plaintiff: He said he had a motor car. Did he say this money was to bind the bar, gain Did he say he would give you 305. and share profits for selling this reflector?—No, he never mentioned profits. . .

Did he give you some reflectors for you to get an opinion on them?---Yes! I could not give them away. They are in Warrington now. Did you not come to the final arrangements verbally by which you would join him and pay .E80?—No.
Do you know these reflectors are made for one penny and sold for sixpence or sevenpence?—lt is a big profit if it is so. Have you tried them?—l have nothing to try them on.

Harold Gough Brandwood gave evidence as to delivering furniture at plaintiff's house, and Mr. Webster, in Illingworth's presence, com- plaining about the delay in delivery, saying he had lost ss. that day through plaintiff not work- ing. He afterwards said to witness he had to make a bit of a show, and invited witness to have a drink. He refused. DEFENDANT'S VERSION.

Daniel Webster said he explained the business about the reflectors to plaintiff very thoroughly. He agreed to pay him 305., share profits, and travelling expenses, and plaintiff agreed to start on a certain date. The £lO was to go towards building a garage for the motor which plaintiff was to use. He had lost a lot of money through plaintiff acting as .he had done, for it was now too late to get the reflectors out, and he had relied on plaintiff. - - .

Cross-examined by Mr. Wallhead, defendant said the agreement he drew up was a basis for a further agreement. The business was his father-in-law's, and that gentleman also was the tenant of his (defendant's) house. Mr. Wallhead : The business was your father-

Defendant: The reflector business was mine, and that was what plaintiff was going to do. I told him the business was my father-in-law's. Mr. Wallhead: You were inducing Mr. Illing- worth to go into a business that was not yours? Witness: He was to learn the cycle and motor business. He agreed to the terms and then backed out.

Robert Whiteford, employed by defendant, and Thomas Golding, employed by the War- rington Corporation Sanitary Department, gave evidence to the, effect that from conversations which they had heard between the parties they were under the impression that plaintiff had fully agreed to go into the business on the terms mentioned.
Cross-examined by Mr. Wallhead, Golding said that plaintiff did not tell him he was going in the business.
Re-called, Illingworth denied that Webster told him the business was his father-in-law's.
His Honour thought that plaintiff put his money down under a misconception. He gave judgment in favour of plaintiff for the amount claimed, with costs.
The money defrulant agreed to pay at £2 per month.

div.head: EXAKENER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAKENER, SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1914.
Ii DISTRICT PIEWS
STeeKTON 1-IE74.TH.
charged he made no reply and would give no clne to his identity.—For the defence it was sub-

mitted by Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, that prisoner was a canvasser for photographic enlargements. Two pictures were exhibited, in court which had been received at his lodgings whilst he had been in prison.—Prisoner said it was dry humour when he showed the sovereign to the men, but it was done principally to show that he did not want to find Mr. Davies to obtain charity.—The Chairman (Councillor H. Roberts) said undoubtedly prisoner had brought the trouble upo t himself by not stating the nature of his busii..,ss in the first case. If he had told the tale to the police as had been heard in court, he would probably not have been ar- rested.—The case was dismissed.

div.head: TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.
div.p: TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

The Parochial Committee are humorists. They transact business along with mirth. There were several amusing items to Enliven the prosaic business on Tuesday. "Only a pair of corsets," or rather A poster depicting that necessary article. Caused a certain amount of humour. Were the modest bachelors on the committee Shocked at the corsets, as was the curate In " The Private Secretary" when he dis- covered
Them in the bag he had exchanged in nns- take?

The powers of the Parish Council Chairman are limited. He has not yet developed into a Hercules. Therefore the irate ratepayer who asked him To go to Grappenhall-road and take up A weighty telephone pole dumped there By the Post Office Authorities' orders, I Must have misunderstood Councillor Whitley's powers When he asked him to become a modern Samson.
However, if Councillor Whitley was not quite able To remove the objectionable telephone pole By forcible means, the Parochial Committee May yet have it removed by peaceful persua- sion.

The idea of a Wakes Week for Stockton Heath, To synchronise with that proposed for War- rington, Is taking shape, and such a decision would be A very sensible one, as it would conjoin the holidays. Amateur gardeners are now hard at work. The gardens are beginning to assume an appearance Which ought to go a long way to appease the Garden Society.
Members Present.—The members present at the Parochial Committee on Tuesday were: Councillors G. Pilling (in the chair), J. Whit- ley, McDermid, Mclntyre, C. Dukes, Pearson, Clark and C. Hallows.

A Danger Spot.—lt was reported at a meeting of the Parochial Committee on Tuesday that the question of the danger spot in Walton-road, where a motor fatality recently occurred, was receiving the attention of a sub-committee of the County Council,—Councillor Whitley: The surveyor has been and taken particulars.

Lumb Brook . Nuisance.—At the Parochial Committee on Tuesday a letter was read from the contractor denying an allegation made at the parish meeting that objectionable matter was deposited at Lumb Brook.—Councillor Whitley said that he had closely watched the matter and fouraA that the chief nuisance arose from the wharf on the capal.—Councillor Pear- son said as chairman of the Sanitary Committee he would investigate the matter.

A " Can-y " Deputation.—At the Parochial Committee on Tuesday, Councillor Pearson an- nounced that they had got samples of new ash cans and pails.—The Chairman Mr. Pilling): Where are they?--Councillor Pearson: In the yard.—Councillor Mclntyre: Will you bring them in?—Councillor Clark: Send a deputation out for them. (Laughter.)—Several members went out and returned laden with the pails, which were inspected amidst a considerable amount of good humoured banter.

A New Light.—Councillor Whitley, at the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee on Tues- day, pointed out the necessity for a lamp at the junction of the passage behind Chapel-lane and Carlisle-street. Steps were constructed there, .and it was necessary to light the spot, otherwise it would be dangerous.—Councillor Mclntyre: Absolutely dangerous without a lamp.—The new 'light was agreed to. , ' Smart Firemen.—Councillor McDermid, re- Porting on the recent fire at Stockton Lodge School, said the fire brigade made a quick turn- out and were away to the fire five minutes after the alarm. They succeeded in confining the outbreak to the room in which it occurred. The turn-out and the work of the men were most satisfactory.. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman (Councillor Pilling) : It is a very satisfactory report. (Vear, hear.) _

The Sewage Question.—Mr. Wright, the sur- veyor, submitted plans for the installation of a water carriage system of dealing with the sewage, to a meeting of the Parochial Com- mittee on Tuesday.—Councillor McDermid said he had now been assured the existing sewers would be capable of dealing with the extra sew- age.—Councillor Whitley said he was told differ- ently, and there would be a difficulty with the syphon.—Councillor Dukes suggested the obtain- ing of the opinion of an expert.—Councillor Pearson agreed that such would be the better course.—Mr. Ashton (the clerk) suggested that they should get the opinion of Mr. Diggle, the expert to the Runcorn Rural Council.—On the motion of Councillor Dukes, seconded by Coun- cillor Pearson, this was agreed to.

"A Most Lovely Place."—While a number of cases of scarlet fever were under discussion at the Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday a member expressed surprise that the cases were not removed to the hospital at Dutton.— The Chairman (Councillor Pilling): Yes,lwe have the accommodation there. It is a most lovely place, and the children who have been there cry when they have to leave.—Councillor Dukes: If it is so lovely you might issue picture postcards to let the people see whqt the place is like. (Laughter.)—The Chairman: We would like anybody to come and see it.

Charge Dismissed.—At Stockton Heath Occa- sional Court on Wednesday, Walter Harris alias Walter Alfred, lodging at 201, Knutsford- ' road, Warrington, was charged on remand with frequently London-road for an unlawful pur- pose.—The evidence for the prosecution showed that whilst two men were on London Bridge on March 23, the prisoner went to them and asked if a Mr. Davies lived in the district, and as he commenced to make inquiries about Mr. Davies' business the men refused to give him any fur- ther information unless he disclosed his own business. He asked one of them if he wanted paying for giving the information, at the same time showing a sovereign. The following day he was again in the district, when he was stopped and handed into custody. When

div.head: PROPOSED WAKES WEEK.
div.p: PROPOSED WAKES WEEK.
Should Stockton Heath Follow
Warrington?

Should Stockton Heath follow the example of Warrington in establishing a Wakes Week? was the question raised at the Parochial Committee n Tuesday. ' Councillor Dukes Said 'there was every bleb- 'mod that Warrington would adopt a Wakes Week, and it seemed to him that the Stockton Heath Walking Day. was going to suffer for the reason that everything would be spent, and the iddies would not be dressed to take part in the walking. Councillor C. Hallows : It is a matter for the Church, as it is a Church festival. Councillor Mclntyre said the field used by the Stockton Heath children would be occupied by the children from St. James', Warrington. It might mean that the Stockton Heath chil- dren would lose the use of the field.
Councillor will be other way about.

FOR FURTHER CONSIDERATION. \ Councillor Pilling (chairman): When the Warrington scheme goes through we may be able to deal with the question. Councillor Dukes said the Warrington scheme was adjourned for three weeks, but the meeting was in favour of the Wakes Week commencing on Walking Day. That was the unanimous feel- ing. Other Lancashire towns had such holi- days. He had a list of 73 towns, covering a population of 11. .millions, all of which had adopted a Wakes Week holiday.' Unfortunately these towns wanted to change their holiday dates to that of Warrington, so the Warrington People would not have the full advantage of the resorts. The Chairman: We had better consider the matter later, after Warrington has decided. This course was agreed to.

div.head: THAT BRIDGE ONCE MORE.
div.p: THAT BRIDGE ONCE MORE.
Lighting Question Again Discussed by Parochial Committee.
A MORE POINTED COMPLAINT.

The alleged danger to traffic on the Swing Bridge through the absence of a lamp for illu- minating purposes was again discussed at the meeting of the Parochial Committee on Tues- day night, and some strong remarks were made about the matter. Company to the letter he had sent Mr. Ashton, the clerk, read a reply from the Ship Canal Pany on behalf of the committee, and in the course of this the company stated that they could not see their way to fix a light, as it would inter- fere with the navigation of the canal. For this reason none of the canal bridges had lights. They wished to mention that the matter was brought before them by the committee in 1909 and 1912, and the request was declined for, the same reason. Councillor Dukes: How does it interfere with navigation? BADLY LIGHTED.

Councillor Whitley said the reason given was that when the bridge was turned the li ht would reflect on the ships and cause confusion to the officers. At the inquest on the youth who was drowned, the Coroner had suggested a, two- sided lamp. The Ship Canal Company's repre- sentative said there were no lights on other bridges, but these bridges were not so long as the Stockton Heath bridge. It was about 90 yards in length, for it ex- tended over the old canal, as well as the Ship Canal, and the other bridges on the Ship Canal were only about 60 yards long. The lamps at either end were quite 120 yards apart. On the Stockton Heath side they had two good incandes- cent lamps showing clear, but on the Warring- ton side there was only one light, and it was behind a tramway "standard. It was like hid- ing their light under a bushel. (Laughter.) Councillor MeDermid : A light is needed in the centre of the bridge.

div.head: FRIVOLOUS OBJECTION.
div.p: A FRIVOLOUS OBJECTION.

Councillor pukes: It is a frivolous objection. It is easy to cover the light when a ship is pass- ing. They could see how that is done if they have travelled at night in a railway carriage. Councillor Clark said the accident had occurred to one of the Ship Canal employes because there was no light on the bridge. Some- thing ought to be done to provide a light, and the reflection difficulty could easily be over- come.

Councillor Whitley : I move we send a more stron gly-worded representation to the company. The Chairman: We might point out that pub- lic feeling has grown stronger since the accident to the company's servant. Councillor McDermid : There will be a very serious accident some day on the bridge through the absence of light. Councillor Whitley: By the company erecting the bridge there they took away the advantages and conveniences of the general public, and the company ought to meet us in every possible way for giving them the advantages and conveni- ences they now have got. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was adopted unanimously,

div.head: TOO GREAT AN ORDER. Amusing Request to the Chairman of the Parish Council.
div.p: TOO GREAT AN ORDER. Amusing Request to the Chairman of the Parish Council.
AN OBJECTIONABLE POLE.

In his capacity' as Chairman of the Parish Council, Councillor Whitley was asked to lift a mighty telephone pole out of the ground by an enraged ratepayer. This bit of humour came out at the Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday, when a telephone pole which is con- sidered an eyesore , by Grappenhall-road resi- dents was under consideration. / 1 Councillor Pearson said the pole was most unsightly on the south side of the road near Sandy-lane. One of the best roads in the neigh- bourhood was thus undoubtedly spoilt. Would a suggest ion from the coMmittee that the wires 1 be put underground meet the case? He wasl quite aware that the question of the erection of poles had been before the committee. Councillor Mclntyre said if the pole were moved to the corner of Sandy-lane it would be better. At present it caused an obstruction and was unsightly. Councillor Clark: If it were opposite my house I should f (Laughter. iel like knocking it down. )

div.head: TO LIFT THE POLE.
div.p: TO LIFT THE POLE.

Councillor Whitley : It is not the only un- sightly pole in the village. The occupant of the house opposite the pole seemed to have a high opinion of my position and strength as chairman of the Parish Council, for he came and said: " I 'want you to come and lift out that tele- phone pole." (Laughter.) I decided to go and look at it, and I took Mr. Pearson with me to help if we were going to lift it out of the hole. (Laughter.)
Councillor Hallows sa,id that he understood that the Post Office engineer was going to re- move the pole soon. The wires would have to go overhead. ' Councillor Clark: I think it ought not to

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH
continued.
have been placed where it is until we had ap- proved or disapproved of the position.
ALL POWERFUL GOVERNMENT.
The Chairman (Councillor Pilling): I -think representations should be made to the Govern- ment to lift it.

Councillor Whitley: Do you say, Mr. Chair- man, the Government can do as they like in such things? (Laughter.) The Chairman: Oh, yes ! CoUncillor Whitley: Then the sooner we have a change of Government the better.
Councillor club re . Hear, hear. Councillor Dukes: Everybody can do as they like, judging from what they are doing in Ulster. (Laughter.)
- Councillor Pearson moved that an applica- tion be made to the Post Nice to remove the pole. This was agreed to.

div.head: PAIR OF CORSETS..
div.p: A PAIR OF CORSETS..
Do They Constitute An Unsightly hoarding?
COUNCILLORS' LITTLE JOKE.

A pair of corsets, not the real article, but a pictorial description of it, formed the theme of an amusing discussion at the monthly meting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee on Tuesday, Councillor Pilling presiding. , Councillor Dukes said they had had com- plaints before about unsightly hoardings and billposting stations in the Square. He now saw a poster on a shop in the Square which-- Councillor Clark: I spoke about it. Councillor Dukes:- But this has something to do with corsets. (Laughter.} Councillor McDerraid I thought we had some control over these things. A Member: Oh, no, but I object to corsets. (Loud laughter.) Mr. Ashton (the clerk) said -the matter of hoardings was under the County Council. The County Council wrote to each District Council asking their views on the matter of hoardings, and whether there were any parts of the dis- trict in, which hoardings were prohibited. That committee sent the required information, and the Council took considerable time considering the mattes and then decided not to comply with the requests of any of the local authorities.
DANGER OF EXAMPLE. Councillor Dukes: I am speaking of the corner shop where a bill about corsets is posted on the brickwork.
A Member: Again I object to corsets. (Laugh- ter.)

Councillor Dukes: If ,everyone will follow the example the whole village will become a gigan- tic advertisement hoarding. The Chairman: Yon—cannot deal with private Property. Councillor McDermid : I think we ought to re- new our application to get local control. The Clerk said it was not a question of local control, but prohibiting the erection of public hoardings in certain areas. The County Coun- cil had passed certain rules in connection with the erection of hoardings. Councillor McDermid thought the committee had control under the Advertisement Hoardings Act. He moved that they renew their applica- tion to the County Council. This was agreed to and the topic dropped.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.
A TRAMWAY CAR ADVENTURE.
Remy Vines Follow Remarkable Case.

Joseph Keenan, 35, Hood-lane, Sankey, was summoned at the Warrington Borough Court on Saturday for interfering with the comfort of the passengers on a Corporation tramcar and also for using obscene language Qjl the predious Saturday night. The Chief Constable, who described defend- ant's conduct as "monstrous," said that• de- fendant was a passenger on the 11.10 p.m. car on Saturday, travelling in the direction of San- key. When the car was at Rylands-street he pressed a button upstairs, and the driver started the car. That was a dangerous practice, and anybody getting on the car at the moment might have been injured.

On the journey the defendant was continually ringing the bell. His method of working seemed that when the conductor stopped the car for passengers to alight or to board it the defend- ant would immediately ring the bell upstairs, and the driver understanding that to be the signal to proceed, started the ear again, with the result that two or three lady passengers were almost thrown to the ground as they were

'ffhe driver and conductor remonstrated with the defendant about his conduct, and later he struck one of the passengers a violent blow in the face, because the passenger had pointed de- fendant out as the man who was ringing the bell.

The driver of the car, James Taylor, stated that they were delayed 20 minutes on the journey, and that a'number of passengers pre-1 ferred to walk from Barnard-street instead of continuing the journey by car. Joseph Bracegirdle, the conductor, corrobor- ated the Chief Constable's statement about ladies being almost thrown into the street. De- fendant used very bad language. Defendant, who said that the evidence had been made up between the witnesses, was fined 305., including costs, in each case.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Death of Mr. Unsworth.—Mr. Unsworth, of the Chapel House Inn, passed away at noon on Thursday. He was well known and a populas personage in the district. He was an enthu- siastic bowler and a good sportsman. A Con- servative, he did not take any active part in politics.

Exciting Fire.—Considerable excitement was caused on Monday afternoon through a motm luny, owned by Mr. W. C. Taylor, of Shaw, en route from Liverpool to Shaw, laden with cotton, catching fire from some unknown cause at Hall's Bridge, Parnworth-road. The Peuketh Tanning Company's Fire Brigade, warned by the works' "buzzer," turned out, under the command of Captain J. Richardson, and wore on the spot iu record time. They soon got the fire under con- trol. The bales were removed from the vehicle to the roadside, thus saving the engine from being damaged. As the goods in transit were of such a combustible nature, the firemen assumed full control over them, keeping theft hose pipes ready for action in case of an un- expected outbreak, until they 'were removed on the following Wednesday evening. The War. rington Fire Brigade also turned out, but theft services were not required.

The Bible Society.--The annual meeting of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Tuesday evening The Rev. James Richardson, of Manchester, who has resided in Madagascar for 35 years: gave a lantern lecture on that country and th& work amongst the natives. Mr. J. G. Within- shaw was in the • chair. The Secretary (Mrs. Parker), before reading the report, expressed her delight upon seeing such a crowded room, but deplored the fact that the amount collected during the past year did not reach that of for- mer years. Deaths and removals were the chief factors, but it was hoped that very soon other subscribers would replace those who had dropped out.—The Chairman alluded to the great work done by the society all the world over, and the necessity for funds to continue it. The Rev. James Richardson then deliveied his lecture, and this was of a most interesting character. Mr. C. E. Parker drew attention to the fact that if it had not been for the advantages gained by the Bible Society it would have cost the Missionary Societies more than ten times the amount spent to produce the Bible in Malagary. The meeting was closed by the Rev. Harry Middlewood. Mr. James Woodward manipu- lated the lantem ia his usual able manner,

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

Death of Mrs. W. G. Groves.—We regret to announoe the death of Mrs. W. G. Groves, wife of Councillor Groves, who passed away at hei residence, Newfield Villa, at noon on Wednes- day, after a long illness. Though of a very retiring disposition, Mrs. Groves was much esteemed, and was very popular with the mem- bers of the Newfield Mission Girls' Union, in whom she took a great interest.

The Election To-day.—With the cessation of hostilities in Booth's Hill Ward, Heatley has become the centre of all electioneering enthu- siasm. Polling will take place to-day in the Infanta' Schoolroom, Sandy-lane, between the hours of 12 o'clock noon and 8 p.m., and the result of the contest between Mr. S. Critchley. and Mr. J. jolley is eagerly awaited. The figures should be announced at the Council Offices about 8.45 p.m.

Bible Society.—The annual public meeting of the Lymm branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Eagle Brow School- room; under the presidency of Mr. J. D. B. Smith. The Honorary Treasurer's report was read by Mr. R. Hewitt, who announced that the sum of £l5 Os. 11d, had been sent to the head- quarters of the society. The Honorary Secre- tary (Mr. David Mort) read a report of the public meeting held recently at Oughtrington. The Rev. T. A. Wolfendale gave a lecture en- titled "Egypt and Palestine," in the course of which he thanked the audience for their assist- ance, and said that the London Committee ap- preciated their efforts. Speaking of the circu- lation of the Bible, he said that there was a world-wide demand for the Scriptures, and that last year the society had distributed eight million copies, a total‘ which they would pro- bably eclipse by the end of the next period.

Baptist " Busy Bees."—The yearly tea and public meeting held in connection with the Higher-lane Baptist "Busy Bees" took place in the schoolroom on Wednesday, when a splen- did gathering spent a very pleasant evening.— Prior to .the lecture on "Woman's Work in Shantung," given by the Rev. E. E. Lovell, the annual report was read by Miss A. Brundrett, who expressed her regret at the absence of Miss Owen, who had performed the duty for many years. The 'report, which showed an encourag- ing state of the finances of the society, included a list of the subscriptions, collecting boxes, and a summary of the gifts of goods, which were dis- played on the stall and round the room, many of the jackets, quilts, socks, scarves, &c., being the successful achievements of the workers' nimble fingers.—On the proposition of the Rev. E. E. Lovell, it was resolved to send a letter of sympathy to Miss Owen.--,-The lecture was illus- trated by some very good limelight views. Several slides were of the Ching Chow Fu dis- trict, the centre of the labours of Miss Kirk- land, the lady missionary to whom the results of the "Busy Bees'" efforts are sent, and her appearance on the screen gave rise to hearty applause. The lecture concluded with an urgent appeal for assistance in the mission field._

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL ANNIVERSARY.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL ANNIVERSARY.
Sympathy With the Injured Pastor.

The anniversary services of the Congrega- tional Church were held on Sunday, when in- iliring sermons were delivered. The Rev. Wm. Landless, of Partington, preached in the morn- ing and the Rev. T. T. James, of Warrington, at night. On Monday evening the lady members of the church provided an excellent tea. This was followed by a public meeting, presided over by Mr. J. H. Holt, at which the Rev. T. T. James delivered his lecture on " The Pilgrim Fathers." Mr. Holt expressed his regret at their pastor's inability to be present owing to his suffering from an unfortunate accident. He thought they ought to send Mr. Penaliggon a message of sympathy in his trouble, expressing their hopes for his speedy recovery, and denoting their ap- preciation of the services he had rendered dur- ing the past year. Speaking of the apparent lack of enthusiasm for Christian service amongst modern church workers, Mr. Holt said that if they only I had to fight for their religious liberties as their forefathers had done, they would probably be bettet Christians.

The Rev. T. T. James introduced his subject as "a talk about one little part of that great movement for spiritual independence and free- dom." The audience were told of the origin of the Independents, or Congregationalists, and a racy account of the early members and customs was given.

div.head: CHORAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
div.p: CHORAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
Daring Scheme Proves Successful.

It was thought to be a rather risky procedure for the Lymm Choral Society to give a public repetition of most of the items rendered recently at the Drill Hall, but their performance in the Eagle Brow Schoolroom on Tuesday night, despite a considerable decrease in the number of singers, passed off quite successfully, though the insufficiency of male voices was noticeable in " 0 happy eyes " and "Moonlight." During the brief interval between the two concerts ,the society have been busy with several new pieces, and their interpretation of "Judge me, 0 God" (Mendelssohn), proved to be their best item of the evening. Evidence of further practice was manifested in the animated and yet dignified rendering of "Tile Voyagers," whilst Caldicott's , pretty part-song, "The Message," was sung with grace and expression. Elgar's two part-songs, for female voices, "The Snow" and "Fly, Singing were given to the violin accompaniments of Miss Hill and Mr. Andrew, the former piece being exceptionally good. The ladies also sang Cowen's duet "Cleansing Fires." That Miss Ada Guest, the lady soloist, has been success- ful at several musical festivals, one did not , doubt after hearing • her delightful singing on Tuesday, and the audience demonstrated their appreciation of her efforts in the request for encores. Ample scope for her resonant and sweet soprano voice was afforded by the songs "Far Greater," "Were I a moth," "The Black- bird," and "The Enchanted, Forest." Mr. W. M. Mitchell was a baritone above the average and created a favourable impression with , his contributions of "Blow, blow, thou winter wind," "When shadows gather,' "Son of mine," "Bantry Bay," and "The Little Irish Girl."

Instrumental music was provided by Mr. Albert Andrew, the favourite violinist of a Lymm audience, who was accorded a warm wel- come. His items were "Ii Trovatore," " Caval- leria Rusticana," "Chanson Polonaise," and Rubenstein's "Melody in F." Pianoforte ac- companiments were skilfully played by Messrs. F. Champ and B. Hill.

div.head: PA DGATE.
div.p: PA DGATE.

Wesley Guild,The usual weekly meeting, held on Monday evening, took the form of a social. Members of the Latchford Guild were present and provided a short entertainment, in which a pianoforte solo was played by Miss Pigot, and an amusing sketch, "My Wife's Itela- tions," was contributed by several of the visitors. The Rev. E. Morgan welcomed the Latchford members and spoke on the value of Guild work. Mr. Cox, on behalf of the visitors, thanked the Padgate friends, and expressed the hope that they would pay a return visit.
