QUAINT AND AMUSING.

Two children only out of five on the books were attending Aughton School, believed to be the smallest in England, when the Government inspector recently visited it. He miule a report to this effect to a meeting of the Lancashire Education Committee and added: "The master continues to give careful attention to his duties." Aughton is a parish seven miles north- east of Lancaster.

div.head: Beer and Spirits as " Poison."
div.p: Beer and Spirits as " Poison."

. . Representatives of the Anti-Saloon League are to introduce a measure in the New York State Legislature providing that all beers and spirits sold within the State boundaries shall be sold in bottles or other vessels labelled with a skull and cross-bones printed in red ink, and marked. with the word "Poison." The promoters of the measure declare that it represents the first real step towards prohibition in New York State. The proposed label also bears the words : " This preparation is a habit-forming, irritant, narcotic poison."

Carrying Coals to Newcastle. As showing the openings that exist for mixed farming in Canada by settlers from this country the Canadian Trade Commissioner for New Zealand reports that the steamer Wakura, which sailed from Auckland to Vancouver late in December, had on board 26,698 boxes of but- ter, which was the largest shipment of New Zealand butter ever taken to Vancouver. The steamer also carried to Canada 1,197 quarters of beef, 362 carcases of veal, and 170 sacks of various meat. This seems very much a case of the old familiar "tarrying coals to New- castle."

div.head: Successful Immigrant.
div.p: A Successful Immigrant.

Two years ago a man left London for New South Wales (says a Sydney paper), and was assisted by a friend in England to acquire a Property in the north. During the two years he has paid off the whole of the liability in con- nection with the purchase of the property, and is now making a substantial profit. The result is that the friend, in England, has decided to leave at an early date to assist in the working of the property, and will bring with him an expert pig-breeder and butcher and dairy hand. Each of these men will emigrate with his family.

The Fox Farming Industry. To meet the demands of the British and other fur markets, the new Canadian fox farming industry grows apace. Fifteen more very hand.. some silver foxes, worth about £3,600, have been taken to farms in Prince, Edward Island and Nova Scotia, where the fox breeding industry is being carried on. They were the property of a fur buyer of Isle la Crosse, in Northern Saskatchewan, and this cargo of foxes is the third of its kind which he has taken to the East. Only seven of them are of the pure silver variety, the others are crosses; they all have, however, that silver tinge in their fur which helps to give the pelts such a high market value.
The "No Hat" Craze.

While it is well to keep the scalp dry and well ventilated and exposed to both light and air, there does not appear to be any valid ground for the belief that going bareheaded, particu- larly in the sun, in any real way promotes the vigour of the hair, says Dr. Woods Hutchinson, in "Common Disgasefi." Experts are unanimous in declaring that an excessive exposure of the already thinning hair to the direct rays of the sun will not only not check the process, but often accelerates it. Like the shoe, the hat, while a good deal of a nuisance in many ways, and a frequent source of inconvenience, discomfort, and absurd extravagance, is probably more helpful than harmful, not merely to the head, but to the hair.

div.head: An Amphibious Steamer.
div.p: An Amphibious Steamer.

The unsophisticated visitor to the lumber districts of Canada may occasionally see what is to him a very remarkable sight, a primitive. looking steamboat high and dry on a road, crawling along quite comfortably, apparently just as much at home as in its natural element, These boats are known as " alligators," and are used for towing the rafts of logs down the rivers and lakes to the mills (says the "Wide World Magazine"). Sometimes it is desired to transfer one of these craft to a new sphere of dperations which can only be reached overland, and the boat is then hauled out of the water, placed upon rollers, and travels to its destination by means of its own power.

div.head: Great Wall of China.
div.p: Great Wall of China.

Few people realise what an almost perfect condition prevails along ex a i dalaiiii.getel i in'atil.tie of the great wall of China. The bricks of the parapet o are as firm as ever, and their edges have stood the severe climatic conditions of North China ,wilt,loipstcliaarrceAlyieaoic break, e , ans magazin, The paving along the top of the wall is so smooth that one may ride over it with a bicycle, and the great granite blocks with which it is faced are smooth and as closely fitted as when put in place over two thousand years ago. The entire length of the wall is 1,400 miles, it is 22ft. high, and 20ft. in thickness. At intervals of 100 yards or so there are towers some 40ft. in height.

Frozen Coal Mines. It was not until 1883, when Poetsch invented the " freezing method," that Holland's coal- fields became ,of any practical value. Where, coal is encountered immediately under the solid rock there is a stratum of drift sand that con- tains great quantities of water. This condition of things made it practically impossible to build the shafts. The freezing method, however, has, successfully solved the problem. On the spot where the shaft is to be dug from twenty-five to thirty borings are made down through the drift sand to the solid rock in ft circle five feet larger , in diameter than the projected shaft. Pipes are then sunk into these bare holes, and through these is circulated by powerful freezing mach- ines a chemical solution pooled down to below zero. In this way the drift sand containing thei water is frozen as hard as a rock, and a shaft is then dug and lined from bottom to top with strong segments of cast-iron securely soldered ' tbgether 'with lead.

div.head: WORLD OF LETTERS.
div.p: THE WORLD OF LETTERS.
New Books.
Labor and Administration. By John R. Com- mons.
London: Macmillan and Co., Ltd. 7s. net.

Prof. Commons, of Wisconsin 'University, has in this volume gathered together a number of articles and addresses which he has published from time to time during the past ten years. They deal with a variety of topics, but there is a common centre of interest, a unifying ele- ment, in the various ithapters, which justifies their inclusion in this book under the general title of "Labor and Administration." They all deal with labour in some measure, and the point of view of the author is that of administration. Prof. Commons strikes the note of his book in the first chapter on " Utilitarian Llealism." He applies the conception of idealismtto the ordin- ary work of the world, and this is one of the greatest needs of the present day. The work of the ordinary man is long and so exhausting that he has little time to think of any idealism in connection with it. This leads at once to the first great problem of modern democracy, how to get a fair living by reason- able hours of work, leaving enough leisure for both childhood and manhood. The second pro- blem, as Prof. Commons indicates, is education —the use of leisure. "Leisure is opportunity. It may be used or abused. What kind of educa- tion is called for? It is that which will develop the idealism of work—now instinctive, but too often suppressed. The ethical ideal of work is service to others: the esthetic ideal i a perfect product." The "idealism of work," as Prof. Commons conceives it may be too much to look for at present, but we feel sure that it is only on the lines that he lays down that it is to be attained.

One of the most valuable of the articles in this book is that on " American Shoemakers, 1648-1895." .Prof. Commons gives us a most in- teresting account of the efforts of the varibus Shoemakers' Unions in America to secure better wages. He shows that in the boot and shoe trade the line of development has been in the extension of the market, and in this develop- ment the merchant is the leading figure. " Throughout the course of industrial evolu- tion," says Prof. Commons, "the part played by the merchant stands out as the determining factor. The key to the situation is at tll times the price—bargain. It is the merchant who controls both capital and labour. If the mer- chant has a market he can secure capital. Even the modern 'manufacturer' is first of all the merchant. The conflict of papital and labour' is a conflict of market and labour, of merchant and wage-earner, of prices and wages." Prof. Commons' analysis of the history of the American shoe trade is a Masterly piece of work, and will be of the greatest interest to economists generally. His account of the. "Wis- cousin Industrial Commission " shows what some of the American States are doing for the betterment of labour conditions. This commis- sion has enormous powers, but, instead of irri- tating employers and employes by its use of these powers, it has gained the confidence of both with the result that they are co-operating in order to obtain a wise administration of the

It is satisfactory to find that Prof. Com- mons is an enthusiast for industrial education, and after outlining a policy, he says—and his words are no exaggeration—" It reaches into almost every workshop and every home in the State. It goes to the very sources of prosperity and poverty. No greater undertaking could be espoused by a democratic people. No other possesses greater promise of usefulness. Failures here and there will occur, but successes here and there will confute them. So important and vital is the movement that the failures must be promptly corrected and the successes be made universal. Then we maysexpect that industrial education will be accepted and enlarged; that it will contribute a decisive share toward, the reduction of dependency, and tho-''elevation of independence." Prof. Commons discusses a host of inter- esting and important subjects connected with labour, and always in the same hopeful and inspiring manner. His book is valuable as a contribution to current labour controversies, and, dealing as it does with American condi- tions and offering American solutions, it may be confidently recommended. to all who are con- cerned in labour matters, and who wish to see what the most progressive nation in the modern world is doing to meet the new demands and the new conditions of labour.

div.head: MR. BIRRELL'S GHOST STORY.
div.p: MR. BIRRELL'S GHOST STORY.

Mr. Birrell has told a ghost story. In refer- ring to a recent speech,by Dr. Silvanus Thomp- son on the importance of science, Mr. Birrell said: I don't know, My Lord Mayor, whether YOU ever had bad dreams, but I have been haunted ever since I was almost a boy by the constant repetition of one and the same dream. It comes to me again and again. It is this. I dream I am walking about somewhere in some plain or desert, and I suddenly encounter the agitated ghost of Sir Isaac Newton. He ap- proaches me, his eyes almost starting out of his head; he tells me who he is, and how ignorant he is of all that has happened in the world of science since he left. "Now," he says, " I want you to tell me in a few words, for I have only a quarter of an hour left, all that has happened to the race; the progress. How is it? I know what it was when I left it. What is it now?" My heart sinks, and, covered with confusion, I stumble, I stutter, I stammer, I become more i and more involved, my gnorance becomes more and more apparent, and at last the unhappy ghost, throwing up his hands, leaves me with dismay. That dream constantly comes to me. The only difference is that the moment the un- happy Sir Isaac Newton sees me now he says,l "Oh, that old ignoramus," and departs.

div.head: WHERE TO SPEND A BREEZY GOLFING
div.p: WHERE TO SPEND A BREEZY GOLFING
HOLIDAY DURING EASTER. i -

On the sunny healthy shores of the Belgium North Sea coast lies the golfer's ideal resort. Amidst the softly undulating sand dunes he can enjoy himself to his heart's content on what is admitted to be one of the finest 18 hole courses on the Continent, with plenty of natural hazards and the invigorating sea breezes over all. A second golf course is in course of con- struction, and will he ready for play in the summer of 1915. Le Zoute-Knocke is also n great favourite with flue lovers of the game on account of the quiet restful stillness that broods over everytbiog, broken only by the soft lulling murmur of the waves as they sluggishly roll up the wide sandy beach, so beloved of the chil- dren. A recent discovery has added an additional charm to the place. A natural Thermal spring has come to light, to freshen the tired visitor with its cooling draughts. In short, to the over- worked city man, to the jaded politician, to every one who feels the need of shaking off winter's load of cares and responsibility, this spot appeals particularly, for here he finds the complete rest, combined with the exercise his tired system is in need of, to brace him up for another bout of strenuous activity. CHAS. KNOTT.

Whilst the resat of the ballot of Accrington trade unionists on the proposed holiday changes has not yet been officially announced, the figures as to the members of the Weavers' Asso- ciation have been completed, and it is clear that there is an overwhelming majority in favour of altering the holiday date.

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.

PREVENTION OF CRUELTY TO PIANOS. If I were desirous of adding another to the numerous leagues which are founded to enable faddists to convert other faddists to the views which they already hold, I should certainly start a "Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Pianos." Considered as a mere receptacle for rugs, flower-vases and photograph-frames, the efficacy of the drawing-room piano would be improved by exchanging the keyboard for a writing desk, and in many households this plan would save the expense of having the piano opened onee a year by a tuner. But if it is ever used the results are frequently pitiable. . . But in recent years a new influence has been gradually making itself felt, which bids fair to obviate the need of a Society. for the Preven- tion of Cruelty to Pianos. The pneumatic piano-player with its library of perforated rolls, has had to encounter the opposition of many sceptics, but it is slowly and surely finding its way into our midst, and giving people a love of music and an interest in their pianos which they never previously possessed. . . . The success of the pneumatic player is largely due to the great quantity of the best music which has been published for its libraries; but an equally important feature is that, while accu- rately rendering the notes, it leaves the expres- sion; and interpretation very largely under the individual control of the " player-pianist." Listening to concerts can never give the same pleasure that an enthusiast obtains by playing the compositions himself when he likes and adapting his interpretation to his particular frame of mind. The mere rhythm of music stimulates in many people a keen desire to beat time; and the pedals and levers of the player respond to this instinctive tendency by giving greatly improved interpretation. The makers advertise that you can learn to play in half an hour, but they carefully omit to say that a piano-player places everyone in a position to begin to learn the art of playing the piano, that a very little time and trouble brings forth rich fruit in the greatly enhanced pleasure and satis- faction afforded by the music, and that it is possible to go on for years always increasing one's powers of interpretation and one's appli- cation of these powers to particular composi- tions.—From "The Piano and its Players." by Professor G. H. Bryan, F.R.S., in the "Corn- hill Magazine."

div.head: MODEIIN MEXICO.
div.p: MODEIIN MEXICO.

"Modern Mexico," by R. J. Mac Hugh, is an excellent book on Mexico, in which he sketches the history of ancient and modern Mexico, and deals fully with Mexican characteristics and politics, with present conditions, and with the resources and industries of the country. It is with the question of her relations with the United States that, at the moment, most people are concerned, and Mr. Mad-high has written with care on this subject. Long before the present trouble broke out one of the highest authorities on Latin-America wrote that the national transformation of Mexico was the work of the magnates of Wall-street, and that-Mexico was becoming a zone of influence for the United , States. To the eye of this close observer the "Yankee peril" was the one disturbing feature of the long period of Diaz's rule. There are people in this country who think that because the United States in 1847 did not meet with serious opposition in Mexico, the work of an American invader now would not be heavy. But the French with their expedition, and their huge army, found the Mexicans too much for them, and Mr. Mat:Hugh, who knows the Mexican soldier of to-day—and who .sees his weaknesses—takes 110 light view of the troubles in store for any invading army. The United States is marking time; but nothing has yet occurred to confirm the far too sanguine views' expressed by President Wilson last summer: It is pleasant to' turn from tales of past wars and 'future troubles. to Mr. Mac Hugh's account of the enormous resources of Mexico, and to read what he says of her excellent climate and fruitful soil. All that is required, in his opinion, to make Mexico one of the richest and most prosperous countries of the world is stable government and adequate protection for the en- terprises financed by foreign capital. There are glowing accounts of oil still waiting to be tapped, and, in passing, we note the remarkable position of Great Britain in the matter of , Mexican railways—England being first and the rest of the globe nowhere.

div.head: PRIMITIVE BAKONGO.
div.p: THE PRIMITIVE BAKONGO.

"Among the Primitive Bakongo," by John H. Weeks,' a record of thirty years spent among the Bakongo and other tribes in Equatorial Africa, is a companion volume to his book en- titled "Among Congo • Cannibals." The Bakongo may truly be described as a peculiar people. Uncontrolled passions and lax princi- ples are among their characteristics. Mr. Weeks knew Dons Pedro V. (he is dead now), their king, who stood 6ft. 4in, and was 60in. round the waist. When the author arrived in San Salvador, the capital of the kingdom of Kongo, in 1882, the king sent him a pig. One day Mr. Weeks sounded him on the subject of a little present. A shirt or two, strong, was the king's choice, and he gave an old one for purposes of measurement. A good needleman he was, and his twenty-five wives clever farmers. The chil- dren of your maternal uncle are spoken of as yours in the quaint land Over which the jolly Dom Pedro reigned for thirty-two years, and you are spoken of as their father; but the chil- dren of your maternal aunts,- no matter how old you are or young they may be, regard you as their child. Sometimes men drink the blood and eat the livers of their victims in a fight. They think that on sneezing the spirit leaves the body. So when a person sneezes, another sitting by says, "Come back quickly," and when a baby sneezes the mother calls out, "Come back quickly." The status of the departed in the next world depends on the family burying him grandly, which means plenty of gun-firing, shouting, trlimpet-blowing, and women wailing. When a. person dies it is generally believed his spirit goes to reside in a great mysterious forest. Mr. Weeks never found an atheist among them, but their theism is very hazy "The name for a Supreme Being (Nzamhi) is known all over the Lower Congo, and, indeed, among all the tribes throughout the watershed of the Congo River; but the knowledge Con- cerning him is very vague. He is regarded as the principal Aentor of the world and all living • creatures; and it is thought that after His work of creation He withdrew Himself, and, since then, He has taken little, if any, further interest in the world and its inhabitants. Ile is spoken of among the natives as being strong, rich and good—so good that He will not hurt them, hence no sacrifices are offered to Him, no prayers to Him ever pass their lips, and they never worship Him. As the Supreme One, He is very remote from them, unconcerned in their welfare, and harmless, therefore they consider there is no need for them to trouble about Him."

Mr. Weeks' former volume dealt with a river- line tribe on the Upper Congo; the present one reflects the mind of the Lower Congo native.' Common to both is the author's conviction that . polygamous marriages are not happy. For one happy union, lie says, there are ninety-nine un- happy ones. ,ITe is even firmer in his views here that polygamy makes neither for morality nor large families.

OUR PRIZE WINNERS. My dear Children,— The entries for our competition were not so numerous as I expOcted, still some good and interesting essays were sent in. As the space is required for the publication of your essays I shall say no more at present than to announce that the prize winners are: BICATRICII MARSHALL, 75, Folly-lane. MABEL 4. la EENHALGII, 25„ Dixon-street. Book prizes will be sent to our competition winners in the course of next week. Your loving UNCLE JACK.
IN PLACE OF MOTHER.
Dear Uncle Jack,—

This is what I should like to do in my Easter holidays. My mother is going to Scot- land for the week-end, so I should very much like to take her place at home, as mother, and why I should like to do so is because I could look after my father and have his meals ready for him, and clean the floors and do the shop- ping. Look how nice that would be to think I was clever to take mother's place, and for her to think she had got such a clever little girl. I am nearly ten years old now, and I am think- ing I ought to do something to help mother. Now I will close, with best love from your loving niece, 75, Folly-lane.
BEATRICE MARSUALL.
LOVER OF THE COUNTRYSIDE.

Dear Uncle Jack,!--- During the Easter holidays I should like to spend a week in the country. I should like to see the trees just beginning to bud, and hear the birds singing their morning songs. I should also like to see the flowers beginning to show forth their beautifully coloured petals. I should be in my glory if I was going to the country, because there the air is pure, and it would be quite a change from the dirty smoky town, and the noise of the busy factories and workshops.— Your loving niece,
IiABEL GREENIIALGII.
25, Diion-street.
A COUNTRY RAMBLE.
Dear Uncle Jack,—

I think you have given us a very nice subject for a competition this time. I intend going into the country during my holidays and gather some of the wild flowers which are just beginning to grow. We sometimes get a "Nature study" lesson in schopl.j The teacher makes it very, interesting and Mike it, very much. I think that by gathering some of the flowers teacher has told us about I may learn something new about the shades and shapes. We have painting every Tuesday, and we paint the different kinds of flowers.—l remain, your loving niece. 125, Wellfleld-street.
J ESSIE 11. MUIR.
TO KEEP A SHOP.

Dear Uncle Jack.— I was so pleased to hear and to see for myself that another competition was going to take place, the subject being " What we will like to do durhig the Easter holidays." I think I should like to go to Manchester, either to mind the shop which Aunty keeps, or else keep baby in a good mood and so help Aunty in some way.—l am, your sincere niece, 68, Steel-street.
LUCY CARET.

div.head: Bi-Gentenary of a Familiar and Valuable
div.p: The Bi-Gentenary of a Familiar and Valuable
Scientific instrument.

div.head: FAMOUS MEN WHO HAVE LABOURED UPON THE THERMOMETER.
div.p: FAMOUS MEN WHO HAVE LABOURED UPON THE THERMOMETER.
BY ARTHUR M

It is just two centuries since the thermometer, as we now have it, took shape and began to fulfil an everyday function. The anniversary merits some notice if only for the opportunity it gives of recording the various stages by which it reached usefulness, and the names of the cele- brated and patient scientists who laboured for its perfection. Its inventor was Galileo Galilei, the famous Italian, whose genius gave us the telescope, the pendulum and 'a proportional compass. A native of Pisa, where he was born in 1564, Galileo became in 1592 tutor in mathematics at Padua, and there laboured until 1610. .It was here that his telescope took shape, and it was here also that the first crude thermometer was made. THE FIRST THERMOMETER.

Someone who saw it and was interested, wrote a brief • description: "He took a glass vessel about the size of a hen's egg, fitted to a tube the size of a straw and about two spans long; he heated the glass bulb in his hands, and turned the glass upside down, so that the tube dipped in water held in another vessel; as soon as the bulb cooled down, the water rose in the tube to the height of a span above the level of that in the vessel." Wine was substituted for water as being more easily seen in the tube, but the instrument could not have been very useful as a measure of heat and cold. No two read alike, and, worst of all, as there was no known method of mark- ing the scale which was used, the readings were of no practical value. Ingenious Italians took up the idea of a heat and cold indicator, and working upon Galileo's tube, made several small advances towards a useful instrument. There were no patent laws then, and the only limitation was the cost of ex- periments and the prejudices against innova- tions. - About the year 1634 there lived in the South of France an obscure physician, Jean Rey, who made two discoveries of real value, lie was far in advance of the thinkers of his day, and his accomplishments, though of momentous value, were not thoi understood or appreciated. The first was that lead and tin, when calcined, increase in weight; but much more valuable was the discovery and application of the fact that liquids expand and contract under the influence of beat and cold. He was familiar with the thermometer of Galileo. Indeed, he made use of it in the treatment of fever patients who came under his care. His instrument had but one bulb filled with water, and the tube was open at the top—a very unsatisfactory ther- mometer, but still one which, after a dull fashion, would indicate changes of temperature. Nine years later a priest named Athanasius Kircher mentions the use of mercury as the fluid used in bulb and tube. This is an interesting step forward, but he does not say who was the first to use it, nor does lie make any reference to a scale. up to this time, 1643; everyone had made Ids own scale. Naturally there was no uniformity about the instruments, and they were regarded as so many curiosities only, and not of any real value to mankind.

div.head: LARGE STEP FORWARD.
div.p: A LARGE STEP FORWARD.

The 'next step in the evolution- Of the ther- momeier was made by Ferdinand 11., Grand Duke of Tuscany, in 1654. lie was a patron of literature and science and devoted much time to practical research. - Taking a thermometer, the bulb of which was at the lower end, he filled • it with coloured alcohol, and after heating the alcohol, sealed the tube herthetically by melting the glass tip. The closed instrument was then graduated by degrees marked on the stem. This was the first instrument which was independent of atmospheric action, Of • course, there were difficulties. The in- equalities in the bore of the tubes and the vary- ing scale made accuracy very uncertain. As yet scientists had not agreed on any particular instrument as the standard, although they all could see that some method of arriving at a common scale was necessary. All sorts of mark- ing were arranged, some absurd, some imprac- tical, some useful, all upheld ,for a time and then dropped. Some turious instruments were made. Otto de Guericke, burgomaster of Madgeburg, made one which was twenty feet long and gorgeous with blue paint and gilt 'stars. It consisted of a large globe fastened to a tube, both of copper. The tube was bent upon itself to form a veryl narrow U, in which was placed the requisite amount of alcohol. One arm of the U was shorter than the other and open at the top. On the liquid was a float, to which was attached a cord passing over a pulley. At the other end of this cord was hung a gilt angel, its finger point- ing to a scale on which the degrees were painted.

div.head: BRITISH EXPERIMENTS.
div.p: BRITISH EXPERIMENTS.

Sir Isaac Newton, interested in the ther- mometer as in everything scientific, made a scale, but it did not find acceptance. lie also Proposed to use " lint seed" oil instead of alcohol. His standards of heat and cold, it may be mentioned, were the heat of the human body and melting snow. A British experimenter, Robert Book, settled the standard of cold. He placed zero at the point where the mercury stood when the bulb was placed in freezing distilled water. Distilled water, it had been noticed, always freezes at the same temperature, while other water might contain ingredients which would hinder or assist the process.

A standard for heat was still requisite. This was first used and given to the world by a Dutch mathematician, Christian Huyghens. He took the point at which distilled water began to boil. The puzzle then presented itself how to divide the scale between those two extremes. At first the division Was into eight parts, but this was unsatisfactory. Some divided the space 'into inches and tenths of inches, but this marking was not accepted by all.

div.head: FAHRENHEIT.
div.p: FAHRENHEIT.

Then came Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit. Bornl in 1686, a German physicist, he hied in England and Holland studying natural physics and the manufacture of meteorological instruments. In 1714 he brought to the Chancellor of the University of Halle two thermometers which agreed so perfectly in registering temperatures that they were considered marvels. Some of his success, possibly the greater part of it, was due to his skill in the working of the glass, a branch of labour in which lie had studied and experimented. He combined with his knowledge and powers of original thought, a good business instinct, and, for commercial reasons, kept his, methods secret for eighteen years. Ho reached the height of his fame and ' Prosperity between the years 1715 and 1725. His thermometer; famed for its splendid accuracy, came into use the world over, and the standard he had adopted took a place which it has ever since retained. We still speak of so many de- grees " Fahrenheit" nor does it seem likely that the passing of the years will lessen the popularity of his standard.
THE DIFFERENT STANDARDS. Lest the thermometer standards should pre- sent eowe iiiyetery it way be well t 9 describe

div.head: IUNFIELD.
div.p: IUNFIELD.

and compare them. We take first that of Fahrenheit. It runs from zero to 96 degrees. Zero is found by immersing the bulb in a mix- ture of ice, water and sal-ammoniac in a thick fluid state. The freezing point is determined by placing the bulb in ice and water only, and is marked 32 degrees. Blood heat is found by Placing the bulb in the mouth of a healthy man and keeping it there till it acquires the tem- perature of the body. This is marked 96 de- grees. Boiling point is marked 212. Another standard was made by a French scholar, De Reaumur, and has only two fixed points—the freezing of water and the boiling point of water, between which it is divided into eighty parts. Of this scale we see and hear little in modern England.

div.head: MYSTERY OF CENTIGRADE AND FAHRENHEIT.
div.p: THE MYSTERY OF CENTIGRADE AND FAHRENHEIT.

A third scale, and one still very widely used, was invented by a Swede named Celsius,. but, while the other two are named from their in- ventors, this is named from the method of mark- ing. It is called centigrade, and has 100 marks or degrees. In this, zero is placed at the freez- ing point of water, and the boiling point is marked 100 degrees. It is used by men of science the world over, and seems likely to be- come the universal scale; superseding Fahren- heit and all the rest.

In reading of a temperature given in a scale with which one is unfamiliar, some confusion arises, and it is convenient to know how to com- pare the two. To reduce.the reading of a centi- grade to a Fahrenheit scale, subtract ten de- grees from the given temperature, from this remainder subtract one-tenth of itself, double the result and add fifty degrees to the answer. To reduce a Fahrenheit reading to centigrade, subtract 50 degrees from the given temperature, divide the remainder by two, multiply this quotient by ten, divide the product by nine, and add ten degrees to the last quotient. Another method less open to the objection of brain fag is to pay sixpence for ft thermometer which is marked Centigrade on one side and Fahrenheit on the other.

div.head: WHEN MERCURY BOILS.
div.p: WHEN MERCURY BOILS.

There are many points of interest in the measuring of beat and cold. The ordinary in- strument contains either mercury or alcohol. Mercury will record up to 660 degrees. At this Point it boils. But the man of science is not at thv end of his resources. After this he can use metals, the expansion and contraction of which are known. For very low temperatures alcohol is used. Cheap thermometers are seldom correct. Scarcely any two read alike. The making of a good one requires a specially prepared and costly quality of glass and great care in making the tube. When they are sorted and tested many tubes must be rejected as imperfect. The greatest care must be taken in pouring in the mercury and carefully sealing it, in order to ekclude all air, and the scale must be accurately engraved on the glass of the tube. All this re- quires workmanship of the highest order, as well as time and patience.

The finest thermometer in the world—so at least the Americans bOast—is at the Hopkins University of Baltimore. It is a rare piece of work, seemingly perfect, and cost £2,200. So fine are the gradations on the glass that they must be magnified in order to be read. . _

This chapter might be lengthened by a description of the clinical, the submarine and the earth thermometer, but we only set our- selves to commemorate Fahrenheit, and perhaps we have covered the points of popular interest. In course of a generation or so there will be other chapters to add to the story of the ther- mometer. In the matter, for instance, of the fixing of zero, much experiment is being made. Our best thinkers are coming to the opinion that there is an absolute zero at which all matter becomes inert; a zero, needless to say, much lower than anything Fahrenheit ever dreamed of.. Professor Dewar's experiments with hydro- gen will be remembered as one branch in n wide and interesting inquiry. Some day the zero point will be changed and its depth will give surprise to ordinary folks. If it is not too late we had better add that the word " thermometer" comes from thermo, heat, and meter, measure.

MANUFACTURE OF OPTICAL GLASS. Optical glass, according to "Engineering," is melted in pots, of a capacity of about Newt., and resembling in shape an " Odol" bottle. These pots take from one to three years to finish unburnt before they are slowly heated for ten days, to drive out the water of combination; the furnace in which this heating is done con- tains only one pot. The finished pot passes into the glass furnace, in which 'again one pot only • stands, supported on a brick pillar.. The front of this furnace is bricked up until red heat is reached. Then broken glass of the desired com- position is introduced into the pot to produce glazure or enamel on the inner surface, a pro- cess which takes two or three hours. The proper mixture of material is then gradually put into the pot, and high heat is kept up for perhaps eight hours, to drive out the gas bubbles. This is one, of the most delicate in the many important operations; the tempera- ture has carefully to be regulated. If too low, bubbles remain in the glass; if too high, the .pot is attacked, and the whole glass is hopelessly spoiled, the ,clay taken up from the pot form- ing small flakes floating into the melt. Next comes the stirring for a period Up to 15 hours; this is done by an iron rod, so mounted that it can be swept round in a circle. The stirring is very hard work, which the men in front of the furnace cannot stand for more than a few min- utes sometimes. The front of the furnace is then sealed, and the pot allowed to cool for fourteen days; in modern practice the pot is removed into a cooling furnace, so that the other furnace is ready for melting again. Not infre- quently the pot cracks in the upper portion dur- ing the melting. If 2cwt.- of good glass is se- cured out of the Newt. of materials, the ramiu- facturer is well satisfied.

div.head: LONG COUNTRY WALKS.
div.p: LONG COUNTRY WALKS.

Dear Uncle Jack,— You ask me where I should like to go for the Easter holidays and why? Well, I think if the weather should he nice, I would like to go for some long walks in the country, for in spring I think the country is at its very best. Some of my reasons for choosing the country for a holiday are not only is it enjoyable and healthy, but I shall learn a lot about Nature. I shall see the trees beginning to look quito green, and the farmers will be quite busy tilling the land and sowing the seeds. The birds will be chattering along the hedgerows and building their little nests. Then there will be the cows in the fields, and at milking time, if I get an op- portunity, I shall try to see the dairykaaid milking them. So I am very sure that if it is nice weather I shall have a very enjoyable holi- day, and one that will give me something to think about when it is over.—Your loving niece, NEL= MASOX. 174, Longford-street.

div.head: GRAND PARTY.
div.p: A GRAND PARTY.

Miss Nellie M'Carty gave a grand party.' And who do you think were there? Marigold Mary and Viscount Canary, And Violet fragrant and fair; Saucy Miss Buttercup and Johnny Jump-111) A boat-load from over the bay. They danced to a fiddle with " hands down the middle," And went to bed sick the next day

div.head: HOW RAIN IS MADE.
div.p: HOW RAIN IS MADE.

Rain falls from the clouds, which get the moisture in them chiefly from the sea. Heat causes some of the water in the sea to rise like steam, but invisibly, and to form clouds, and, when the clouds are cooled, this moisture falls 'as rain. The rain sinks into the earth and forms springs, which in their turn give rise to brooks and rivers. These brooks and rivers take the water back to the sea, from which it at first came.

I Rain ia often disagreeable, especially when it spoils pleasure-parties, but on tho other hand it does much good. It helps plants to grow, and gives animals water to drink. Snow and hail are frozen rain, aml do very much the 15ame work as rain.

div.head: WOMAN'S WORLD.
div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.
CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MAJOR lE.

When the King and Queen visit Paris to- wards the end of the month, they will be accompanied by Sir Edward Grey, the Duchess of Devonshire, and a large -suite. If nothing untoward interferes with the projected arrange- ments, trie visit will extend over four days. It is quite a new departure for the British Foreign Secretary officially' to accompany the King on such an occasion, and his presence will un- doubtedly add to the diplomatic importance of the Royal journey. All that is to happen, and to be said, and all the ceremonies to be observed, are the subject of previous agreement with the French Government, and the whole programme is set out in the minutest detail in a document which will goven every movement and action of the King and Queen, whilst their Majesties are in France. It is thus already pre-ordained what the President will say at the banquet at the Elysee, and what the King will say in reply. The terms of all addresses and replies are settled beforehand, as are also the uniforms to be worn, the honours, courtesies and recognitions to be given and received; so carefully prepared are the precautions that no faux pas should occur. Short Luncheons.

The desire to shorten the time formerly given to luncheon and dinner, is as apparent in French as in English society. The meal com- posed of two dishes is now finding favour in the French capital, even for luncheon—the chief meal of the day—since fashionable men and women have contented themselves with a light evening repast. In fact, it would seem that the example of the middle classes and the peasants is being followed by French leaders of fashion in this matter. The bourgeois and the country folk of the labouring classes take a solid meal at noon, the evening repast consisting mainly of soup, and a vegetable, followed by cheese.

• The Heir of Brunswick. Great have been the rejoicings in Germany over the birth of an heir to the House of Bruns- wick. The infant is a Prince of Great Britain and Ireland, on his fatheA's side, and a great grandson of the Empress Frederick, who was Princess Royal of Great Britain and Ireland, and the eldest child of Queen Victoria. The infant's birth was officially certified by a repre- sentative of King George, who travelled to Brunswick for the purpose. The Duchess of Brunswick was eighteen when she last visited this country. It is said that since her marriage she has gained in dignity and good looks. The impression she made on the occasion of her visit here was most favourable, and she is as popular in the Duchy as she is beloved throughout Ger- many. Woman's Church.

The Women's Church at Wallasey, which is to have an ordained congregatiolialist woman minister, bas had sev,eral forerunners in America, and a woman who can preach with power invariably succeeds in making an impres- Sion on working class congregations. Much more so than many eloquent ministers, who are the exception rather . than the rule in the churches, and one reason why so many places of worship are habitually half empty is the preacliing of indifferent sermons. 7Sermons can be bought, like most other things, and although the Bishops condemn the practice of preaching second-hiind sermons, these are often much more effective than original sterile productions.

But what on earth could Walter Graydon see in Mabel Forrester? And Mabel must be a deceitful little minx, for everybody, had been thinking she hoped one day to be .Mrs. Warne- Green. Poor Jimmy Warne-Green would be cut up. Anyway, she hoped that Mabel and—and Mr. Graydon wo ild be very happy. A curate, after all, was not such a mighty person. Than she came back to the other, thought that man was base. It was time—wine(' woman— shackles—break chains . And Walter Gray- don was the very worst of base men: All the mothers of Disdale rose and bobbed a curtsey as Miss Winifred Wilson entered the sehrolrcom where the fortnightly Dorcas meet- ing was held. "Now, don't let me interrupt," said the girl. "I've come to help." She took off her hat and balanced it on a blue globe of the world. "What can I do?" "Well, miss," said Mrs. Sawley, a lady of great girth, the wife of the grocer at the top of the street; " it's not—not for the likes o' you ter bother about scwin'. " "Oh, but a woman ought to be useful." "That's 50, miss. As I was sayin' this very mornin' ter our Sally Jane, tit' Lord 'elps 'cm as helps theirselves. An' my man 'e says ter me —an' I'm a good wife, miss, an' allus 'ears what my man says, fur I'm not one o' them there women as is abs a-naggin' on their—" "Yes," said Winifred, picking up a stray pil- low-case and marvelling at what point the hem- ming commenced. Dangerous Colour Wigs. • Various experiments have been tried in Paris to " fashionise " the colour wig, and this latest " elegance " has made various flitting appear- ances on the London stage. It is not a mode that would appeal to any but those women who are always ready to follow freak fashions, and the question of expense alone would prevent the majority of women from adopting it as part and parcel of their everyday attire, but those who are not deterred by these considerations should heed the warnings of the doctors, who assert that plague, leprosy, and other dangers May lurk in colour wigs. Oriental human hair is largely used in these productions, and cases of illness have been traced both to the dyes used, and the fact that the cleansing processes the hair undergoes may not in every case remove the danger of it conveying loathsome diseases. Fashionable Embroideries.

Those women who are adepts in the art of embroidery will find their skill of real value now, for hand-worked decorations are to be the rule4his summer.. An,exclusive charm may be given to a simple lingerie, muslin, or silk blouse, if adorned with Irish satin stitch, or fin- ished with collar and cuffs in broderie anglaise, or Punto-tagliato. Small floral designs, tiny spots, and diamonds,Vorked in fine embroidery cotton, floss silk; or any of the new threads, are seen side by side with the boldest patterns, and these are 'worked on all kinds of fabrics. In white and black these embroideries are exceed- ingly smart. There was a glow of colour about Winifred's face, not entirely due to the breath of summer, that drowsy afternoon. Somebody had been telling her something. Of course it didn't affect her. She didn't care two pins if the Rev. Walter Graydon married Mabel Forrester or half a down Mabel Forresters. Why ehould she? So she took her big sun hat, with the string of wild king-cups chasing round the brim, and savagely drove two long pins right through it. But she wasn't angry. Doris, who had imparted the news, was lying back in a camp chair beneath the verandah, playing with the tendrils of a variegated creeper. .
"Don't you think it horrid of him?" she suggested. • •
"I don't think anything about it." And Wini- fred stabbed a king-cup to the heart with one of those murderous pins. "And after his being so awfully nice," added Doris.

"1 don't—don't think Mr. Graydon has been any nicer than—than a curate generally iy,." Winifred took hold of a spray of the clinging creeper, gave it a tug, and fastened a few of the rich coloured leaves at tb-D waist of her muslin frock.
"But I thought that you—that is. that ho----"

"Then you're a silly girl." She stood for a moment ori the edge of the verandah, with the light playing about her dark hair, and the colour dancing on her sun-kissed cheeks. She looked idly across the lawn and watched the fluttering o the noisy crows in the tree-tops of the plants tion beyond. "1 think I'll go down to the school," she said. "The school!" repeated Doris.

Summer Washing Frocks.

Washing materials have now made their ap- pearance, and are wider in range and more fascinating than ever. For children's dresses the choice is almost infinite in variety. Per- taps cotton crepe, by reason of its many virtues, must be given pride of place in this connection. The plain crepes are made in every imaginable charming shade, and .the figured varieties are delightful in pattern and equally beautiful in colouring. As a background for the many different embroideries thAt will be used as lav- ishly on the dresses and other garments of chil- dren as on those of their elders, nothing could he better than a new cotton voile. It is par- ticularly filmy in appearance, and very fine in make. A heavy conventional pattern suits it admirably, whilst bold designs of broderie anglaise are most effective also. A Djibbah for a little girl, in dark blue crash, was worked round the neck and on the wide sleeves in a soft durable cotton thread. The colours were bright orange, yellow, blue, red, and green, beautifully combined, and the effect was most pleasing. _

New Leather for Shoes. The latest living creatures to be included in the list of those that contribute to our ward, robes are the frog and the shark. In America the skin of the former has been carefully pre- pared and tanned and the leather derived from it is described as beautifully marked and very pliable. Shark skin is handsome, too, also dur- able, and easily worked, and there is a certain demand for both these products, more particu- larly for the freakish type of shoes. .

MEMS. FOR MOTHERS.
The Small Child's Feet.

The little feet of children often do not receive the attention they deserve. They are in waking hours almost always on their feet, and therefore too great care cannot be taken to avoid discom- fort or pain. The feet and legs should be regularly washed before going to bed, and special notice taken of probable ingrowing nails, hardened skin, or an incipient corn. Socks and stockings should have no seam on the foot, neither should there be a darn, unless it is very skilfully done. home-knitted foot- wear is best for young children, but the wool should not be too thick or coarse.
Fine, pure wool is quite as warm as a thick, heavy make. Never let the stocking, be too short in the foot; allow plenty of space, and buy shoes accordingly.

div.head: IN DAMP WEATHER.
div.p: IN DAMP WEATHER.

Special care is necessary in wet -weather to avoid damp feet. At the first sign of a thin, worn sole, the shoes should be repaired. 11W). bers (or goloshes) are very cheap, and are made in all sizes. A thin pair of shoes may be worn with perfect safety if rubbers are worn over them.

Children's shoes should be light in weight; and they must be wide, and not tightly laced or buttoned. If they are wet, dry them slowly and thoroughly. Do not put 'them on the oven, or the hot plate; this will'quickly ruin them. The best plan is to tie them together by the laces, or button them together, and hang them either from the gas piPe in the centre of the mantelpiece, or on a screw hook. The leat from the range will dry the leather slowly. A child must not go to bed with cold feet. A hot water bottle will be a great comfort; or, failing this, a warm flat-iron may be wrapped in a piece of flannel and put into the bed.

div.head: COOKERY CORNER.
div.p: COOKERY CORNER.
Articles Now In Season.

Fruits in season in April are :—Apples, bananas, figs, grapes, lemons, melons (Spanish, water), oranges, prunes, rhubarb. Vegetables.—Broccoli, cabbage, carrots, horse- radish, lettuce, leeks, onions, parsnips, potatoes, ditto new, spinach. Fish.—Bloaters, cod, crabs, dory, flounders, lobsters, mackerel, salmon, shrimps, skate, smelts, sprats, trout, turbot, whitebait. Poultry.—Chickens, ducklings, pigeons, quails, teal.
Meat.—Beef, lamb, mutton, pork, veal.
BOILED LEG OF LAMB.

Try this recipe. Put the lamb, which will be a small joint, into a large saucepan, with water to just cover it; let it boil up once, add a teacup of cold water, and then allow it to simmer, first removing the scum which the cold water has caused to be thrown up. Continue simmering until the lamb is about half-cooked, then add a teaspoonful of Salt, and cook again until done. Boil apart some new young carrots, garnish the lamb with these, serve with caper sauce.

div.head: NICE BREAKFAST DISH.
div.p: A NICE BREAKFAST DISH.

Instead of the usual dish of ham and eggs, try this recipe: Fry some rashers of bacon, and when done keep them hot in the oven or before the fire. Have ready some cold potatoes left from the previous day, cut these up, rather roughly, and fry them in the fat in the pan left from the bacon. Let them get crisp and brown; just before taking them up sprinkle over them some pepper, le,mon juice, and finely minced parsley: Serve them on a hot dish with the bacon on the top.

CHEESE AND SEMOLINA. This is a very tasty and nourishing dish with- out meats. Grate four ounces of cheese, bring half a pint of milk to the boil and stir in one ounce of semolina, stir over the fire till it thickens, remove from the fire and stir in the grated cheese, a pinch of cayenne, and the yolks of two eggs well beaten, also the whites beaten to 'a stiff froth; add salt to taste, and stir into a buttered pie-dish and bake gently for about half hour, or steam in a greased purlding basin for 40 minutes. Serve with friend tomatoes.

div.head: HEALTH HINTS.
div.p: HEALTH HINTS.
A Doctor's Recommendations'.

Dr. David Paulson, writing in that bright little Magazine " Good Health" for April, gives the following useful hints : Do not eat a morsel between meals. If you keep your digestive mill constantly grinding it will soon wear out. Food must be well relished in order to be well digested.
Many dietetic errors are due to a low concep- tion of eating. Avoid iced foods and drinks. Do not make a cold storage plant out of your stomach.
Fletcher has well said : "Do not eat when you are mad, or bad, or sad; only when you are glad."
- It is not only necessary to bring a good appe- tite to the table, but it is ulso important to come with a good state of mind.
Remember your teeth are put in your mouth, not in your stomach; so the first thing to do is to chew. Chew for your life. If you chew long you will live long; and you will not need to eat so much.

If you taste your food before you swallow it, you will not have to taste it afterwards. Eat your bread with gladness. "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine." When one eats in an ugly, dissatisfied, con- temptible, hateful state of mind, he is sinning toward God -and is wronging himself. The great ideal is to continue feeling thankful all through the meal.

div.head: DRUGS, SPICES, AND CONDIMENTS.
div.p: DRUGS, SPICES, AND CONDIMENTS.

Intemperate eating is infinitely more common than intemperance in drinking. Use salt sparingly. Condiments should be wholly discarded, because they irritate the stomach, tending to produce gastric and intes- tinal catarrh.

Tea and coffee are drugs, not foods, and should come from the drug store instead of the kitchen. Avoid mustard, pepper, tind highly-spiced foods that taste hot when they are cold, for they continue being hot after they are swallowed, and even after they are absorbed into the blood. Mustard plasters may proiierly be applied exter- nally, but they should not be used internally. It is because we have so little scientific cookery that so many have to resort to nmstard, pepper, and other fiery condiments and spices. These things that taste hot when they are really cold, that give the palate a twist, also injure the nervous system.

div.p: SMART PEDESTRIANS.
Two Warrington Cracks Run Well ' In the International. \
ANTROBUS FOURTH MAN.

The two Warrington runners who represented England in the Cross-Country International at Chesham, Bucks, on Saturday, did good work, Antrobils especially so, for he finished fourth in a large field of seasoned cracks. Price (Wales), at the start, went into the lead, and at the end of a mile was leading from Ruffen. :(England), Wallach (Scotland), Glover (England), Ryder (Ireland), Murray (Ireland), and the Wilsons (England and Wales) close together. However, when it came to the real cross-country test, Price was found wanting, and he began to tire, and come back to the run- ners when the ploughed land was entered upon. Glover then took the lead, and George Wallach was sticking to him very determinedly, the pair being 20 yards ahead of Ruffell and Antrobus, and the Wilsons next in order. Afterwards Wallach took the lead, with A. H. Nicholls (Southern champion) in close attend- ance, and between this pair a well-contested race ensued to the end. Over the last mile Nicholls made a great effort, and drawing away from his 'opponents, won amidst cheers in 60min. 23 4-ssec., the order of finishing being as fol- lows:

M. S. 1. A. H. Nicholls, England , 6O 23 2. G. C. L. Wallach, Scotland 6O 46 3. E. Glover, England 4. F. Antrobus, England 5. J. Hughes, Ireland 6. J. Wilson, England 7. A. S. Wilson, Wales 8. J. Lindsay, Scotland 9. M. Lalaimode,,Prance 10. C. F. Price, Wales

div.head: LATCHFORD BADLY BEATEJI.
div.p: LATCHFORD BADLY BEATEJI.
110 w the Contest for the Minor Medals is Progressing.
STOCKTON HEATH'S CUP DEFEAT.

div.head: By di Linesman.”
div.p: By di Linesman.”

In the second round of the ,Warrington Minor Medal Competition the ties were played on Saturday,' four games being down for decision. Three were definitely decided, while St. George's Mission and Longford United will have to meet again. The Latchford Works Competition is progres- sing very satisfactorily, and some very keenly- contested games have been witnessed during the week.

duced. Hough was injured and had to retire for a short time, and during his absence the home forwards made an attack on the visitors' goal. Winnington beat Knight with a beauty and equalised the score. The home men con- tinued to play the shady game and several were cautioned by the referee. Millington placed the visitors in front, and at the interval the scores were: Emmanuel, two goals; Acton Village, one. On resuming, the home side showed-much ex- citement and wild kicking. Free-kicks were very frequent. Yoxall, being injured, had to retire, and he waS soon followed by Winnington, the home team thus having their ranks reduced. Acton were penalised. Millington took the kick and Collier saved the shot, but in the next minute Rowe made amends and scored the third goal for the Old Boys. Ward, of the home team, had to be sent off for infringement, and Acton now had only seven players left. Hatton scored again for the Old Boys, and the final was: Emmanuel, four goals; Acton Village, one.

div.head: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. Lostock Gralam v. Latchford. '
div.p: NORTH CHESHIRE LEAGUE. Lostock Gralam v. Latchford. '

The return fixture between-These—Clubs was played on the ground of the former. The home away,yf d. After twelve ollowe and after being. re- pulsed play the home team opened the score, a strong appeal for offside being ignored. The t team were wemreid-fiheal d first pla home team pressed again, but failed to increase their lead, after which the visitors transferred to the opposite end, but could not penetrate thc' home defence. At the interval the soore was one goal to none in favour of the home team. On resuming, the visitors became aggressive, but could not get past the home defence, and from a breakaway the locals increased their lead. Owing to the visitors net being fully represented in their defence, the homesters began to have the best of the exchanges, and further goals were added without the visitors being able to respond. The final result was: Lostock Gralam, 5; Latchford, nil.

div.head: NORTHWICH JUNIOR CUP COMPETITION Semi-final. Stockton Heath Y. Barntan Rovers. _ .
div.p: NORTHWICH JUNIOR CUP COMPETITION Semi-final. Stockton Heath Y. Barntan Rovers. _ .

The semi-final tie between the above clubs was played at Northwich before a very pool number of spectators. Barnton set up a very fast pace, and soon became dangerous near the "Heathens" goal. A penalty was awarded the Rovers for "hands" against Sankey, from which they opened the score. The "Heathens" attacknow took n h o up tte foyers'h e running, g 0 goal, b d madeutw oai n prolonged gto bad marksmanship they failed to score. The Rovers' centre-forward increased the lead with a rattling shot. Half-time: Barnton Rovers, two goals; Stockton Heath, nil. On resuming, play was chiefly in mid-field. Then the "heathens" got into the danger zone, when Stubbs was just wide with a good shot. From the goal-kick the Rovers improved and gained a free-kick in the " Heathens' " half. The Rovers' outside-left centred well in front of goal, and the inside man registered the third goal. The "Heathens" now became more desperate and made strenuous efforts to open their account, when Jones, with an easy open- ing, shot over the bar. The "Heathens" con- tinued to have most of the game, but failed to score. Following a goal-kick, the Rovers took up the running and transferred the scene of action. From a centre near the corner-flag they registered their fourth goal. The "Heathens" were now in a hopeless position and could make no headway against the opposing defence. Time was called with the result Barnton Rovers, four goals; Stockton Heath, nil.

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. Great Sankey v. Weaver Refiners. This postponed fixture between the above clubs was played on the Penketh Recreation Ground. Teams: Great Sankey—Bond; Glover and Stephens; H. Ditchfield, Gardiner and Payne; Darlington, Illidge, J. Ditchfield, Pout. ton and Houghton. Weaver Refiners—Collier; Newton and Woodward; Evans, Newton and Powell; Bayliss, Jones, Wilkinson and Beans. Referee, Mr. S. C. Essenhigh. The visitors only had ten players. J. Ditchfield set the ball rolling, and the opening exchanges were evenly contested. The home team were the first to become dangerous, but were erratic in their final shots. The visitors did not appear able to settle down, and their goal was attacked and Collier had to concede a corner. Houghton placed well in front, where Gardiner missed a splendid opening. This gave the visitors' defence relief, and their forwards took a turn at the home goal, but, owing, to excitement, they allowed several easy chances to go. Poulton now came into collision with one of the visitors, and had to retire for a short time. The inter- val arrived without any score being recorded. In the second half the homesters set up a rare pace and made tracks for the visitors' goal, when the ball was handled in the penalty area. Herbert Ditchfield, taking the kick, regis- tered the first goal. This suee-ss acted as a stimulant to the home team, 'd they were I soon in the visitors' quarters a tin, Gardiner scoring the second goal with a ilne shot. At this point Poulton returned to the field and was loudly cheered, and returned the compliment by scoring the third goal. The visitors at this juncture appeared to be hopelessly beaten, and their goal was subjected to continual bombard- ment. After a grand run on the left Houghton scored the fourth goal, and Illidge added a fifth shortly after. The Sankeyites now eased a little ovsete and allowed the visitors' defence some relief. Later Darlington registered a sixth goal for the lme fi n eßesult:rs,nil. Great Sankey, goals; virrear ers i six

WARRINGTON MINOR MEDAL COMPETI- TION. Vulcan Mission v. Orford St. John's. On the ground of the former. The following players lined up: Vulcan Mission—Dennett; Phythian and Baker; Clarke, Roberts and Littler; Marsh, Cliffe, Rowbottom, plumpton, and Gleave. Orford St. John's—Porber; W. Smith and Harrison; Denny, Stretford and Atherton; Tickle, Meachin, Millward, nankin- son and Smalley. Referee, Mr. J. Smith. Row_ bottom set the ball rolling, and Stretford, with a good kick, set his forwards going, but they were driven back by Phythian. By good combination on the home right the game was carried to the visitors' quarters and •their defence was kept busy for a short time. A goal-kick brought re- lief to the defence, and Meachin and Tickle transferred play to the opposite end. Dennett wasecla)olloerd cluepaornancseevsebryalthteimheosm, eand, backs, toekle closed in, drove past Dennett and registered the first point for the' visitors. The homesters now made tracks for the other goal, and play was chiefly in the strangers' half. The final efforts of the home forwards were very erratic, and an aonfitlie hometlessc goal, the visitors made n and, from a good centre by Smalley, Baker miskicked, and the ball went through Ids own goal. Even play followed, and at half-time the "Saints" were leading by two goals to none. Play became very keen and more even, and each goal was visited, Millward proving a source of trouble to the home backs, who now fell off in their play. Baker again being at fault with mis- kicking, Tickle raced up and beat Dennett with a low shot. This reverse stung the homesters and they played desperately to reduce the arrears, but the visitors: defence proved them- selves equal to the occasion. Result: Orford St. John's,.three goals; Vulcan Mission, nil. Smith, Stretford, Atherton, Millward and Tickle were most prominent for the visitors, and Phythian., Roberts, Cliffe and Plumpton for the home team.

div.head: Acton Village v. Emmanuel Old Boys.
div.p: Acton Village v. Emmanuel Old Boys.

At Acton. In the first minute Millington missed by inches. The visitors, playing very keen, attacked the home goal, and Rowe, gain- ing possession, beat Betley and scored at the end of five minutes' play. Rough tactics were intro-

div.head: St. Barnabas' v. Fairfield .United.
div.p: St. Barnabas' v. Fairfield .United.

_ At Lovely-lane. Shuttleworth started the game, and the visitors' goal was soon in danger, but their backs defended well. Even play fol- lowed, and for a time the half-back lines were most prominent. From a big kick by Spruce, Vernon gained possession, and after eluding the attentions of several opponents he passed to his partner, who opened the score for the home team. This reverse nettled the visitors, and they retaliated. Woodhouse beat the opposing centre-half and worked his way towards the left wing, when he equalised with a good shot No further score was made before the interval, each side having one goal to their credit. After the usual breather the game was re- sumed, and it was soon evident that some of the Players were trying to acquit themselves to the satisfaction of a portion of their supporters than to the merits of the game, and the referee had to caution some of them, as well as some of the spectators. For the next quarter of an houz play was not so keen, until the visitors were awarded a corner. This was well placed, but Spruce got the ball away to Vernon on the left, who raced away, beat several opponents, and scored with a good low shot, the visitors' goals keeper having no chance. Encouraged by this success, St. Barnabas' set up a fierce attack on the United goal, and several easy chances were missed owing to excitement. However, Shuttle- worth put the result beyond doubt when he ob- tained the third goal for the homesters a few minutes before time. Result: St. Barnabas' three goals; Fairfield United, one goal.

St. George's Mission v. Longford United. On the Fairfield ground, with the followinti players: St. George's Mission—Roberts; Tulley and Brown; Goulding, Livesey and E. Marsden; Dunbavin, S. Hands, T. Hands, Thomas, and H. Marsden. Longford United—Barber; Mosley and Holdings; Darbyshire, H. Finch and Lea; Darbyshire, Holloway, Sherratt, Finch and Helsby. Referee, Mr. B. Howell. A smart run by Marsden was checked by Livesey, who worked the ball nicely into the United's quarters, and a melee in front of the 'United's goal nearly re- sulted in their downfall, Mosley clearing at the critical moment. Even play followed, and from a breakaway the Mission defenders were penal- ised. Sherratt, taking the kick, missed scoring. Both teams now showed good combination, the' Mission having slightly the better of the game. Dunbavin opened the score for them, and shortly after T. Hands scored a second goal. The United made strenuous efforts to reduce the arrears, but half-time arrived with the Mission , leading by two goals to nil. The second half opened very smartly, and the United became more dangerous. A fine centre by Holloway came to nothing. The Mission defence were now having a very busy time and Roberts distinguished himself on several occa- sions by smart goalkeeping, but spoilt his pre- vious good work when lie allowed a bouncing shot from Sherratt to beat him. This reverse had a great effect on the Mission players, and they became very keen and excited. Roberts was penalised for kicking at a player, and H. Finch equalised from the penalty. Both teams now strove hard to gain the lead, and good defensive play was witnessed on each side. Neither managed to score again and the game ended in a draw of two goals each.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
NV arrington Workingmen's Ass ocia-
N.A. CENTRE.

At present interest is being taken in angling, although there are several close season specials to be won, having been offered to keep our locals interested during these months. Mr. 'Worthington, Shrewsbury Arias, Mickle Trafford, writes the Secretary to say he will give ss. for the, best trout, and 2s. 6d. for the second best. At a meeting of the joint committees it was agreed to hold matches, one in a canal and one in the Dee, providing reasonable terms cannot be had from Northwich to fish the Weaver. The committees were unanimous in agreeing that the terms offered at present were quite beyond their reach. _ _
NOTICES A general meeting will be held at the Bay Horse Hotel on Tuesday. Members would do well to attend, as there is an item on the agenda that is most important to the club. A. S.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
AMATEURS AT ANNUAL MEETING.
A Happy Augury for the Coming
Season.

There was one outstanding feature at the annual meeting of the Warrington and District Amateur Bowling Association in the Pelican Hotel on Tuesday evening, and that was the record number of delegates present. As the Chairman, Mr. G. Ball, said, it augured well for the coming season. The delegates present were R. F. Anderton, H. Whittle and T. Horrabin (Senior Conserva- tives), A. Regan (Bull's Head), J. T. Edgington (Horse Shoe, Croft), R. Hitchmough and T. O'Brien (Liberal Club), J. Roberts, J. Russell Mid J. Dagnall (Walker's Brewery), E. Williams and F. Dean (Whitecross), J. Lawson and W. Bolton (Earlestown Vulcan), J. Sinclair and J. Newton (Rylands' Recs.). R. Harrison, E. War- burton and B. Jennings (Crosfield's), J. Monks and J. Higham (Bing and Queen), W. Bibby and J. Lythgoe (Rope and Anchor, Woolston), J. Finch and E. H. Ashton (Penketh Tannery), S. Jenks and J. Weston (Farmer's Arms, Fearn- head), T. Garnett and A. H. Denham (Ceme- foxy), B. Higham and C. Bowers (Junior Con- servatives), J. Hibbert and G. Langley (How- ley Tannery), with Mr. J. T. Wood (secretary) and Mr. G. F. Freeman (treasurer). Mr. Freeman submitted the statement of accounts, which showed there was a balance\ in hand of Bs. 3d. Mr 4 J. Newton (auditor) said the accounts were well kept, and the decreased balance was due to a smaller number of teams, a decrease in subscriptions, and extra cost of printing and stationery.
The statement_ of accounts was passed.

On the proposition of the Secretary, the fol- lowing new clubs were accepted: Earlestown Viaduct Institution, Vulcan Locomotive Works Institute, Rope and Anchor (Woolston), and Hutchinson's Tannery. Walker's Brewery Club and Croft Bowling Club had already been accepted.

div.head: COMPETITIONS.
div.p: THE COMPETITIONS.
Mr. Wood proposed the following resolution: "That it would be advisable to run the Cham- pionship and Consolation Competitions on the system of eight players to comprise a team of home and away."

The cora‘petitions, he said, dragged on too long now, and with the 12 a-side system the green was monopolised for the whole afternoon, and that probably caused much friction amongst the members. If the new system were adopted, games starting at 3 o'clock would finish about 5 o'clock, which would give the other members a chance for a game. The system would benefit the Association 'and .the clubs connected with it. There would be eight men on the home team and eight on the away team. Mr. T. Garnett said it would encourage the smaller clubs. The Cemetery Hotel were in favour of it.

Mr. Harrison said they at Crosfield's were in favour of it. Several delegates expressed themselves in favour Of the reduction, but on the proposition of the Howley Tannery representative it was decided that the teams consist of seven a-side-- seven at home and seven away.

div.head: REVISED ENTRANCE FEE.
div.p: REVISED ENTRANCE FEE.

Mr. Harrison (Crosfield's) proposed the reso- lution: "To revise the entrance fee to the Asso- ciation, so that the Championship and Consola- tion winners may have better value and further- more if the above motion is carried, the Associa- tion will have to find more prize money on account of more players participating in the Competitions." He proposed 14s. instead of 125., but after dis- cussion it was decided that the subscription be 15s. per team.. The following gentlemen were appointed a sub-committee to go into the rules, fix the dates, decide in regard to neutral jacks, and consider the advisability of an Emergency Committee: Messrs. Bowers, Regan, Lawson, Finch, Harri- son, Monks, Sinclair, Whittle and Jenks. The sub-committee will meet in Walker's Club at 7.30 p.m. on Tuesday next.

MR. A. H. CROSFIELD AS PRESIDENT. Mr. A. H. Crosfield was unanimously re- elected President of the Association; Mr. G. Ball, chairman; Mr. F. Dean, vice-chairman; Mr. G. F. Freeman, treasurer; Mr. J. T. Wood, secretary; Mr. J. Newton and Mr. A. E. Bur- dett, auditors. On the proposition of Mr. Russell, it was de- cided to give the auditors an honorarium of ss. each. It was also decided to become affiliated to the British Crown Green Association, and that the decision of the last council meeting that the Meetings should be held in different club rooms in rotation be confirmed. Votes of thanks to the officials concluded the meeting.

WARRINGTON "A" v. ST. HELENS RECS. A first-class match should be seen at Wilders- pool to-day between the "A" team, who were beaten at Rochdale on'Saturday by eight point, to five, and St. Helens Recs. The Warrington side will include J. Brown, who makes his first appearance since his severe injuries sustained in the Salford match at the end of last year. The Warrington team will he:— J: Brown; Baker, Steele, Nicholls, Taberner; A. Brown,,Dainteth; Critchley, Harmer, Shep- herd, Green, Bevan, and Broadhurst.

div.p: GOOD FRIDAY'S MATCH..

. ...—... _ A strong attraction will be provided at Wil- derspool on Good Friday. Dewsbury, who defeated Warrington- at Crown Flatts, a few weeks ago, are the visitors, and as the home men are anxious to avenge that defeat, the match ought to be particularly interesting. Warrington probably will play a team similai to that which is doing duty at Barrow to-day, although the side will not be definitely fixed until next week.

div.head: RYLANDS' LEAGUE CHAMPIONS.
div.p: RYLANDS' LEAGUE CHAMPIONS.
Championship Now Is Safe.

Rylands' have now made their claim, to be Manchester and District League champions safe. This was the result of their victory over Flixton at Gorsey-lane on Saturday. A. Hill commenced operations for Flixton. Good work by Hill and Wallwork took play to the railway end, Horrocks, saving. Even play followed, until from passing and re-passing be- tween Warren, Morris and Griffiths ended in the latter scoring a good try, Warren adding: the extra points. Half-time arrived with the. score : Rylands', 1 goal 1 try (5 points); Flixton, nil. Morris commenced the second half fox Rylands', who made things warm for Flixton. llorrocks was well tackled on the line, but in another breakaway he forced his way through and scored. Warren again adding the extra points. Good passing between Griffiths and Warren ended in the latter player scoring under the posts, the same player goaling. Flixton, although playing up pluckily, were well beaten. Dobson, for Flixton, kicked a splendid goal from half-way. Slater scored for Rylands., the goal- kick failing. A pleasant game ended in Rylands' winning by 3 goals 4 tries, (18 points) to Flixton 1 goal (2 points). Warren, Dorrocks and Griffiths played well for the home team.

Teams for To-day. Rylands' Recs. meet Salford 'A," at Gorsey- lane, in a friendly, with: P. Horrocks; J: Grif- fiths, T. Laws, A. Horrocks (captain), P. Morris; G. Warren, J. Gallop; J. Brandwood, J. Whit- tak4r, H. Morris, D. Slater, J. Broadhurst, H. Welsby.

In the St. Helens and District League, Rylands' Recq. "A" meet St. Helens Rovers, at, St. Helens, with : Potter (captain); Nunnerley, Hardman, Warren, Richardson; Cummings, Adcroft; Peers, Dumbell, Cooper, Hackett, Thorniley, Cooper.

It might have been worse. It might have been better. A drawn game was not so bad. Still, on the play, Warrington were Deserving of a good victory. After all, it was a great match, Only a "wee bit" disappointing. Wilderspool folk could have done with Two points instead of the one received. However, if we do as well at Barrow To-day little cause for a general Grumble will be left behind.

Who was the Warringtonian, late cai Saturday, I Went to a policeman on duty And said: "Say, your boss played "A pretty good game for a novice"? The cOnstable was quite justified In feeling that he was a bit mystified. The worthy questioner was a bit mixed. You see the two names are alike. He meant the new threequarter back, And jumbled up his ideas of persons. Still Nicholls, late of Pemberton, Did play a pretty good game for Warrington..

Waywell always got away well, And Brookes did not brook the Attacks of Corsi or Jones, did he? This was a strong threequarter Way-well's try was a stinging one. The way he dived over the line with The ball after Stan Young had worked A tricky and smart opening was great work. Jolley- has kicked good angle goals, But this one was too much for the expert. It was, however, a pity he did not score, As it would have been a brilliant finish to a brilliant try.

e e ff) Two tries were disallowed to Warrington. •Was this due to a referee-ing mistake? It looked to most as if it was. Waywell was not in touch 'when He ran over—he was inches off the line. Then Nicholls did not throw forward The pass which enabled Taberner to cross the line. Had these two tries been allowed The result would not have been a draw The pass which sent West away with The Rochdale try looked quite more Of a forward one than that of Nicholls.

div.head: BANK QUAY CLUB.
div.p: BANK QUAY CLUB.

The annual meeting of the above club was held on Tuesday evening at the headyiarters, the Bowling Green House, Liverpool-road, when a fairly good number of members were present. Mr. Frederick T. Bennie was unanimously re- elected the President of the club and the whole of last season's vice-presidents were re-elected. The Treasurer (Mr. William Campbell) and the Secretary (Mr. William E. Clare) were also re, elected.

The Secretary gave his report on the past season's work, and also submitted the balance sheet, which showed a sum to be carried for- ward to next season of ..t2 3s. 10d., which, he stated, was most satisfactory, and was sufficient proof that the club was making much headway. It was announced that the green would be formally opened, to members of the club only, 'on Tuesday evening, the 14th of April, at 6 pan. The green has been very- carefully I attended to during the winter and is now in Very fine condition. As it is proposed to again I have an opening main, intending members will do well to make early application for member- ship if they are desirous of being eligible to enter such .main. ether bowling engagements are also being arranged, and a very enjoyable season is anticipated.
