div.head: Mistakes Disney:Ted In the Old and flew Testaments.
div.p: Mistakes Disney:Ted In the Old and flew Testaments.
STRIKING ADULT SCHOOL LECTURE,

At the Sankey Bridges Men's School on Sun- day morning Mr. Charles Wilcockson gave the first part of a lecture on "Errors in the Bible: Real and Apparent" The speaker at the outset said he was opposed to those people who, from the best of motives, either denied the existence of errors or advised young people , not to probe too deeply into Biblical problems. , There were unquestionably errors in our Bible, and it was useless to deny it. The speaker then Pointed out a number in detail, especially in the Book of Genesis. In examining how these mis- takes came to be made, the lecturer paid a tribute of praise to the research work carried out by the Higher Critics, especially those who had worked at the Old Testament. He deplored the fact that it was difficult to compare the Old Testament literature with that of other countries, but where this was possible the agree- ment was striking.

Dealing with the New Testament, Mr. Wil- cockson expressed the view that in several cases the early documents had been tampered with by early copyists. In conclusion, the lecturer said that Biblical study should be encouraged. The moral and religious value of the Bible will al- ways stand, and the more closely it is studied the more it will be appreciated.

div.head: BEWSEY MEN'S.
div.p: BEWSEY MEN'S.

An interesting story of travel. was related by Mr. J. H. J. Hampson on Sunday morning, en- titled "Early recollections .of a voyage on a Troop-ship." The speaker prefaced his remarks by a description of the West Indies and their inhabitants. The West Indies were blessed with almost eternal sunshine, and, in consequence, flowers and plants flourished in a most profuse manner. Apart from the natives, who origin- ally came from Africa, the islands contained many nationalities, due to the government being in the hands of the British, French and Ger- mans. The journey in the troop-ship was first to Malta, where the party of returning British soldiers landed on their way to the Mother Country. Mr. Hampson gave' a picturesque description of Malta, and the Maltese. It ap- pears that the soil of Malta had been carried there from other lands by Orders of the Knight Templars, and instead of the island being a barren area, it possessed a soil whereby the natives could grow potatoes and much agricul- tural produce. It possesses several very beauti- ful cathedrals and it official religion is Roman Catholic. Continuing the journey, Portsmouth was at last reached. It was strikingly impres- sive for the members of the school to learn of the homage which the inhabitants of the West Indies paid to the Mother Country, and Mr. liampson spoke of the great joy of reaching the homeland. Coming from the hot climates to the temperate one of England, one of the first things to impress a stranger was the beautiful white skins of the English, and the different condi- tions of English life.

div.head: hearty rote of thanks was given to the lecturer for his interesting story.
div.p: A hearty rote of thanks was given to the lec- turer for his interesting story.

ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S. A scholarly. exposition was given by Mr. Sutton on the subject of "Citizenship" on Sun- day morning. He traced the etymology of the word and compared its literal meaning with the interpretation now put upon it. Its definition, he said was " the share of a unit in a community, formed for mutual protection and help, and this share ought to consist of (1) all the advan- tages which the State can secure for the indivi- dual, protection of life and property, help in difficulty or distress, and a portion in the general prosperity; (2) the obligation to secure for fellow-citizens the same benefits. The obli- gation may subordinate private interest to pub- lic welfare, but vested interests in local or Imperial government should be persistently opposed, and representatives who carry their! conscience in the same pocket as their money should be displaced.

A true citizen must think Imperially as. well as about his immediate surroundings, and must support every agency for increasing the general Prosperity and happiness. He must obey the laws approved by the majority whether accept- able to himself or not. Dissentients, however, were justified in allowipg their protest to go into Court, and to thus have public protest through the Press, but should not further resist the law.

Conscience claqses, the speaker considered, were undesirable as tending to increase the diffi- culty of carrying the law, into efiect rather than mitigation, reference beirg made to Passive Resisters and Home Rule questions.
A lively discussion ensued on the claims ol minorities.

div.head: STRIKE TO CO ON.
div.p: STRIKE TO CO ON.
Negotiations for Peace in Fletcher, Russell's Dispute Broken Off.
LAST NIGHT'S DECISION.
The strike at Messrs. Fletcher, Russell's, now in its fifth week, is to go on. This was the decision of a large mass meeting of the men last night._

_ „ During the week a conference had been held, and there were signs of peace, but an announce- ment by the firm that disputes must first be referred to the foremen and manager, and if they could not decide it the directors would meet a deputation, who could be accompanied by one outside official, has not met with the I men's approval. The firm could not go any further towards a settlement.

Following a telephone c-On;ersation, when, it is understood, the men proposed certain condi- tions, Mr. A. Bennett wrote to the firm stating: "Our Joint Committee have considered your pro- posed agreement, which, we understand, you have already agreed to verbally, that if any complaint is made by a workman from any department he must make it to his foreman, and if he cannot decide it, it must be submitted to I the works' manager, who shall meet a deputa- tion of the men, along with an outside union official. If you can endorse this agreement, kindly reply stating date when you will again meet our deputation, along with Messrs. A. Hutchinson, C. Dukes and 11. Sinclair."

div.head: MEN'S STATEMENT.
div.p: THE MEN'S STATEMENT.
Yesterday the men, before they received a reply, issued this statement :

"We wish to _point out that the proposed agreement by the firm would necessarily delay the clearing up of any grievances, whereas under our amended agreement, should the foreman be unable to put matters right, an interview be- tween the manager and a union official would have the desired effect without the case having to be deferred until a meeting of directors could be convened. It will be seen from this that it is not our desire to take matters past the man- agement and to treat only with the Board of Directors, as we have been accused of request- ing. The above suggestion is the working method of all agreements, and embodies all we asked for at the commencement of the strike."

EMPLOYERS' REPLY. The men later received the following from the Secretary of the Company: "The object of the resolution was that any workman's complaint must first be submitted to his foreman, and if he cannot decide it, then to the manager of the works, and if he could not decide it, as a last resort it would be brought by a deputation of the workmen to the Board of Directors, and because you said that the workmen were incom- petent themselves to amend the complaint (as to which I may say my directors do not agree) they decided that the workmen might be accom- panied by an outside official to speak for them. I feel it useless, therefore, to call a meeting of the Board to decide the question already decided."

div.head: RECOGNITION FIRST.
div.p: RECOGNITION FIRST.

Mr. Bennett last night replied: "My com- mittee instruct me that our desire to amend your resolution is in order to facilitate working arrangements. In doing so we feel confident that any difficulty may be set right more quickly by the works' manager meeting the men con- cerned with a union official rather than await- ing a meeting of the directors. As our suggested amendment has not been considered by the directors we cannot accept the ordinary resolutioh as an answer to our proposed amend- ment, we beg, therefore, for an early considera- tion of its contents. We further wish to point out that we have not termed any section of the workmen incompetent to deal with grievances, but, as experience proves, outside officials may I meet the management on a plane of equality not usually conceded to workmen. The men have decided at a mass meeting today to leave the present grievances in abeyance until the terms of union recognition have been decided." The matter has thus reached a critical point, and negotiations are broken off in the meantime.

div.head: MINERS' RELIEF SOCIETY. Lancashire and Cheshire Association.
div.p: MINERS' RELIEF SOCIETY. Lancashire and Cheshire Association.

The 41st annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Permanent Relief Society was held on Saturday, at the Mining College, Wigan. Sir William Scott Barrett presided over a representative gathering. The Chairman said the past year had not only been the most important in their history, but the report was the best one they had ever issued. The number of members, 62,231, was the highest on record, whilst their investments reached £15,000, and the benefit fund stood at .R 161,000. The rate of accident pay was very high at pre- sent, being 234.4 per member, and that was one point which would have to be carefully watched. Mr. John Denn (the chairman of the Board of Management) mentioned that three or foui agencies had communicated with the Board, pointing out that, as the National Insurance Act provided medical benefit for insured persons, the Permanent Relief Society should dispense' with the surgical benefit 'which had hitherto been provided for its members. He pointed out that there were still 126 of these members upon the funds, and while this was so it was undesir- able to make any alteration in either contribu- tions or benefits during the interval of a valua- tion period. The Board of Management would be glad to consider during the current year the desirability .of increasing the allowance of these members. Mr. Alfred Hewlett was re-elected president, Sir William Scott-Barrett and Mr. James Latham vice-presidents. The Board of Man- agement was elected as follows: Honorary mem- bers, Messrs. C. F. Bouchier (Platt Bridge), T. G. Dobb (West Leigh), L. R. Fletcher (Leigh), G. A. Haworth (Wigan), R. B. Mawson (Wigan) ; ordinary members, Messrs. A. Baker (Leigh), T. Grundy (Leigh), W. Ingram (Hindley), J. Latham (Atherton), P. Lon (Skelmersdale), F. Ryding (Standish).

A Reason. "What you see in that creature to admire I can't see," said Mrs. Dubbleigh. "Why, she's all made up. Her hair, her figure, her com- plexion—every bit of her is artificial." "Well, what of it?" retorted Dubbleigh. "If the world admires a self-made man, why shouldn't it admire a self-made woman?"

A Strong Argument. , A Devonshire lady once sent to her son a pair of trousers by book post, which is, of course, cheaper than parcel post. The postal officials wrote to her : "Clothes cannot be sent by book post. If you will refer to the post-office guide you will see under, what conditions articles May be sent by book post." After a few days the lady replied : "I have looked in the post-office guide, and find that articles which are open at both ends ma 'y be sent by book post. And if trousers are not open int both ends, I should like to knor what is."
WORKERS' MOVEMENT.
Postal Servants' Deputation to Mr.
Harold SMith.
GRIEVANCE OVER HOLT REPORT.

Warrington postal servants, in conjunction with their brethren all over the country, have a grievance over the Holt report, and this they placed before Mr. Harold Smith, M.P. Two deputations waited upon him on Wednesday, one from the postmen and the other from the postal clerks. . , The postmen's deputation gave a brief history l'of the events leading up to the Holt report. The Hobhouse report was in 1908, and that was where they began to go back. They started with wages of 17s. and went to 255., which was a shilling reduction on the maximum and thie minimum. They still were able to get six , stripes, which took 25 years to attain. The Holt Commission was appointed in 1912. The Board of Trade also inquired concurrently into the cost of living of the working classes, and upon the result of that inquiry the postal ser- vants based their main objection to the Holt report. There was an increase in the cost of living equal to 11.3 per cent., so that they should have had an increase to that amount to maintain their 1908 standard. They claimed that the proposed maximum was inadequate.

div.head: REDUCED ONE SHILLING.
div.p: REDUCED ONE SHILLING.

In 1908 the maximum wage at Warrington office was reduced by is., so that in actual fact 49 per cent. of the men got no increase at all. For some reason the Holt Committee recom- mended a shilling increase only on the maximum of towns in classes 1, 2 and 3, while two shillings was granted in every other case. According to the report submitted to the Board of Trade no inquiries were made into the cost of living in 1912 in Warrington. Since 1913 rents in the town alone had increased from 4 per cent. to 15 per cent. for houses containing three, to five rooms. Another complaint at the Warrington office was the split attendance and rotary system of duties. Under the llolt Committee recommendation 51 per cent. of the staff received a shilling rise and the remainder nothing, with the exception that they reached the maximum in 21 years' time instead of 25 years.
245. 2d. PER WEEK.

According to the official statement, the aver- ' age weekly wage of postmen in 1910 was 275. 5d., In Warrington it would be lower, and according , to the evidence submitted by the Postmen's Federation to the Holt Committee, the average pay, including money allowances for stripes, was estimated at 265. 6d. per week in class 3 offices. Apart from these allowances the pay at Warrington averaged about 245. 2d. per week, compared with Corporation employes, such as scavengers, &c., wages, which were averaged at 245. Mr. 11. Smith said that had he been in London that day he should himself have formed one of a committee who were receiving a deputation of the Post Office workers' head officials in regard to the matter discussed. It was a committee of his colleagues in the party to which he belonged, who for some time had realised that there were distinct grievances. The remedy for the chief grievance was wrapped round the question of wages. He did not believe that postmen ob- jected to work, but they did properly demand adequate remuneration. The hours of duty which they had mentioned presented a problem which lie had to confess he could not at the present grapple. The Holt Committee were making a reduction in the wages, and he could not see how that could be defended, for if it was to be defended, it must be shown that the wages before were too high. Mr. Smith was asked to support the claim for Is. an hour maximum increment, annually in- stead of triennially, and for Id. an hour for auxiliary labour.

div.head: POSTAL CLERKS' DEPUTATION.
div.p: POSTAL CLERKS' DEPUTATION.

The deputation from the postal clerks stated that three-quarters of the staff received nothing from the Holt report. The officals on scale got nothing from it in any shape ta• form. They also complained that the young pbstal clQrks were not given the necessary elementary train- ing they should have. Mr. Smith replied in somewhat the same terms as to the previous deputation, promising them his support.

UNFLINCHING LOYALTY TO PREMIER. Messages From Lancashire and Cheshire. Liberal women of Lancashire and Cheshire on Monday expressed their determination to stand by the Government in the struggle for Home Rule, and they sent a message of their unflinch- ing loyalty and support to Mr. Asquith. This encouraging assurance was given at the Spring conference of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Women's Liberal Associations, held at Olive Hall, Waterloo, Liverpool. Lady Haworth appealed to Liberal women to stand more loyal to the Government than ever before. Home Rule must go on—(cheers)—just the same. There could be no drawing back now. Let them, both men and women, say nothing that would cause the Liberal party to falter for one moment in its great work, and she urged that they should send a message of loyalty and of zeal to the Prime Minister.

From Everywhere. Lobsters travel in regiments. Heaven won't be nearly exclusive enough to suit some people. A man who gives himself away is apt to lose his self-possession. "What are you laughing at, dear?" asked a fond mother of a little four-year-old miss who seemed to be greatly amused. "Oh. at something funny that happened," was the reply, "but it's no use to tell you, because it isn't funny enough for both of us to laugh at."

r HOCKEY. • LATCHFORD DEFEATED. Latchford had a visit last week from a Bow- don eleven, captained by F. S. Church, the Che- shire County captain, and which included Bloomfield, Greenhow, Eric Church and Brown. The visitors were clearly superior, and won by 5-0, but there was hardly the disparity be- tween the teams that the score would suggest, as Latchford missed several chances in front of goal, and played better all round against their accomplished opponents than for weeks past. The visitors made a brilliant start, their centre-forward scoring a fine goal from a corner with a lightning shot, and adding another before the interval. Latchford forced several corners, but these were rather badly placed and nothing came of them. In the second half the Bowdon centre-forward scored two splendid goals in quick succession, and F. S. Church scored a fifth with a curious shot. Wilkinson and Pearson had hard lines in not netting for Latchford. Bruhl was quite good in the home goal, making some daring saves, and he had no chance with the shots that scored. W. Fletcher played an excellent game at right back, and was, in fact, one of the best defenders on the field. V. H. letcher played well at left back, and the two brothers defended coolly and skilfully, although opposed to such a warm forward line. Albinson and Allanson were the best of the halves, and Pearson and Colton the most promi- nent forwards. To-day's Match. The first eleven finish the programme to-day, when Sale Ist are the visitors. The Latchford eleven is: J. Bruhl, goal; P. Allanson and C. Billington, backs; J. Albinson, J. B. Wilkinson and A. B. Starkey, halves; R. A. Dale, J. E. Pearson, W. H. Minards, H. R. Colton, and A.
